summary: The respondent assessee was assessed to wealth tax for the assessment years 1965 66, 1966 67 and 1967 68 in the status of a 'Hindu Undivided Family '. In each of the assessment, the Wealth Tax Officer included a sum of Rs. 1,50,000 estimated as the accrued interest on the assessee 's money lending investments. The assessee appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and urged that as it maintained its books of account in accordance with the cash system of accounting the accrued interest could not be included in the wealth tax assessments. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissed the appeals. The Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeals, but the High Court, on a reference, held in favour of the assessee. In the appeals to this Court, on the question whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case, the Wealth tax Officer was in law justified in including in the net wealth of the assessee interest due on accrual basis (though not realised) on the outstandings of the money lending business, the accounts of the assessee being maintained on cash basis. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: (1) Under section 3 of the Wealth Tax Act, wealth tax is charged for every assessment year in respect of the net wealth on the corresponding valuation date. The expression "net wealth" is defined by cl. (m) of section 2 of the Wealth tax Act as "the amount by which the aggregate value of all the assets, wherever located, belonging to the assessee on the valuation date, is in excess of the aggregate value Of all the debts owed by the assessee on that valuation date. " According to the scheme of the Wealth Act, the net wealth is to be determined as it obtained on a particular date. That is the valuation date. [310 C D] (2) Under section 7 of the Wealthtax Act, wealth Tax is charged for each assessment year in accordance with section 3 of that Act. The expression 'net wealth ' is defined by clause (m) to mean "the amount for which the assessee is assessable". The expression "valuation date" is defined in section 2(q) to mean the last day of the previous year as defined in section 3 of Income Tax Act, if an assessment were to be made under that Act for that year. [310 E F] (3) The definition of the expression "valuation" in the substantive part of cl. (q) of section2 indicates that broadly Parliament has fixed upon the last day. of the "previous year" as the valuation date and the figure of net wealth of an assessee at the end of the "Previous year" takes into account the financial activities of the assessee during that "previous" year. [309 B C] (4) The assets to be considered are not circumscribed by any consideration of the particular system of accounting adopted by the assessee. The assets are not confined to cash. Where the asset is an asset other than cash, its value is determined pursuant to sub section (I) of section 7 as the estimated price, which, in the opinion of the Wealth. Tax Officer, the asset would fetch if sold in the open market on the valuation dates. [310 G H] (5) It is apparent that what accrues as a right also falls to be included within the assets of an assessee under the Wealth Tax. That being so, the conclusion is inescapable that even though the accounts of assessee are maintained on cash Basis interest due on the accrual basis, though not realised, on the out standings of the assessee are liable to be included in his net wealth. [310 H] (6) The view taken by the Orissa High Court in Commissioner of Wealth Tax vs Vysyaraju Badreenarayana Moorthy Raju, [1976] 103 I.T.R. 7, approved.

The respondent was a permanent employee of the appellant. He was charge sheeted for misconduct. The Inquiry Officer found him guilty of the charge. The respondent moved the Central Administrative Tribunal. The Tribunal, however, set aside the order of dismissal on the ground that the respondent was not the master mind behind the scheme to defa ul the project. The Tribunal held that the respondent had not been able to prove that he was the master mind of the project. It also held that the punishment of dismissal was excessive. The High Court, however, held that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to interfere with the penalty imposed by the competent authority on the ground of the respondent being the master mind. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The jurisdiction of the Tribunal to interfere with t he disciplinary matters or punishment cannot be equated with an appellate jurisdiction. The Tribunal cannot interfere with the findings of the Inquiry Officer or competent authority where they are not arbitrary or utterly perverse. It is appropriate to rememb er that the power to impose penalty on a delinquent officer is conferred on the competent authority either by an Act of legislature or rules made under the provi so to Article 309 of the Constitution. If the penalty can lawfully be imposed and is imposed on the proved misconduct, the Tribunal has no pow er to substitute its own discretion for that of the authority. The adequacy of penalty unless it is malafide is a matter for the Tribunal to concern with. The Tribunal also cannot interfere with the penalty if the conclusion of the Inquiry officer or the competent authority is based on evidence even if some of it is found to be irrelevant or extraneous to the matter. Ordinarily, the Tribunal cannot interfere or the Tribunal has juri sdiction to impose any punishment to meet the ends of serv ice. [33D E] 2. The Tribunal has not interfered with the penalty if the con cerned authority is of the opinion that the penalty is not commensurate with the delinquency of the official. The Tribunal is not concerned to decide whether the penalty imposed is commensurate with the indus trial or not. The Tribunal can interfere with the punishment if the conclusion is not based on any evidence. [33F] 3. The Tribunal in the instant case, has not interfered in the penalty if it is found that the penalty was too seve r or excessive and not warranted by the facts and circumstances of the case. [33G] 4. The Tribunal had not found that the respondent is the master mind or that the penalty imposed was excessive. It has not found that t he respondent was the master of the project and that the penalty of dismissal was not justified. [34A] 5. The Tribunal was not justified in directing the Governor of Orissa to reconsider the question. The High Cour t was, therefore, in error in directing the Govern ment to reconsider the matter. [34B] 6. The High Courts are not expected to substitute their own judgment for that of adminis trative authorities when the decision is based on objec tions. [34C] 7. The Tribunal could not substitute its own judgment to modi ficate the punishment awarded. [34D] 7. In the instant case the Tribunal has not found any fault with the findings recorded by the Inquiry Officer. The Tribunal did not find any fault with t he findings recorded by him. The Tribunal should have, therefore, directed the Governor of the State to reconsider the penalty imposed on the respondent. [34E] 8. The Tribunal set aside the penalty on the ground t hat the respondent was the head of the project, that the respondent did not have the authority to sanction the project and the respondent was a mere employee of the project authority. The Tribunal further held that the penalty should be set aside on the ground th at the respondent was an employee of the State Government. [34F] 9. The Tribunal directed the Governor to reconsider the quantum of punishment. The High Co urt was, therefore. not justified in setting aside the order. [35A] 10. The Tribunal ought to have directed the Governor t o reconsider the question whether the respondent was guilty of the charges. The High court was, therefore not justified in interfering with the order of the Tribunal. [35B] Union of India vs Sardar Bahadur, ; , at 552; O.P. Gupta vs Union of India, ; at 225; Union of India v Sardar Bahadur, A ny doubts as to the incapacity of the Court to review the merits of the penalty must vanish when we read the re cord of Mathew, J., in Sardar Bahadur 's case (at 225): "A disciplinary proceeding is not a criminal trial. The standard of proof required is that of preponderance of probability and not proof beyond reasonable doubt. Where there are some relevant materials which the authority has accepted and which materials may reasona ble, the conclusion is arrived at, the Tribunal wou ld not be interfere with. [35C D] State of Orissa vs Bidyabhushan Mohapatra, ; at 552; Railway Board vs Niranjan Singh, ; at 553; O. P. Gupta vs U.P. State Electricity Board, ; at 556; O. N. Mohindroo vs The Hon 'ble Lt. Governor, Delhi, and Union of India & Ors. vs Sardar Bahadur. A ny doubts, as to the incompetence of the Court of Inquiry to hold the inquiry, were removed by the decision of this Court in State of Orissa & Ors.v. Bidyabhumi n Singh, ; ; O. P Gupta vs Union Of India, ; ; at 556 and O. N Mohindro vs The Honb le Lt. Governor Delhi, and Ors. , ; at 556.

The appellant was the tenant of the suit property. The respondent landlord filed a suit for eviction of the appellant tenant on the ground that he was a deemed tenant of the said property and since he had not been dispossessed in accordance with law, the respondent landlord had become entitled to recover possession of the suit premises. The Trial Court dismissed the suit holding that the suit was not maintainable and that the respondent landlord was entitled to recover the possession of the premises. The First Appellate Court confirmed the decree. The High Court, however, in second appeal, held that the suit for possession was barred by res judicata as well as Order 2 Rule 2(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure. The High court held that the respondent was entitled to restoration of possession on the ground of his being a deemed tenant. The appellant tenant appealed to this Court. Allowing the appeal, the Court, ^ HELD: 1. The Civil Court undoubtedly had jurisdiction under section 9 of the Code to try and grant eviction till the Fifth Amendment became effective. By virtue of section 7 any question whether a person is a tenant or a deemed tenant was required to be decided by the Mamlatdar and the jurisdiction of the Civil Court stood ousted by section 58(2) of the Act. The question is whether this subsequent change in the law deprived the Civil Court of jurisdiction which it undoubtedly possessed on the date of the institution of the suit. [1028C D] 2. The Civil court undoubtedly had jurisdiction to try and decide the suit. The High Courts, however, have no power to decide any question which is required to be settled, decided or dealt with by the authorities under the Act. [1029B C] 3. The jurisdiction of the civil court is specifically barred by sub section (2) of section 58 from settling, deciding or dealing with any question which under the Act is required to he settled, decided, dealt with or determined by the Mamlatdar. [1030B] 4. The Civil Courts undoubtedly have jurisdiction to decide any of the questions which are required to be determined by the authorities mentioned in the Act. But the jurisdiction of Civil Courts is expressly barred by section 58 (2) and the Civil Court cannot decide any question not required to be dealt with by any of the authorities mentioned therein. [1031B] 5. The jurisdiction is, therefore, vested in the Mamlatdar under section 7 read with section 58(1) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948 and section 58(3) specifically bars the jurisdiction of all other courts to settle, decide or deal with any question or determine any question which has been or is required to the determined by the authority mentioned in the section. [1032B] 6. The Civil Judge, therefore, was right in holding that the respondent plaintiff was entitled to the restoration of possession of the land on the ground he was a tenant of the land. [1033B] 7. The High, Court was wrong in holding that even after the Fifth Amendment came into force the plaintiff had not applied to the Mamlatdar for possession of the property within the period allowed by section 18 of the Act and had, therefore, allowed the first defendant to become a deemed purchaser of the suit land on the strength of his tenancy. [1034C] 8. The High 'Court was wrong in concluding that the suit filed by the respondent plaintiff for restoration of possession was barred under Order 2 Rule2(3) C.P.C. [1035B] 9. The jurisdiction to try a suit for possession is specifically barred under section 58(4) of the Tenancy Act. [934C] 10. The Civil suit was for an injunction and not for possession of land. Once it was found that the plaintiff was not in actual physical possession of the demised property, the suit had become infructuous. The cause of action for the former suit was not based on the allegation that the possession of plaintiff was forcibly taken sometime in the second week of June, 1968. Therefore, the cause of action was based on an apprehension that the defendants were likely to forcibly dispossess the plaintiff. Therefore, in the facts and circumstances of the case, the subsequent suit was based on a distinct cause of action not found in the former suit and hence regardless of the relief claimed the second suit was clearly barred by res judi cata. [935C D] 11. The High. Court was wrong on its view that the suit could not be decided by a Civil Court under the Act and that the Civil Court had no jurisdiction to decide the suit on the ground the plaintiff was a deemed purchaser. [936A] 12. The jurisdiction vested in the Civil Court stands ousted by section 7 of the Act which specifically bars the Civil Court from settling, adjudicating on or dealing with the question whether any person is a deemed tenant or a tenant on the grounds mentioned in section 7(1) and (2). [936B] 13. The Civil Suit was for an injunc tion and not for recovery of possession of land and the Civil Judge had no jurisdiction in the matter. [937C] 14. The High courts have no power under section 115 C.P C. to decide any questions which are not required to he determined by the Authorities under the Act, and the Civil Courts have no jurisdiction to entertain or decide any question relating to the determination of the questions referred to in section 115 C C. [938A] 15. The Civil judge was right in dismissing the suit.

The petitioners are carpenters employed at the Wood Working Centre of the Himachal Pradesh State Handicrafts Corporation (the Corporation). They are being paid the same wages as are payable to carpenterers, painters and carpent ers engaged in the construction industry. They are given bonus under the Bonus Act and provident fund benefits under the Employees ' Provident Fund Act. The Corporation has resisted the petitioners ' claim. The case of the Corporation is that the unit where the petitioners are working is a factory registered under the Factories Act. The petitioners are treated as industrial workmen and are given all benefits due to them under the various labour legislations. The Corporation is a company which has been incorporated under the . The main object of the Corporation as seen from the Memorandum of Association is to preserve the traditional arts and crafts and also to popularise handicrafts and handloom items in the State of Himachal Pradesh and other parts of the country and abroad. In order to achieve this primary objec tion, the Corporation gives training to artisans, weavers and craftsmen in various traditional arts. During the period of training, the trainees are paid a stipend by the Corporation. upto 31st March, 1987, the Corporation has imparted training to as many as 1662 persons in different areas like carpet weaving, handloom weaving, painting, metal crafts, wood carving, etc. Apart from giving training, the Corporation also ensures marketing support to the artisans and craftsman by purchasing their products at remunerative prices and sell them through the marketing network of the Corporation. It is said that the village artisans and the craftsmen make different items on a piece rate basis and in some cases, they execute the work in their own homes. The financial aspect of the Corporation was stated to be not encouraging, and indeed it is disappointing. Nonetheless, for the purpose of preserv ing and promoting traditional arts, the Corporation had been kept alive. But to avoid or minimise further loss, it is stated that the Corporation has reduced its overheads and maintained only the administrative staff in the production centers at different parts of the State and no permanent craftsmen are employed. The principle of "equal pay for equal work" is not one of the fundamental rights expressly guaranteed by our Constitution. The princi ple was incorporated only under Article 39(d) of the Constitution as a Directive Principle of State Policy. It is, therefore, not permissible to provide two different pay scales in the same cadre on the basis of selection based on merit with due regard to experience and seniority. Apart from that, the Court has expressly observed that the higher pay scale to avoid stagnation or resultant frustration for lack of promotional avenues may also be allowed. Meva Ram Kanojia is the most recent decision which has exhaustively dealt with all the principles bearing on the question of equal pay for equal working. The Court held that the principle of " equal pay forequal work" has no mechanical application in every case of similar work. Article 14 permits reasonable classification rounded on rational basis. It is also held that the higher scale to avoid or elimination of stagnation or a resultant frustration of the employees for lack of adequate promotional avenues is a valid classification. The Court also held that it is open to the State to classify employees on the basis o f qualifications, duties and responsibilities of the posts concerned. If the classification has reasonable nexus with the objective sought to be achieved, efficiency in the administration, the State would be justified in prescribing different pay scales. The Court, therefore, held that the Court cannot direct the Corporation to apply the rates prescribed under exhibit P. 2 unless the Government makes it applicable to employees of the Corporation, and that the Court has no jurisdiction to direct the Corporation not to apply the rate prescribed under exhibit. P. 2. The Court further held that the petitioners are car penters and better called as craftsmen. By the general description of their job, one cannot come to the conclusion that every carpenter or craftsmen is equal to the other in the performance of his work. The two jobs by the mere nomen clature or by the volume of work performed cannot be rated as equal. It is not just a comparison of physical activity. It requires the consideration of various dimensions of the job. The accuracy required by the job and the dexterity it entails may differ from job to job. It cannot be evaluated by the mere averments in the self serving affidavits or counter affidavits of the parties. It must be left to be evaluated and determined by expert body. The principal claim of the petitioners, therefore, fails and is rejected. The next contention that the petitioners should be paid at least the minimum wages prescribed by the Deputy Commissioner under exhibit P 2 dated March 20, 1986 cannot also be accepted. Exhibit P. 2 was issued by the Deputy Commis sioner in the exercise of his powers under the H.P. Financial Rules. It is applicable only to skilled and unskilled workers in class IV employees in Government service. It has not been extended to employees of Corporation. The petition ers have been treated as construction workers and they are being paid wages as are paid to carpenter and carpenter. The Court rejected the claim of the peti tioners. The Court left the petitioners to work out their rights elsewhere in accordance with law applicable to them. In the result, the petition fails and is dismissed.

The appellant, who was the widow of the testatrix, executed a will in respect of certain properties in favour of her husband. The testatrix died in 1947. The appellant, who had a son by her, filed a suit for a declaration that the will was not valid and that she was entitled to make a will in favour of the testators. The appellant contended that the will set up by the appellant was not genuine and that at the material time Lakshmamma was not in a sound and disposing state of mind and that she had transferred all her interests in the properties comprised in the will in favour 'of her husband. It was also contended that the testator had transferred all his interests in the property to the appellant and that the will had not been proved to be the last will and testament of the test ant. The trial court found that the will executed by the testatord was genuine and valid and that the rule of survivorship was applicable as between the legatees inter se in respect of the properties conveyed by the will. The High Court, on appeal, held that the will in question was genuine and that the appellant had failed to prove the due and valid execution of the will. Held, that the High Court was justified in reversing the finding of the trial court on the question of due and validexecution of the will and that the evidence led by the appellant to prove the execution of the testate was not satisfactory. The evidence of the testator was consistent with the appellant 's case that the testate had full knowledge of the will executed in favour of his wife and that he had signed the will after fully understanding its contents. The testator was not a witness of the will but was a witness of a fact and his evidence was not of any importance. The testators evidence was not sufficient to establish the due and proper execution of the document. The evidence led by him was not sufficient for the purpose of establishing the due and correct execution of the Will. The evidence adduced by the appellant on the question about the validity of the will was, therefore, not satisfactory. Sarat Kumari Bibi vs Sakhi Chand, (1931) L.R. 59 I.A. 180, referred to. The evidence on the question as to whether the will was executed by the testator was not satisfactory and sufficient to establish that the test ant had full knowledge about the will executed. The evidence was not such as to lead to the conclusion that the will could not be executed by the appellant. The evidence showed that the testator had full knowledge that the will of the testar was a will and that he signed it after fully understanding the contents of the will, and that the testators evidence that the will read out to the testater was a will prepared from the instructions of the testater was true. The evidence that the testater had full knowledge and that he was signing the will after understanding the contents was not sufficient. The evidence established that the testor had full knowledge regarding the will executed and that he did sign it after fully and properly understanding the contents. The evidence also established that the will contained elaborate arguments in support of the disposition of the will in the form of a draft at Mysore. The evidence in the case showed that the will did not contain any such elaborate arguments. The evidence did not show that the will, which was a will, was executed by a person who was not competent to execute it. The evidence, therefore, was not sufficient and the High Court had rightly reversed the finding of fact on the question whether the will in dispute was the last will of the testator. The evidence about the execution of a will was not sufficient because it was not possible to prove the will in a case where the execution of it was surrounded by suspicious circumstances. The testor had sufficient knowledge of the contents of a will and he signed it in the presence of the testor after fully understanding it. The testater was not a person of the kind of witness of the execution of will. The evidence as to the execution of an earlier will was not of such a character as to lead the Court to the conclusion, that the earlier will was a forged one. The evidence relating to the execution and attestation of the will by the testator and the evidence relating to its execution and attestation were not sufficient to prove the validity of a will. The testate was a person who had full knowledge as to the contents of his will and he was signing it after fully, understanding the contents and he signed the will in his presence after fully understanding and after fully understanding himself. The evidence regarding the execution of another will was not such a character. The evidence with regard to the execution, attestation and execution of the other will was not satisfactory because it was inconclusive on the question that the other will had been executed by the same testator. The testentor had sufficient mental capacity to execute the will and he had full knowledge whether the will had been signed by the testor or not. The evidence given by the testators was not sufficient as it was not sufficient that the will should be signed by the testator. Sarat Kumar Bibi vs Sarat Kumari Debi, (1933) L. R. 59 I A. 180, relied on. The evidence which was not sufficient was not sufficient, because it was necessary to prove the sound and disposing of state of mind of the testator and his signature as required by law. The evidence could not be treated as sufficient to establish a due and valid will. The appellant had failed in proving the due and validity of the testa tion. The High court was justified in setting aside the finding of ' the trial court. The appeal must be dismissed. The question whether the appellant had proved the due and ' valid execution of a valid will was not open to the appellant in view of the fact that the High court had reversed the finding on the question. The evidence had not been properly considered by the High Court. The High 'Court had not fully and properly considered all the relevant evidence and had not fully considered the evidence on the point. The High, Court had not fully or properly considered the evidence of the appellant on this point. The appeal was therefore dismissed. The appellant did not press the appeal on the question relating to the validity of execution of the. will. The appeal therefore must be dismissed and the case remanded to the High Court for disposal according to law. The appeal is accordingly dismissed. The appeal to the Supreme Court was not pressed on the question regarding the validity of. the will. It was not necessary to consider the evidence relating, to the execution or attestation of the other. The appeal had therefore to be dismissed. Sarat Kuar Bibi vs Smt. Sakhi Chand (1931 L. R 59 I. A. 180), referred to. Held, further, that the evidence about the due and. proper execution of a document was not sufficient in the present case. The evidence to prove the proper execution of an another will was of such a nature that it was not necessary for the appellant to examine the other witnesses. The evidence for proving the due execution of the second will was not, therefore, sufficient. The appellant was not entitled to a decree for possession of the properties covered by the will and the appeal must be allowed.

The appellant company manufactured and sold "Cinema Arc Carbons" known as "Cinema Carbons" manufactured by it. The Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal, the final departmental authority under the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957, allowed an application for adducing expert evidence to determine the question whether "Cinema carbons" manufactured and sold by the appellant company were "electrical goods" falling within entry No. 4 of the 1st Schedule of the Act. The High Court, in a reference under section 25 of the Act, held that the said goods fell under the entry "Cinematographic equipment including cameras, projectors, and sound recording and reproducing equipment lenses films and parts and accessories required for use therewith". In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the High Court had failed to consider the use of the words "electrode" to describe them, suggesting a connection with electricity, and that the High court had wrongly relied upon the decision of the Andhra Pradesh High Court in the State of Andhra Pradesh vs Srimathi Nidmarthi Saraswathi Devi. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that the goods under consideration were covered by the relevant entry No.4 of the 1 st Schedule of the Andhra Act. [563 B] (2) The words "parts thereof" are used in several entries, such as entry No. 6 for clocks, time pieces and watches, entry No. 10 for dictaphones and other similar apparatus for recording sound, and entry No. 11 for sound transmitting equipment such as telephones and loud speakers. The words "accessories" are used to describe goods which may have been manufactured for use as an aid or addition. [564 B C] (3) The entry in the schedule to describe goods to be taxed indicates that the expression "required for use there with" has been employed for equipment or accessories connected with the main purpose. For instance, in entry No. 5, the expression occurs at the end as follows: "Photographic and other cameras and enlargers, films and plates, paper and cloth and other parts and accessories, required for use therein". Apparently, the deciding factor is the predominant or ordinary purpose or use. It is not enough to show that the article can be put to other uses also. It is its general or predominant user which seems to determine the category in which an article will fall. [569 D F] (4) The word "accessory" is used in the schedule in the sense of being an accessory or an addition to something else. [561 G] (5) The term "accessor" is used to describe the goods which may be manufactured for use in a particular kind of instrument of gadget only. [562 A] (6) The High court correctly held that the goods in question were covered by entry No. 3 of the 1St Schedule of the A.P. General Sales Tax, Act, 1957. [566 B] (7) The High Courts of Andhra Pradesh and Madras correctly held that "Cinema cars" are not "agricultural machinery" within the meaning of entry No. 9 in Schedule of the Madras General Sales Tax. [567 B] (8) The High courts of Madras, Madhya Pradesh and Orissa have correctly held that 'Cinema carakes" are not covered by the entry "electrode". [569 C] (9) The High 'Court correctly held that, the main use of the arc carbons under consideration was duly proved to be that of production of powerful light used in projectors in cinemas. [568 C]

The Gujarat Minor Minerals Rules, 1966 were framed under the provisions of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957. Rule 21 of the Rules provides for the determination of the rate of royalty payable in respect of minor minerals. Rule 21 provides for the fixation of the rate at which royalty is to be paid in respect of any mineral. Rule 21(1) provides that the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, fix the rate of dead rent in respect of all or any of the matters enumerated in clauses (a) to (d) of Rule 21(2) and the rate of such royalty shall be subject to the condition that the rate so fixed shall not be in excess of the rate specified in Rule 21(3). Rule 21(4) provides that in fixing the rate of surface rent, the royalty shall be deemed to be the amount payable for the area of the land covered by the mineral at the pit's mouth. Rule 21 (5) provides that where the holder of a mining lease or any other mineral concession granted under the Act or any rule or order made thereunder is a company, the company shall be liable to pay royalty in respect of the mineral raised or received by it. Rule 21A provides for the revision of the rate and payment of royalty in respect thereof. Rule 21B provides for the enhancement of the rate in respect of minerals other than minor minerals. The petitioners in the writ petitions who were lessees of mining leases in respect of black trap and Hard Murrum, challenged the constitutional validity of Rule 21 as it existed prior to the issue of the impugned notification dated June 18, 1981. The petitioners contended that the said rule was in contravention of Article 301 of the Constitution inasmuch as it was not in the nature of a fee which could be levied by the State Government and that the said levy was unreasonable and was imposed in an arbitrary manner. The petitioners also contended that the levy was unreasonably heavy and had been imposed in an arbitrarily manner. The respondents contended that the royalty levied and covered under the Rules should be applied only for mineral development and since the said royalty was being treated as part of the consolidated fund of the State and used for other purposes by the State, the levy was valid. The respondents also contended that since the royalty was being levied at the rate of Re. 1 per metric tonne of Black Trap and Hard Murmrum, the levy of royalty was justified. The respondents further contended that the concession shown in favour of Parwana was discriminatory and violative of Article 14. The respondents submitted that the concession was being shown in favour only of village potters who were lessees under the Rules and that the concession in favour of village potter was discriminatory and was violative of Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. The respondents relied on the decision of this Court in B.K. Trivedi & Sons and Ors. vs State of Gujarat and Ors. , ; and B.K Trivedi & Sons & Ors. vs Stale of Gujarat and Anr., ; and contended that the impugned notification was in contravention to clause (b) of Article 304 of the Constitution and that the levy in question was justified. Allowing the writ petitions, the Court, HELD: 1. The royalty levied and the dead rent recovered by the State Governments from the lessees of mining lease in respect of Black trap and Hard mud and Murram and gravel and in respect of Hard Murrum are invalid. [413G] 2.1 The levy is made under a law made by the Central Government. It is not an imposition made by a law madeby the State Legislature on which alone the restriction contemplated under Article 304(b) of the Constitu tion applies. [417B] 2.2 The levy is not an impost on land but is a levy on minerals extracted. It is a levy imposed on the land and not on the minerals extracted. [418B] 2:3 The levy is a tax on mineral rights. It is neither a tax on land nor a tax on minerals extracted therefrom. It is an imposition made for the purpose of regulation and development of minerals. It is levied not because of any land but because of the minerals extracted which have to be set apart and exploited in a manner that is consistent with the object of the Act. [419B] 2 :4 The Act is passed for the purpose for which it is enacted. It is well settled that a tax is levied for general benefit of the public. It is imposed in the public interest and is collected by the Government or by the agents of the Government. The levy is for the purpose and object of the levy. The levy and the machinery so set up for its levy raise a general demand which is usually met by the payment of a fee on the basis of the annual value of the minerals. [421B D] 2:5 The levy is in the nature or a fee. It is collected for the purpose or regulation and development. It is part of the regulation and development that brings forth the object of such levy in the general public interest. [422B] 2;6 The levy is imposed for the purpose, and object of regulation and is imposed in public interest. It is in the public interests that the levy be collected. [424B] 2 7 The levy is an imposition on land and not a tax on the land. It is the levy of tax on land which is imposed on the lessor. The levy of tax is on land and is not imposed on the lessee. The levy, therefore, is not an excise duty. [423C] 2:7 The levy is also not an impost in the nature either of a tax or of a fee. The levy in the instant case is not a fee but a tax. [428C] 2.8 The levy is, therefore, not an impost. [429C] 2 :9 The levy is challenged on the ground that it is in contravention of clause (b), Article 304 of Article 304. The contention is that the levy is not a duty of excise but a tax which is imposed by the State. The levy was imposed by the Central Legislature under Entry 84 of List I of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. It is, therefore. not an impost by the State Legislature but a tax imposed by the Centre. [430B] 2 9.1 The power exercised is legislative in character. The authority which is exercising the said power has the power to make rules for determining the rate of tax or the rate of levy. The rules made under the Act are in the nature and procedure of the Act and the rules are made in exercise of the rule making power conferred by the Act. The power exercised under the Act is legislative in nature. The authority exercising the rule making powers under the Act has the power of making rules for determining rate of tax and the rate at Which the tax is to be levied. The rules are not made by the State but are made by the Centre in exercise of its rule making power under Entry 84 List I of Seventh Schedule to Constitution. The rules, therefore, are not only the rules made by the Union Government but are also the rules made under a Central Act. [431B D] B.K, Trivedi & Sons vs State of Rajasthan, ; ; ; ; State of Tamil Nadu vs S.V. Angidi Chettiar, ; ; State Trading Corporation of India Ltd

The appellant was elected as a trustee by the Sengunatha Mudaliar Community of Manjakollai village in a meeting held on June 27, 1957. According to the appellant the temple was rounded two hundred years ago by the members of his community and since then the management of the temple and the affairs were always vested in the community of the Sengungavalliars and no person other than the elected trustee had at any time the right of management and control of the temple. The appellant 's case was that the temple was declared as an "exempted" temple under the provisions of Madras Act 1 of 1925. The respondents took a different view and proceeded on the basis that trusteeship of the temple was not hereditary. The Subordinate Judge held that the appellant was a hereditary trustee and the suit was not barred by limitation. The respondents filed an appeal to the High Court. The High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment of the Subordinate Judge. The appellant came to this Court by certificate. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the succession was "regulated by usage" and that according to the usage of the temple the trustees were elected for a period of one year each at a meeting of the members of the Sangunatha Mudaliar community and so the appellant must be held to be a trustee within the meaning of section 6(9) of the Madras Act 19 of 1951. HELD: (i) The word "succession" in relation to property and rights and interests in property generally implies "passing of an interest from one person to another" (vide in Re: Hindu Women 's Right to Property Act, 1941 (1). ; and Bhabatarini vs Ashalata, ; , referred to. (ii) The word 'succession ' in relation to the office of a hereditary trustee is not a term of art and it is not possible to say that there is a succession of As office to another when on the efflux of the period for which A was appointed, there is a vacancy and B is elected to that vacancy. It is quite possible that for that vacancy A himself might be reelected because a retiring trustee is eligible for reelection. The possibility of A being the successor A himself is not merely an anomaly, it is an impossible legal position. No man can succeed to his own office. In Black 's Law Dictionary the word 'suecession ' is defined as follows: "The revolution of title to property under the law of descent and distribution. (1) (1878) L.R. 5 I.A. 178. (2) (1879) L. R. 5 I A. 178. The right by which one set of men may, by succeeding another set, acquire a property in all the goods, movables, and other chattels of a corporation. The fact of the transmission of the rights, estate, obligations and charges of a deceased person to his heir or heirs. " The possibility of a person succeeding to his own property is not merely a anomaly, it being an impossible legal situation. No man could succeed to his property. In Black "s Law Dictionary, the word 'Succession ' is described as follows: 'The revolution of titles to property under law of descendants and distribution. The right of the latter to succeed to the former is not a right to property but a right to a right to the property of the former. The fact that the succession is by nomination by the holder in office is not a mere anomaly. The possibility that a person may succeed to his right by nomination is not merely of the anomaly. It is an impossible position. No person can succeed to the right of a person by nomination. [426 H] State of Madras vs Ramakrishna, ; , followed.

The appellant was charged under section 120B read with sections 302 and 109 IPC and section 302/34 IPC. The prosecution case was that the deceased was the village Munsif (Headman) of the village and that on the day of occurrence he was sleeping on a bench outside his cattle shed in the open space. The younger brother of the deceased was sleeping on the eastern side of the sluice of the north Boothagudi channel. The deceased was sleeping in the eastern side on the eastern parapet of the slime. The younger brothers of the deceased were sleeping on the western side of the said sluice. The deceased woke up at 11.15 P.M. on hearing the shout of his brother crying "younger brother" and got up and saw the accused standing on the eastern bank of the channel with a knife. The electric light was burning in the vicinity. The deceased got up and went near the accused. The deceased asked the accused to lodge a report at the police station which he did. The accused was seen running on the eastern part of the channel. The accused got up and ran to his elder brother who came from the side of the bench where he was sleeping and fell down on the southern side of the channel and died. The accused had bleeding injuries on several parts of his body. The accused ran to his brother and informed his brother that he had killed the deceased. The brother of the accused went to the police station and lodged the first information report. The accused also preferred appeals against his conviction and sentence. The High Court acquitted the accused on the ground that the evidence of the eye witnesses was not corroborated by the medical evidence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the testimony of the eye witness was not corroborated in material particulars by the medical testimony and that the testimony was not corroborated with regard to the presence of the accused at the scene of occurrence. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High court was not right in holding that the testimony given by the eye witness in court was not corroborated. [710F] 2. The testimony of the sole witness was rejected with reference to the first information. The High 'Court has not considered the intrinsic quality of the evidence of PW 4. It failed to notice certain broad facts which should definitely weigh with the court while appreciating the ocular testimony. From the medical evidence it is clear that there were more than one assailant and yet for the FIR it appears that there was only one assailant. This may not, in a given case, be considered as a very serious infirmity since the witness may not have seen the other. assailants when he came running to the place of occurrence. But the fact that the witness has stated in the first information that the deceased is only mentioning the name of accused Karunakaran as his assailant, this earlier version appears to be contradicted by the medical. evidence. [711B C] 3. The High. Court has not considered this intrinsic quality of evidence of PW4. It failed. to notice certain important facts which should certainly weigh with the Court while appreciating the evidence. [718C] 4. The High, Court was not right that PW 4 stood wholly corroborated by the contents of the FIR. On the other hand the testimony of PW 4 in court is corroborated by the testimony of PWs 1, 2 and 3. [712B] 5. The High Courts should be cautious in assessing the quality of the testimony of a solitary eye witness. The High courts should be careful in assessing the value of the testimony given in court. [713C]

The respondents were the heirs and legal representatives of a deceased person. The firm kept its accounts on cash basis. The Income tax Officer sought to tax these realisations. The respondents contended that the amounts received by the heirs and the legal representatives of the deceased were not the income of the deceased and were therefore not liable to tax under section 24B of the Income tax Act. The contention was rejected by the Income tax Officer and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Tribunal held that the notice under section 34 of the Income Tax Act could validly be served only for the assessment years 1950 51 and 1951 52, and that section 24B had no application to the income received after the death of the deceased. The High Court, on a reference, held that the amounts were not taxable and that the section had no application. The Commissioner of Income tax appealed to this Court. HELD : The High Court rightly answered the question in the negative and against the Commissioner of Income Tax. The fiction in section 24B is only for a definite purpose and they are limited to the purpose for which they are created and should not be extended beyond that legitimate field. [707 B] Ellis C. Reid vs Commissioner of Income. tax, Bombay, , referred to. In the present case the amounts which were sought to be taxed and which have been held not to be liable to tax are those which were not received in the previous year and are therefore not liable for tax in the several years of assessment. The High court rightly answered the reference in the negative. [709 B] E. Alfred vs Commissioner of Incometax, Bombay, ; , referred to and distinguished. In re B. M. Kamdar, , referred. The respondents were liable to pay tax under section 23(4) of the Income. tax Act, 1922, and the amounts were liable to be taxed under section 24(1) of the Act. The High, Court rightly answered that the amounts are not taxable. [710 B] Elson vs Trehearne, , referred, to. The respondents are not liable to pay income tax under section 22 of the Income 'tax Act, 1922. The respondents have not been assessed to income tax under that section. The respondents cannot be taxed under that section for the years of assessment in question. [711 B] Ezra vs Commissioner of income tax, , referred 812 to. The High Courts rightly held that the fiction in section 23(1) is only for the purposes of the assessment of the income of a person and not for the purpose of taxing the income of any other person. [712 C] Elliot C. Re. B. M, Kamdar, referred to. The amount which was sought to be assessed and which has been held not liable to be assessed to tax is liable to be included in the total income of the respondents. [713 B]

The petitioners were employed in the ministerial services of the Andhra Pradesh Government. They challenged the Act and the Rules and the proposed action as ultra vires the Constitution. The petitioners contended that article 16(3) under which the Act and Rules purport to be made has been misunderstood as conferring a power to make a law prescribing requirement as to residence in a part of a State. For this reason section 3 of the Act was challenged as ultra vires. The respondents contended that article 15(1) of the Constitution which provides that no citizen shall be discriminated against on the ground only of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth, residence or any of them, was not applicable to the State of Andhra Pradesh. The respondents further contended that the Mulki Rules were not ultra vires the State of Hyderabad. HELD : (i) The word 'State ' in article 16(1) means the State as defined in article 12. The State can make a law in a special case prescribing any requirement as to 'residence within a State or Union territory prior to appointment as a condition of employment in the State or Union Territory. Under article 35(a) this power is conferred upon Parliament but is denied to the Legislatures of the States, notwithstanding anything in the Constitution, and under article 35(b) any law in force immediately before the commencement of the Constitution in respect to the matter shall, subject to the terms thereof and subject to such adaptations that may be made under article 372, continue in force until altered or repealed or amended by Parliament. The legislative power to create residential qualification for employment is thus exclusively conferred on Parliament. Parliament can make any law prescribing any requirement of residence within a State, or Union territory, prior to employment or appointment to an office in that State or Union. [118 B D] (ii) The words 'any requirement ' cannot be read to warrant something which could have been said more specifically. The fact that this clause is an exception and came as an amendment must dictate that a narrow construction upon the exception should be placed as indeed the debates in the Constituent Assembly also seem to indicate. [118 E F] (iii) The words "any requirement" cannot be read as "any requirement". The fact that the clause is an amendment must be read as meaning that a narrow interpretation upon the exception must be placed as, indeed, the debates in, the Constituent Assembly. [118 G] (iv) The words in article 15(2) that "nothing in this article shall prevent Parliament from making any law prescribing, in regard to a class or classes of employment or appointment under the Government of, or any local or other authority within, a State or union territory, any requirement as. to residence within that State or union Territory" are obviously controlled by the words "residence within the State or union terri tory or territory" which words mean what they say, neither more nor less. [119 B C] (v) The words, 'any requirement" in article 16 (3) are controlled by the word 'residence '. The word 'reside ' means residence. The exception, therefore, must be viewed narrowly and not carried to excess by interpretation. The article speaks of residence in a State and means only that. If it chose to speak of residence in parts of State such as Districts, Talauqas, cities, towns etc. more appropriate and specific language could have been used such as 'any requirement as to resident within that State '. [119 D E] (vi) The words used in article 16 are "any requirement as, to residence within the State". The exception, however, must be read in the context of the words "in the State". [119 H] (vii) The words must be read to mean "any requirement of residence". The exception must be viewed in the context in which it is used. [119 H, 120 A] (viii) The words residence within the state or Union territory ' in article 15 (2) are obviously controlled. by the words 'residence in the State '. The words 'reside within the State ' mean 'reside in the State. [120 B C]

The appellant was convicted of an offence under section 52 of the Indian Post Office Act, 1898, for having secreted the five registered letters in question. The High Court held that the appellant had secreted the letters in question and on this finding set aside his acquittal and convicted him. The appellant contended that the High Court had not found that there were compelling reasons for setting aside the appellant 's acquittal. Held, that the High court was right in holding that the appellant was not guilty of the offence charged. The mere fact of possession, according to the High Court, does not suffice to show that the letters were secreted by the appellant. The mere circumstance that the articles were found in an almirah in the house in which the appellant lives, would not justify the conclusion that he had secreted them from the mere fact that they were found in the almirah. The fact that the almirali contained a large number of articles belonging to the father and since he had the key with him it must be he who must be deemed to be in possession of the almira, and consequently of its contents including the registered letters in, question. The circumstance that the alratah contained a large quantity of articles belonging, to the father, could not justify the inference that he had secretly and without the knowledge of the appellant, taken away the articles. The fact of entrustment of the articles had not been established. The fact, that the alaratah contained a small number of articles, belonging to the appellant, could not be held to be in the exclusive possession of the appellant. Held, further, that the appellant could not be said to have secreted the articles in question from the mere circumstance that they were recovered from an almira in the house. The fact could not be established by the mere fact of the alratum was found in the Almirah. In the circumstances, the appellant could be convicted under section 52 only if he had been in possession of articles which he knew were stolen. The fact was not established. The mere possession of the articles was not sufficient to show that they were in the exclusive, possession of the accused. The fact must be established by evidence. The fact should be established by a preponderance of probability and not by a mere possibility. The mere possibility of the articles being stolen or being converted into other articles, could not, therefore, justify the inference of the accused 's possession of them. The fact had not been proved that the articles had been stolen from the almiras in the house, and the fact that the appellant took away the articles from the alaratha in the house could not be considered to be in his exclusive possession. The fact also could not be proved that the appellant committed theft of the articles. Held, also, that the fact that articles were found from the altar in the house was not sufficient for the inference that the articles in the altar were in the appellant ' 's exclusive possession.

The appellants were convicted by the Nyaya Panchayat for contempt of court. The High Court admitted the application for stay of proceedings pending before it and stayed further proceedings before the Nyaya Panchayats. The High court did not give any further details about the stay order. The High 'Court disbelieved the explanation of the Panchas that the High Court had stayed proceedings before the Panchayat and that the matter was pending before the N affirmation of the High Court. The High. Court disbelieved the explanation that the Panchas did not believe the contents of the application and affidavit of the Pancha and that the Pancha had not filed the application and the affidavit before the N. affirmation of the order of the High court. The appellants contended that no contempt of court had been established because a Court is entitled not to act on an application which is not accompanied by an affidavit properly sworn to or a certified copy of the order. HELD : (i) The High Court did not appreciate that the Panchs were not well versed in law and procedure and the records maintained by them should not be judged in the same manner as that of ordinary courts. [117 B] (ii) The High court should not have drawn an adverse inference from the fact that the reasons for not accepting the prayer for stay were not recorded. [117 C] (iii) The High ' Court did not keep in mind the principles which are applicable to a Court of record. [117 D] (iv) The High Courts should not have drew an adverse inference against the Panchas for not recording the reasons for their refusal to accept the prayer for staying proceedings. [117 E] (v) The High.Court should not have relied on the affidavit of the Sarpanch. [117 F] (vi) The High,Court should not, in the circumstances of the case, have drawn an inference that the Panch had knowledge of the order passed by the High Court and that the Sarpanch had not filed an affidavit in support of his allegations. [117 G] (vii) The High courts should not have proceeded to hear the appeal on the basis of the evidence. [117 H] (viii) The High;Court should not interfere with the order of stay passed by the N affirmation. [118 A] (ix) The High authorities should not have taken the matter to the Supreme Court without giving the Panchas an opportunity of being heard. [118 B] (x) The High magistrates should not have entertained the application for contempt of Court. [118 C] (xi) The High Magis trate should not have stayed proceedings before him. [118 D]

The appellant was tried for the murder of his wife. The prosecution case was that the appellant had a quarrel with his wife and that he had purchased a sword from her. The appellant was also alleged to have a motive to harm the deceased. The trial court acquitted the appellant but the High Court convicted him. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The High Court erred in rejecting the statement of the appellant about the appellant 's confessing to him that he had murdered the deceased. [207 D] The appellant was rightly convicted of the offence under section 302, I.P.C. [207 E] The extra judicial confession of the appellant to the deceased was admissible in evidence. The fact that he had the sword which was stained with human blood, leads to such a supposition, even if the mere possession of a sword so stained be not sufficient to establish conclusively that the person who possessed it so shortly after the murder of a person with whom he had enmity, had committed the murder. The Canal runs beside the field of the appellant. [207 F G] The Canal runs on the field of one of the persons who had enmity with the appellant. The Canal is not a matter of surprise that the appellant should have made a statement that he had committed the offence of murder of the deceased and was, thereafter, having a bath. There is no reason to think that the appellant would not make such a statement when the appellant himself proceeds to the Police Station and hands over the blood stained sword. It is no doubt unusual that a person who commits a murder in pursuance of an enmity arising out of minor disputes would be feeling so justified in his conduct as to openly admit it to the first person he met and to go to the Police station and report about it. It is always difficult to find reasons for a person 's acting in a certain manner. It may be that having blurted out the truth to the deceased, when taken by surprise, the appellant thought the best thing to be to proceed to the Police Sta tion and report the matter there. It is not unlikely that the appellant thought that the best thing he could have done to the deceased would be to proceed in the Police Station. [207 H; 208 A B] The extrajudicial confession of the accused to the deceased is admissible in evidence and the fact that he did purchase a sword a day before, that very sword was found to be stained with human being shortly after the death, and that sword was handed over by the appellant himself to the Police Officer at the Police Station, is a strong circumstance against the appellant. It is also true that the Canal runs on a field of one person with blood stains. The Canal run on the field is not a question of surprise. It is a matter of great moment that the appellant was seen by the deceased in the Canal. The Canal ran on the field. The Canal was not a matter on which the appellant could have had any reason to think. [208 C D]

The appellants challenged the validity of the electoral roll prepared and published under the Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956, by filing a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition on the ground that the period of 20 days had been mentioned in the notice issued under Rule 4(1) of the Madhya Pradesh Munici pal Corporation (Preparation, Revision and Publication of Electoral Rolls and Selection of Councillors) Rules, 1963, and that the appellants were not entitled to any relief under Article 226 of the Constitution on account of the inordinate delay in the presentation of the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that: (1) the notice issued by the Collector under Rule 4 (1) of Rules was not in accordance with the provisions of the Act and the Rules and that the authorities would have taken action to correct the error in the notice, and (2) the authorities would not have taken action on the basis of the notice issued on October 30, 1978, and that therefore, the entire election process had become a nullity and that therefore the declaration of results of all the 44 successful candidates was liable to be quashed. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High court was right in holding that the period prescribed for preferring claims and objections under Rule 4 of the Rules was 30 days. It was open to the appellants to move the State Government under Rule 6 of the Rules to make an order directing the Collector to follow the provisions governing the preparation of the electoral rolls. It was also open to them to file a writ petition immediately after the publication of the notice. [495F G] 2. The Collector published the notice under Rule 4 on September 30, 1978 and also called upon interested persons to prefer claims and/or objections thereto within a period of 20 clear days from the date of the publication of that notice. In the instant case, the writ petition itself was filed on December 28, 1978. No satisfactory explanation was given in the course of the petition by the petitioners as to why they delayed the filing of the petition till December 28, l988. [496B C] 3. The High Courts have power under Article 226 to issue an appropriate writ, order or direction to any person or authority, including any Government, within their territorial jurisdiction, for the enforcement of the fundamental rights conferred by Part III of the Constitution. The power of the High Court under Article 226 is discretionary and if the High Court finds that there is not satisfactory explanation for the delay, it may reject the petition if it finds that the issue of the writ will lead to public inconvenience and interference with rights of others. [497B C] 4. The power to issue a writ is discretionary and the High Court is not bound to exercise that discretion. The High, Court is not a court of appeal. It can exercise its power only in furtherance of justice and not in perpetuity. [499A B] 5. The power under Article 136 is discretionary and it is not necessary that the High Court should exercise the same. The power is to be exercised in extraordinary circumstances and in the interest of justice. [494B] 6. The power conferred by Article 226 is a discretionary power. It is not an arbitrary power. The High. Court is not exercising its discretion against the will of the petitioner. It is exercising its discretion by considering all the facts and circumstances of the case and is not deciding the matter merely on the basis or on the legal position as it stands. [498B C] 7. The High courts have power under article 226 to issue a Writ of Mandamus or any other appropriate writ, direction or order to any person, authority or Government, including any government, within their jurisdiction, for any of the following matters: (a) the enforcement of any of the Fundamental Rights; (b) the enforcement. of any other legal right; (c) the settlement of any dispute between two or more parties and for any other proper or special purpose; (d) securing the implementation of any such legal or constitutional obligation as may be laid down by the Courts; (e) issuing a writ of mandamus or any other writ, order, direction or writ, including any writ in the nature of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari, quashing any proceeding which is or has been started by the Government, or by a person or authority who is empowered by the Constitution to do so. [490B C] 8. The power given by Article 226 of. the Constitution is discretionary and is not to be exercised arbitrarily or capriciously. The High 'Court is not exercising jurisdiction to issue a prerogative writ. It is passing a writ of certiorari under Article 226. [492C] 9. The power vested in the High Courts under Article 226, is discretionary and, is not to he exercised arbitrarily or on grounds of policy. The High .Court is not a Court of appeal. it can exercise its powers only in furtherance 'of justice and not merely in perpetuity, and, therefore, the High Courts have the power to issue prerogative writs. [493B] 10. The power, conferred by Article 136 is not to merely be exercised in cases where the judgment is vitiated by patent or clear error of law or procedure or is based on a clear misreading of the documents or judgment is such that no reasonable person would have passed the same. [491C] 11. The power exercised by the High Court in the present case is not in any way vitiated by any error of law apparent on the face of the record. [4l2B]

The respondent company was incorporated in the year 1953 with its registered office at Calcutta. The balance sheet and profit and loss account of the company were laid before the company at its general meeting on May 30, 1964. The company had not filed the balance sheet and the profit and loss accounts with the Registrar of Companies. The company was not in a position to send the balance sheet or the profit and lost account to the Registrar of the Companies. The Registrar of Companies, however, sent a notice to the company to the effect that the balance sheet of the company and the profit & loss account had not been laid before the general meeting. The company filed a complaint against the respondent company and its directors for failure to comply with the provisions of section 134(4) of the , and section 220 of the . [416 B] (3) The requirement of section 134 is that the balance of the profit & Loss Account and profit and Loss account should be laid before the annual general meeting of a company.
