The West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1950, was enacted to provide for the speedier trial of certain offences. The Act provided for the constitution of Special Courts and for the trial of cases by Special Courts. Section 5(1) of the Act provided that a Special Court shall try such offences or classes of offences or cases or classes of cases as the State Government may, by general or special order in writing direct. Section 7 of the Act empowered the State Government to direct by notification in the Official Gazette that the trial of all offences or classes or cases or class of cases or classes shall be by a Special Court. Section 7 provided that the State Government might direct by notification that the trial by a Special Tribunal of offences or classes, of offences or class of cages of cases or class or classes of Special cases or classes, or cases or cases or Classes of cases, to be tried by a Special court shall be tried by the Special Court constituted for the area in which the offence or classes of. cases or classes were committed. The State Government issued a notification under section 5(1), directing that the trial shall be by the Special Tribunal. The respondents were tried by the special Tribunal for offences under section 5 of the Act. The Special Tribunal convicted the respondents and sentenced them to various terms of imprisonment. The respondents filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the Act on the ground that the Act was violative of article 14 of the Constitution. The High Court held that the Act did not contravene article 14 of ' the Constitution and quashed the conviction and sentence. The State appealed to this Court. HELD: (i) The Act was not violative of article. 14 of the Constitu tion. The classification implied in the sub section has no reference to, and is not directed towards the singling out of any particular person as an object of hostile State action but is concerned only with the grouping of "offences", "classes of offences" and "classes and classes of cases" for the purpose of being tried by a special court. The Act therefore empowers the State Government, to direct the offences, which in its view require speedier trial, to be try by a Special. Court according to the special procedure provided by it for the speedily trial of those offences. [297 B D] (ii) The Act in so far as it empowers the State Govern ment to direct "cases" to be tried before a Special Court of offences or a class of offences or to a Special Court for the trial 'of cases or classes or classes of ' cases or classes is not violative of the equal protection clause of the Constitution, because, the classification is based on an intelligible differentia which has a rational relation to the object of the Act, namely, the speedier trials of certain offences, and the differentiation is based on the difference in the procedure for the trial by Special Courts and the procedure for trial by Special Tribunals. [297 E G] (iii) The Act is not violative Of article 14 of Constitution because, the Act does not make any distinction between "offences" and "cases". The classification is based upon an intelligible differentiation which has a reasonable relation to the objects sought to be achieved by the Act. [298 B C] (iv) The Act does not violate article 14 of. the Constitution because, it does not make the classification of offences or "classes" of offences or 'cases" arbitrary. The classification is not based on any intelligible differen tice which has a relation to the policy of the Act to try such offences and cases. [298 D E] (v) The Act, in so far, as it empowers State Government to order "cases", to be tried only by a Special, Court, is not violative. of article 14. The classification of offences and cases is based on intelligible differen ic and scientifically relevant considerations and the differentia which is sought to be made out of the classification is founded on an intelligent differentia which distinguished those offences and cases from the offences and cases which are the subject matter of the present case. [298 F G] (vi) The Act cannot be said to be violative of article 19 of the Constitution because the Act does. not make any classification of offences nor does it make any classification on the basis of the commission of offences by a particular person or persons. The classification does not appear to be based on any rational principle and the differen tice is based on a consideration of the nature and circumstances of the offences and the nature and volume of evidence to be obtained in respect of it. [299 B C] The Act is therefore not violative of Article 14 of the Consti tution. [299 D E] The Act does.not make any classification and is not violative, of article 14, because, it is not based upon any intelligible differenti ifictia which has any relation to the differentia on which the classification is made. [300 B] (vii) The Act has not made any classification of cases or cases for the purpose. of being tried only by Special Courts, but has made a classification of offences for the purpose, of being tried in a Special Court by a Special Judge. The classification has no reasonable relation to. the object of. the Act. It is not based.on any intelligible principle and the classification is not founded on any intelligi ble differentia which had a reasonable relation with the object of, the Act. There is therefore no discrimination in the matter of the trial of the respondents by a Special 'Court. [300 E F] (viii) The Act being not violative of articles 14 of the constitution, the High Court was not justified in quashing the conviction and sentences. [300 G] (ix) The Act did not violate article 19 of. the constitution because, the State Government had not made any discrimination in the trial of offences or in the trial by the Special Courts. The Act does, not make any discrimination in respect of the trial by special courts. [301 B C] State of West Bengal vs Anwar Ali Sarkar, ; , referred to. (x) The Act provides for the trial to be by Special Courts only and the Act does nothing to indicate that the Special Court should be constituted only by the State Government. The Act is a special Act applicable to the State of West Bengal and the Special Court has no jurisdiction to try the respondents. [302 C D] (xi) The Act also does not violate articles 14 of.the Constitution because, there is no discrimination in that the Act does,not make any distinction on the basis. of the commission or offences by a certain person or persons and the classification does not bear any reasonable relation to, the object of that Act. [302 E] (xii) The Act makes no discrimination in respect to the trial of certain offi ces by Special Courts but makes a distinction between those cases where the cases are tried by a Court of Sessions or High Court and those where the cases have been committed to it by a Magistrate or Court of Sessions. [303 E] (xiii) The Act only makes a distinction in the matter,of the trial of those cases where a case is transferred from one Special Court to another under the provisions of section 7 of the Criminal Procedure Code. The Act, therefore, does not violate the equal protection Clause of the Constitution and is not void

The appellant was a Radiologist in the Maulana Azad Medical College, Delhi. He was appointed as a Radiologist cum Associate Professor in the Maulaana Azad Medical Collage in 1964. He was later promoted as a Professor in the Medical College in 1966. In 1973, the Government of India promoted him as a Professor of Radiology in the Ma ulana Azad Medical Collegiate College. The appellant was not relieved of his duties by the Government of the India in the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. All that they stated was that he did not fulfil the requirement of the Central Health Service (Amendment) Rules, 1966. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said Rules. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the teaching experience gained by the appellant as a Radiology cum Associate Professor or a Professor of a speciality in a Medical College cannot be taken into consideration for the purpose of determining the question of his eligibility for appointment as a Professor. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant had acquired the requisite teaching experience as envisaged by r. 8(2A) and paragraph 3 of Annexure I to the Second Schedule of the Central Services (Amendment) rules, 1966. He was therefore eligible to be considered for appointment to the post of Professor of Radiological Surgery in the Maulsana Azad MedicalCollege. [27D] 2. The Ministry of Health cannot be heard to say that the appellant has not acquired the status of an Associate Professor of Radiologist cum Professor of Radiologists in the Willingdon Hospital or the Safdarjang Hospital or the Safdarjung Hospital. The mere fact that the appellant was not drawing a teaching allowance of Rs. 200/ p.m. is of no legal consequence because the allowance is attached to the post. [27E] 3. The appellant has acquired the requisite qualification for appointment as Professor of Radiotherapy in the Maullana Azad Medical college. [27F] 4. The Ministry cannot be heard now to say that he has not acquired his status of an Assistant Professor of Radiography cum Associate Professor of a Medical College. [27G] 5. The appellant having been substantively appointed to the post in the Irwin Hospital, he cannot be said to have acquired the status as an Associate Professor. [27H] 6. The appellant, having been substantive in the Irrin Hospital, was eligible to be appointed as Professor of radiology in the Medical college. He could not be appointed Professor of Radiographic in the Ma pauana Azad Medical Colleges. [28A] 7. The appellant is not entitled to be promoted to the post Professor of Radioology in the M.D.M.R.T. and M.B.B.S. courses of studies for the last 17 years. [28B] 8. The appellant cannot be considered for promotion to the post professor of Radiology. [28C] 9. The appellant does not fulfil the qualifications prescribed by the Central Health Services (Amendment Rules, 1966). [28D] 10. The Ministry has also filed the affidavit of Shri N.S. Bakshi, Deputy Secretary to the Government of Indian, Ministry of Health & Family Welfare to the effect that the teaching and other academic qualifications of the appellant are not equivalent to those of a Professor of the Maulna Azad Medical College. The Ministry is unable to support the stand of the Government of Indias that the appellant does not possess the teaching experience of a Professor in a Medical college. The Ministry should have been more specific in its stand. [28E] 11. The Ministry can be heard to state that the appellant had acquired his teaching experience as a Professor and that he was eligible to apply for the post of professor of radiology. [29A] 12. The appellant could not be considered for the post Professor in Radiology in Maulana ' Azad Medical College as he did not possess the requisite teaching qualification. [29B] 13. The appellant did not fulfil qualifications prescribed by Central Health Service Rules. [30A] 14. The Ministry could not be heard to deny the appellant the benefit of the teaching experience. [30B] 15. The appellant would be eligible to apply to the post for which he had been substantively selected. [30C] 16. The appellant should be considered for selection to the post and appointment to the said post. [30D] 17. The appellant will be considered for a post in the Medical Colleges in India. [30E] 18. The appellant may apply to the Ministry of Home Affairs for being considered for selection for the post. The Ministry may consider the appellant for selection to that post. [31A] [The Court directed the Union Public Service Commission to re advertiise the post of Professors of Radiology and to call the appellant for an interview for being considered appointment to that post.] [30E F] [The court directed the Union of India to consider the appellant 's case for selection to Professor of Radios in the Medical colleges in India.] [30F] [The appeal was dismissed. The appellant shall be considered for being appointed Professor of radiological surgery in the Medical Collage of Delhi.] [30G] [The appellant was not entitled to the benefit of teaching experience gained as a Professor or a Reader in a Medical Collage.] [30H] [The order of the Court was confined to the appellant 'Sitting in the Medical Collegiates of Delhi and Delhi.] [31A B] [The Government of India is directed to consider the case of the appellant for appointment to Professor of radiotherapy in Maulna ' Azad Medical Collge, New Delhi.] [32B]

The workmen of the appellant company claimed that the Tribunal should fix the minimum wage in the company 's concern and that the minimum wage should be fixed at the rate of three months ' basic wage in each case. The company resisted the claim on the ground that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to fix the minimum wages in the concern. The Tribunal held that it would not be proper to compare the wage structure for these paper mills with that of the company. The Tribunal also held that the minimum wages should be paid on the basis of the minimum wage prevailing in the other industries in the region. The company appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The principle of fixation of wages on the basis Of Comparison in the region laid down in the French Motor Car Co. 's case was not rigid and, it was not necessary that the minimum. wage in the Company must be fixed at a rate equal to the minimum wages paid in the other comparable industries in the same region. The principle of fixing the minimum wage was not rigid but was not rigid. It was not necessary to fix the wages in the company at the same rate as in other industries. [674 D] (ii) The principle that the minimum should be fixed on the basis that the wages paid in comparable industries in other parts of the country should be the same as the wages paid by comparable industries in comparable industries should be accepted. [677 B] (iii) The principle was not rigid, but was not adopted by the Tribunal. It was for this reason that the Tribunal held that the principle of fixation Of wages on the principle of Comparison in industry cum region was not rigid; it was not for the Tribunal to fix the same wage structure for the industry cum region. [670 C D] (iv) The principle laid down in Associated Cement Companies ' case was not a rigid principle and was not applicable to the present case. The principle was that the minimum was to be fixed on a fair and just basis and that the Tribunal was not to fix the wage structure on the basis as if the wages paid were the same. [671 C D] The principle was also not rigid. The principle that wages paid in other industries should be the basis of fixation of wage structure was not rigid or rigid. It could not be said that the principle was not applicable in the present case because the company had agreed to exclude the workmen in the company in regard to payment of bonus. [673 C D] In the present case, the Tribunal had fixed the minimum wage at Rs. 95 per month. The company had agreed that the minimum would be Rs. 12 per month. [676 D] (v) The Tribunal was not justified in fixing the minimum wages on the ground of the company ' not having produced the balance sheet and profit and loss account of the company for the year 1962 63. The company was paying profit bonus equivalent to three months ' wages. The demand for bonus was for the year 1963 64. The Tribunal was expected to decide the dispute only as referred to it and at the time of reference at least, there was not and there could possibly not be a claim for higher bonus on the basis. of the application of the Full Bench Formula. [678 E F] (vi) The Tribunal had directed that the increase of Rs. 12 p.m. in the total minimum wage packet allowed by it will enure to the benefit of the lowest paid female, badi and permanent dailyrated workers also. The demand made by the workmen was for bonus equivalent to six months ' wages and the argument was that if the Tribunal had worked out the surplus available on the correct basis, that surplus would have justified grant of profit bonus at the rate. of six months ' Wages. [679 B C] (vii) The Tribunal could not have fixed the minimum wages at the same level as in other concerns. The principle laid by the Tribunal was that the wages should be fixed as per the Full Bench formula. The principle could not be applied to the company in the present ease because the company was paying the minimum wage to the lowest paid clerical staff. The demand of the workmen was that the company should pay the minimum wage on the basis, of the Full bench formula. The Tribunal had fixed at Rs. 94 per month. It was, therefore, not correct to say that the minimum of Rs. 95 was fixed on the ground. [672 D F]

The assessee, a partnership firm, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1960 61. The Income tax Officer issued a notice under section 148 of the Income tax Act, 1961, to the assessee, calling upon it to produce its books of account and other relevant papers. The assessee produced before the Income tax Officer a statement showing various creditors from whom it had borrowed on Hundi during the accounting year in question. In that statement it gave the lull names and address of the creditors. After enquiry, the assessee 's total income was assessed at Rs. 69,886/ . On June 3, 1966, the Income tax officer issued a notice to the assessee under section 148, requiring it to produce before him its books of accounts and other relevant records. The assessee challenged the validity of that notice as well as proceedings taken on the strength of that notice on various grounds. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The notice was issued after four years but before eight years of the date of the original assessment. Section 151(2) of the Act provides that the Income tax Officers shall, before issuing any notice under section 147, record his reasons for doing so. The Income Tax Officer has not stated in his report that he had satisfied himself that the income chargeable to tax had escaped assessment for that year. He has merely stated that he had reason to believe that by reason of the omission or failure on the part of the assessee to make a return under section 139 for any assessment year to the Income tax 'Officer or to disclose fully and truly all material facts necessary for his assessment for that assessment year, income chargeable to income tax has escaped assessment for the assessment years in question. [445 E H] (2) The Commissioner of Income tax, Bihar and Orissa, Patna vs M/s. Chugamal Rajpal, Calcutta, , referred to. (3) The Commissioner has mechanically accorded permission. He did not himself record that he was satisfied that this was a fit case for the issue of a notice under s. 148. [446 A B] (4) The Commissioner had mechanically accorded permission, and he did not himself recorded that he was so satisfied. [446 C]

The appellant firm was a firm carrying on business in the manufacture of soap and soap ghee. It was dissolved on January 2, 1934. The firm consisted of Nagjee, Narayanjee and Krishnajee. The firm was carrying on business as commission agents in the name of the firm of solicitors and commission agents. The firm had been carrying on business at Bombay and Calcutta. The firm carried on business in Bombay and Calcutta and at Calcutta. The business of the firm consisted of the business of the appellant firm as commission agents and of the firm as a firm of soliciting and procuring orders from the Government. The firm 's business was carried on at Bombay and at Calcutta and at Madras. The firm constituted by the instrument of 1918 was dissolved on April 1, 1939. The firm continued the business of manufacturing soap and soapghee till it was dissolved on December 6, 1918. The firm, however, continued to carry on business at Madras and Calcutta. In the assessment year 1939 40, the firm claimed that in view of the provisions of section 25(4) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, as amended in 1939, the firm was not entitled to the benefit of section 25 (4) of that Act. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Income tax Appellate Tribunal rejected the claim of the appellant. The High Court, on a reference, held that the appellant was not entitled under section 25(1) of the Act to the benefit. The appellant came to this Court by special leave. Held, that the appellant firm was not liable to be taxed under section 25 (1) of Act, 1922. The firm of solicitor and commission agents was a separate and distinct entity from the firm of Solicitors and so was not entitled as of right to the benefit under section 25. The firm did not carry on any business at Bombay or Calcutta and the business of Solicitor and commission agent was carried on only at Madras and at Madras and not at Bombay and Madras. The business was carried at Bombay and not at Calcutta and so the firm was entitled to the benefits of section 25. Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay vs Sir Mahomed Yusuf Ismail, [1940] 8 I.T.R. 8, referred to. The firm which was dissolved in 1939 was not a separate and independent entity from the business carried on by the firm ofsolicitors and the income of the firm was therefore not assessable under section 25 of the Act. Commissioner of Incometax, Bombay vs Sitaldas Tirathdas, [1959] 36 I.T R. 887, referred to and distinguished. Commissioner of Excess Profits Tax, Bombay City vs The Scindia Steam Navigation Co. Ltd., [1961] 41 I.T,R. 367, distinguished. Commissioner Of Income tax, Madras vs A. V. S. Arunachala Nadar, [19591 36 I. T.R. 687, referred. Commissioner of income tax, Bombay City, Bombay vs The Scindias of India Ltd., [1959] 37 I.T,.R. 151, distinguished. The firm in the present case was not entitled, under section 25, to the benefit as it was not carrying on any business in Bombay or Calcutta. The income of the appellant was therefore not liable to tax under section 25 and the income tax authorities were right in rejecting the claim of tax. Commissioner of Inland Revenue vs The Duke of Westminister, [1938] , referred to. Commissioner of Taxes vs A. W. R. W. Co. Ltd. , distinguished. Commissioner 'of Income tax, Burma vs A. L. V.R.P. Firm, [1937] , distinguished. The appellant firm was entitled under section 26(2) of the Income tax Act to the benefits as it was carrying on the business in Bombay, Calcutta and Madras. Commissioner of lncome tax, Bombay, vs Sital Das Tirathdas. , , distinguished. Held, further, that the business of a firm was not carried on by a firm and the income was not liable under section 25 to tax. Commissioner Of Excess Profits tax, Bombay South vs The Scoble of India Ltd. , referred to and relied on. Commissioner of I.T., Bombay vs The Hindusthan Co operative Insurance Society Ltd., , distinguished. In the present case, the business of solicitor and soliciting orders from the government was carried on by one of the partners of the firm and the business was carried by the firm itself. The firm and the partners were carrying on the same business in the same name and in the same place. The firm carrying on the firm business was not a distinct and separate entity from the other business carried on in the name and style of Soliciting and Soliciting orders. The income was not assessable under the section. Commissioner of Income tax, Madras, vs A.V. S. Venkatachala Nadar. , , referred to, Commissioner of Income Tax, Bombay vs R. M. D. K. A. V., R. M., T. K. M. M. Muthia Chettiar, [1943] , distinguished and held inapplicable. Commissioner of Wealth tax, Bombay North vs The South India Pictures Ltd., , referred to; Commissioner of Income. tax, Bombay Presidency and Aden vs A. C. R. P. Firm, , distinguished. Case law discussed. Commissioner of Taxation, Burma vs Commissioner of Income, tax, , distinguished and distinguished. The business carried on at Madras and the business carried at Calcutta were not the same business carried on under the Act of 1922. The income from the business ofsolicitor and the commission agent was not liable as the business of an independent firm. The income tax authorities had rightly rejected the claim for tax. Commissioner, of Excess profits tax, Bombay Central vs The Scottish Co operative Insurance Co. Ltd, , distinguished, Commissioner of Exce Profits Tax, Madras vs The Sculiny of India Ltd, , referred to: Commissioner of Income 'tax, Bombay City. vs The Scinbia of India Ltd; , , distinguished and applied. Commissioner of Sales tax, U.P. vs Sital Prasad, ; , distinguished. Per Sarkar, J. The firm is not entitled to claim the benefit of the section as it was a separate entity from its other business carried out in the name, and style of, Solicitors. The firm could not be said to carry on any other business at Bombay, Calcutta or Madras. The income derived from the business in solicitors ' firm was not assessable to tax under the section, and the income from the firm was assessable under section 26 (2) of Act 1922.

The appellant plaintiff filed a suit for partition of her husband 's share in the joint family properties. The suit was dismissed by the trial court. The High Court dismissed the plaintiff 's appeal. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the plaintiff ' 's husband 's interest in the coparcenary property would devolve by survivorship upon the surviving members of the coparc entary and not in accordance with the provisions of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The Hindu Succession Act came into force on June 17, 1956. Section 6 of the Act provides that the Act shall not apply to any property which at the time of the death of the deceased was in possession of a female Hindu, and the property was held by her as a limited owner. The proviso to that section contains the formula for fixing the share of the claimant while Explanation 1 contains a formula for determining the share of heirs in the property of a deceased coparcener. The plaintiff 's share, by the application of the proviso, has to be determined according to the terms of the testamentary instrument, if any, made by the deceased and since there is none in the instant case, by the applicability of the rules of intestate succession contained in sections 8, 9 and 10 of the Hindu Succession Act, the proviso to section 6 comes into play and the normal rule is excluded. [767 H, 768 A B] (2) The plaintiff ' ' 's share would be 1/24th. The plaintiff would get 1/24rd. The plaintiff will get 1/4th. The defendant 's share will be 1/4 th. The plaintiff is entitled to 1/24 th. [766 C D] (3) The plaintiff is not entitled to any share in the copartnership property. [768 A] (4) The plaintiff has a 1/4 share in the property. The plaintiff has 1/4 of the property. [769 B] (5) The plaintiff would be entitled to 1 1/4. [761 C] (6) The plaintiff will be entitled to a 1/24 share in the suit property. [770 C] (7) The plaintiff can claim a 1/6th share in the family property. [771 C] (8) The plaintiff cannot claim a share in the partition of the copartner property. [772 C] (9) The plaintiff could claim a 1 1/24 of the property as a matter of right. [773 C] (10) The plaintiff was entitled to 1 /24th share in her husband ' 's property. [783 D] (11) The plaintiff had 1/4rd share in the husband 's property and the plaintiff would get a 1/8th share in that property. [781 D] (12) The plaintiff, by virtue of section 6 of the Hindu Women 's Rights to Property Act, 1937, is entitled to a share in her deceased husband 's family property. The proviso thereto provides that nothing contained in the section shall be construed as enabling a person who has separated himself from the coparcarcenary before the death of his father, the surviving coparceners of the coparce, to claim on intestacy a share in that coparcenery property. [751 E] (13) The plaintiff having 1/4 in the property, would get a share in it. [775 G] (14) The plaintiff being a widow, she is entitled to get a 1 1 /24 share in her property. [757 B] (15) The plaintiff in the instant suit, is not entitled as a matter or right to any share. [758 C] (16) The plaintiff does not claim a share under section 6 of Hindu Succession Act. [759 D] (17) The plaintiff did not claim a 1 /24 of the properties as a matter to which section 6 of Act is applicable. [756 E] (18) The plaintiff claimed a 1/12th share in all the properties of the joint family. The plaintiff was not entitled to claim a share of the properties under section 6. [757 E] (19) The plaintiff must be held entitled to 1.5/24th share. [765 G] (20) The plaintiff should be held entitled only to 1/4 and not 1/24. [767 A] (21) The plaintiff may claim a 1.5th share in any property of the joint Hindu family. [748 C] (22) The plaintiff and the defendant are entitled to 1 5/24th each. [749 A] (23) The plaintiff shall be entitled to the 1/24 interest of the defendant in the joint Hindu Family properties. [747 E] (24) The plaintiff who is a widow is entitled to the share of her deceased husband in the joint Family properties. The plaintiff cannot be entitled to any interest in the joint properties. [752 C]

The 1st Respondent was appointed as a Class III employee in the Corporation on 1.9.1956. He was promoted to Class I post in 1963. He was further promoted to Class II post in 1965. He was also promoted to Class III post in 1965 and was further promoted in 1967. He was again promoted to Class IV post in 1968 and was further further promoted to the post of Assistant Manager in 1969. He was finally promoted to Class 1 post in 1970. He was then promoted to Class 11 post in 1971. He was thereafter promoted to Class 12 post in 1973. He was later promoted to Class 13 post in 1974. He was lastly promoted to Class 14 post in 1976. He was thus in Class I service till he attained the age of 60 years. The 1st Respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the note substituted by the order dated 23.12.1967. The High Court held that the 1st Respondent had been discriminated against and that the note was discriminatory and violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. The High court held that the employees of the Corporation belonging to Class I and Class II who had entered service of the Corporation after 1.9, 1956 were not entitled to continue in service beyond the age of 58 years. The High Courts order was upheld by this Court. The 1 st Respondent filed a Writ Petition in this Court challenging the order of the High Court. The High Cour t held that the Corporation was bound to continue the 1st respondent in its service till he completed the age of sixty years. The Corporation was directed to continue the Respondent in its service in Class I post. The Corporation appealed to this Court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The 1st respondent was entitled to continue till he attained 60 years of age. [223E] 1.2 The High Court erred in striking down the note substituted in the order dated 12.12.1977. The HighCourt erred in holding that the employees belonging to Class III and Class IV employees of the Corpo ration belonging to the Corporation recruited after 1.1.1956 were not entitled tO continue in service upto 60 years of service. [223F] 1.3 The 1st respond ent was entitled to be in service till he reached the age of superannuation of 60 years, but the Corporation was directed not to reduce him in service till the age of retirement. [223G] 1.4 The 1stRespondent was entitled to the benefit of the higher age of retirement as provided in the settlement dated 6.6.1965. The appellants wrote a letter to the President of India with copies to the Chief Justice of Punjab and Haryana High Court, the Chief Minister of Haryana and the Chief Justice and the Prime Minister of India. The letter was signed by 15 members of the Bar Association, Bhiwani. In that letter they brought to the notice of the President that Justice D.S. Tewatia of the Punjab and Haryana high Court visited the session division of Bhiwani and inspected the courts from 14 February, 1975 to 19 February, 1975. During the course of the meeting, the learned Judge criticised the Government 's policy in regard to its attitude towards the judiciary. Besides the learned Judge was openly attacking the Government in its political as well as administrative decision. On the whole, he gave an impression that he was not a Judge but a politician who had come to Bar Room. The Judge also said that the prevailing system of Government was not good in this country and the Government was not in a position to take any action in this regard. The appellants took a copy of their letter to the Chief justice of Punjab and H Haryana High Court. The appellants could not see the Chief Justice or the Judges who visited the Judges ' Chambers from 14 February to 19 February. The Registrar of the High Court informed the appellants that the closed cover could reach the Chief Justice on 19 February, that the closed covers could reach the Hon 'ble Chief Justice on 20 February, that he had not seen the Chief Justice. The appellants did not see the Judges ' Chamber and did not see any Judge who was present in the Chamber. The appellants were not present in the Court when the letter was written. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court. A Single Judge of the High court dismissed the petition. The appellants appealed to the Full Bench. The Full Bench held that the letters written by the appellants were correct. The Full Court of the High. Court took the view that the letters were not contempt of Court. The Full. Bench also held that the appellants had committed contempt of Court and the appellants were liable to be proceeded against. The Full 'Bench held that the letter was not a contempt of Court but was a conditional apology. The Full, Bench also held the appellants guilty of contempt of Court for having committed criminal contempt of Court, and sentenced them to simple imprisonment for two months. The appellants came to this Court by special leave. The appellants contended that the letters addressed by the appellants to the President were not in keeping with the well accepted role of a Judge and that the letters did not interfere with due course of justice or proper administration of law by the Courts. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: (1) The letters written by appellants to the Chief Minister, Chief Justice of India, Chief Justice Punjab and Haryana, Chief Justice, Punjab and Haryana of the Punjab High Court, Chief Justice and Chief Justice of the Punjab & Haryana High Court and the Chief Minister in the Punjab and the Chief Justices of the Haryana High Court were addressed to the President and Prime Minister of the country. The letters were addressed to them in the discharge of their duties as Judges of the High Courts. The letters addressed to the Chief Justices and Chief Justices of their respective High Courts were addressed to all the Judges of the respective High Courts. [246 G H] (2) The letters addressed by appellants to Chief Justice of their respective respective High Courts and Chief Justices and the Chief Ministers of their respective States were addressed to Chief Justices and Judges of the Supreme Court. The letters written to the Chief Judges and Judges of their respective Supreme Court were addressed by the Chief Justices to the Chief Ministers and Chief Justices. The Chief Justices and judges of the Supreme Courts were not personally bound by the letter. The letter addressed to the Judges of their Supreme Court was addressed to the Prime Minister, Chief Minister, the Chief Justice, the Chief Justices, the Chief Ministers, the Chief Judges of the Punjab, Haryana and Himachal Pradesh High Courts. They were not personally aware of the contents of the letter. They were also not aware of the reasons why the letter was addressed to them. The Chief Justice of each High Court wrote to the Chief jus tice Judges and Chief Justices in turn wrote to the Judges. The Chief justice of each High. The letters, addressed to the judges of the High, Court and the Supreme Court were written by them in the course of their duties. The letters did not have the imprimatur of the Chief Justice in the case of the Chief Justices. [247 C D] (4) The letters to Chief Justices, Chief Justices and. The respondent assessee was a Jagirdar of the erstwhile State of Oudh. In 1796 there were certain disputes between him and the Zamindars in the district and the matter was referred by the Collector of Benaras to the Board of Revenue. The quantum of the pension was calculated on the basis of 1/4th of the revenue of the Jagir. The pension was paid regularly from year to year by the Government to the respondent. During the previous year of the assessment year 1949 50 the assessee received a sum of Rs. 36,396/ on account of the aforesaid pension. The Income tax Officer held that it was a regular annual income of the assessee and did not fall within the category of agricultural income tax. He observed that in fact this income arose from a statutory obligation of the Government to pay it, and although the Government recouped this from the person with whom the land was settled, land in the genealogical tree of Malikana appeared in the second degree, its immediate and effective source was the Government 's statutory obligation to pay it and this obligation was not land within the meaning of Income tax Act. He accordingly held that the sum of Rs 36,396 was chargeable to tax under the Act as the income was not agricultural income for "although the pension was determined with respect to the quantum of the rent collection the rent collections or the land could not be said to be the immediate source of the pension. The assessee appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner who held that the alleged cash grant of varying and unspecified amount received by the assessee in relation to land revenue of Seyedpur now Tehsil of District Ghazipur clearly fell within the definition of agricultural income under section 2(1) of the Income tax Act and that the source of the income was a liability undertaken by the Government for extinguishing the proprietary rights of the Jagirdar and when the immediate source was not land or rent collections from land, it was difficult to hold that the receipt of the assessee was agricultural income within the meaning Of section 4(3)(viii) of the Act. The assessee 's appeal to the Income tax Appellate Tribunal was dismissed. The High Court held that from the language of the letter of July 7, 1837 it was manifest that the right which was conferred was a right to a share of one fourth in the net land revenue collections after deducting costs of Tahsil establishment. It relied on the fact that the amount which had been received by the successors of the respondent varied from year to years. The High court accordingly answered the question in the negative. The assessee came to this Court by special leave. Held: (i) The income in question was not agricultural Income as defined in the Act. (ii) The source of the allowance or pension was not in the right to receive rent or revenue of agricultural lands, but rests in the covenant in the deed to receive remuneration for management of the trust. The income of the trust appropriated by the appellant as remuneration was not received by him as rent or revenue or agricultural income. (iii) The allowance was in fact a payment of the compensation for relinquishing the title to those lands. (iv) The allowance varied from year

The appellants in Civil Appeal No. 441 of 1981 were appointed as Supervisors 'A ' on various dates between the years 1962 and 1963. They were promoted as Chargeman II on the basis of the seniority cum merit. The respondents in the writ petition were also appointed as Chargeman II. The appellants in Civil appeal No. 441/81 were appointed as Chargeman I on various dates in the year 1964, 1965, 1966 and 1967. The respondents were promoted as Chargemen tals II on the recommendations of the Departmental Promotion Committee. The appellants of Civil Appeal No, 441/81 who were appointed as Chargemen II on various dates during the years 1962 to 1963 were promoted as Foremen II on the recommendation of the Departmental Selection Committee. The respondents of the writ petition who were appointed on various dates as Chargemen I were promoted as chargemen tals on the recommendations made by the Departmental Selection Commit tee. The appellants were promoted as Supervisor 'A ' only on the basis that they were not found fit for promotion. The respondents who were appointed to the post of Chargemen II were promoted as Supervisors II on the basi s of seniority cum merit and the appellants were promoted to the post. The respondents filed a writ petition in the High Court for a direction to the Union of India to promote them to the post o f Chargeman II. A Single Judge of the High Court allowed the writ petition and directed the Union of india to promote the appellants to the post as Chargemen 11. The Union of India filed an appeal against the judgment of the Single Judge. A Division Bench of the High Cour t dismissed the appeal. The appellants filed a Special Leave Petition in this Court. The appellants contended that the direction given by this Court on 2nd February, 1981 had not been complied with in the manner as it ought to have been by the respondents and they should be required to comply with the said direction. The respondents on the other hand contended that the appellants had been discriminated again st by depriving them the benefit of automatic promotion in violation of constitutional guarantee under Article 16 of the Constitution. Allowing the appeals, HELD: 1. The order dated 28th December, 1965 which provided a minimum period of service of three years in the lower grade for promotion to the next higher grade and the circular dated 20th January, 1966 which provided that promotions in future will be made in accordance with the normal rules and not merely on completion of 2 years ' satisfactory service could not be treated to be one affecting adversely any condition of service of the Supervisors ' A '. Its only effect was that the chance of promotion which had been accelerated by the circu lar dated 6th November, 1962 was deferred and made depende nt on selection according to the Rules. The appellants who had been promoted before the coming into force of the order dated 28 th December, 1965 and the circular of 20th January 1966 stood in a class separate from those whose promo tion was to be made thereafter. It is now well settled by the decision of this Court in State of Mysore vs G.B. Purohit that though a right to be considered for prom otion is a condition of service, mere chances of promo tion are not. A rule which merely affects chances of pro mo tion cannot be regarded as varying a condition of serv ice. [103F H; 104A B] Ramachandra Shankar Deodhar and Ors. vs The State of Maharashtra & Ors., [1982] 3 S.C.R. 824, referred to. 2. The Karnataka State Transport Authority granted two permits to the Karnataka State Tourism Development Corporation, one to the Indian Tourism Development Corporation and two permits to Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation. The Karnataka State Transport Corporation filed writ petitions in the High Court challenging the grant of two permits to them. The High Court allowed the writ petitions and set aside the grant of the two permits to Corporation. The State Transport Appellate Tribunal and the High Court dismissed the appeals of the Corporation. The Corporation has filed these appeals by special leave. The Karnataka Government issued a notification under section 63(7) of the , specifying 50 as the number of permits for each State. The Karnataka Transport Undertaking applied for permits under Chapter IV of the Act. The State Government specified 50 as the maximum number of permits. The Karnataka Road Transport Corporation filed an application for grant of two more permits. The State Road Transport Authority granted the two permits. The Corporation filed appeals to the State Transport Appellate Tribu nal. The Tribunal set aside the order of the State Transport Authority and granted three permits to the Corporation. A number of appeals were preferred to the High Court. The High court dismissed the appeals. The Corporation appealed to this Court by special leave against the order of dismissal of the appeals. Dismissing the appeals, the Court, ^ HELD: 1. The High Courts have not correctly interpreted the proviso to section 63(1) of the Act and the proviso to the effect that preference to be given to an applicant for a stage carriage permit from the State Transport Undertaking should be confined to the State Road Transport Undertaking alone. [1016C] 2. The proviso to section 47(1) for example, provides that other conditions being equal, an application for a stage carriages permit from a cooperative society or a person holding a valid licence for driving transport vehicles shall as far as may be, be given preference over applications from individual owners. There is no problem here since the proviso itself says that the rules of preference will apply only if other conditions are equal. [1017B C] 3. The proviso is not unconstitutional. [1018C] 4. The State of Karnataka has not questioned the validity of the fourth clause of the proviso to Section 63(7). [1018D] 5. The State has not questioned its validity. [1019D] 6. The State is not bound to grant a permit to the Corporation because the Corporation has not obtained a permit under Chapter IV. [1020B] 7. The State cannot be compelled to grant a stage carriage to the Corporation on the basis of the rule of preference. [1021B] 8. The State can be compelled to give preference to an applicant who is otherwise eligible for a permit under section 47(I H) of the Karnataka Act. [1022C] 9. The State should be free to grant a contract carriage permit to the State Undertaking. [1023C] 10. The State shall be free to give a contract carriage to the State undertaking on the basis that the State Undertaking has obtained a permit from the Central Government. [1024D] 11. The State may grant a contract Carriage permit to the Karnataka Road Transport Undertaking on the basis if the State Undertaking is in a position to provide a service of the type proposed to be provided by it. [1025B] 12. The State will be free to refuse to grant a Stage Carriage permit to any applicant who does not fulfil the conditions of the proviso. [1026C] 13. The State, if it thinks fit, may grant a stage Carriage permit to a State Transport Undertaking. [1010C] 14. The State and the Corporation shall be entitled to the benefit of the proviso and the proviso shall be deemed to have been inserted in the Act with effect from the date of the notification. [1010D]

The respondent purchased by a registered instrument the business carried on by one Purushottam Raju under the name and style of All India Trading Company. The respondent denied liability to pay sales tax but his contention was over ruled by the Deputy Commercial Tax Officer. The respondent appealed to the Commercial Tax Officer as well as to the Board of Revenue but the appeals were dismissed. The respondent then moved the Madras High Court under article 226 of the Constitution for the issue of a writ in the nature of certiorari to quash the orders of the Commercial Tax officer and the Board of Revenueres. The High Court held that Rule 21 A of the Sales Tax Rules was illegal and ultra vires and the respondent was not liable to pay the sales tax due from his predecessor in title Purushottam. The State Government appealed to this Court. HELD : Rule 21 A was ultra vires of the rule making power of the State Government under section 19(1) and (2) of the Act. The State 's power under section 19 (1) and 19(2) (c) of the is to make rules to carry out the purposes of the Act, but the section cannot be utilised to enlarge the scope of section 10 regarding recovery and payment of tax from some other person other than a "dealer" under the Act. [664 B C] The State Government has no authority under section 19 of the Act to create a legal fiction by which the transferee of the business is constituted as the dealer liable to pay tax in respect of the turnover of the transferor. The word "assessment" in the scheme of sales tax and income tax legislation is a term of varying import. The word is used sometimes to mean the computation of income, sometimes the determination of the amount of tax payable, and sometimes the whole procedure laid down in the Income tax Act for imposing liability on the tax payer. [665 B C] Badridas Daga vs C.I.T. , , followed. The word 'assessment ' used in section 19(2)(c) does not include the power of recovering tax assessed from a person other than the assessee. It follows therefore that Rule 21A is beyond the rule making powers of the State government either under section 19 or section 19(3) of the Sales tax Act. [667 B C] In the context and background of other sections of the Act the word 'assessment" used in section 10 of the principal Act does not include power of recovering sales tax assessed from the person other than assessee. It is not open to the State Government to rely on the instrument inter vivos between the transferor and the transferee and to contend that there is any contractual obligation between the transferee and the State Government who is not a party to the instrument. [669 B C]

The appellant was a jailor in the State of Bombay. He was served with a charge sheet on March 7, 1954, for accepting illegal gratification from a prisoner. The enquiry was held by the Inspector General of Prisons, who found that the appellant was guilty of the charge. The Inspector General of prisons, after giving the appellant a hearing, passed an order on February 2/4, 1955, dismissing him from service. The appellant filed a suit for a declaration that the order of dismissal was illegal and void on the ground that it contravened the provisions of article 311(2) of the Constitution. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court in appeal, held that the failure to supply a copy of the enquiry report amounted to denial of reasonable opportunity contemplated by article 311(1) of the constitution and that the appellant had not been given a copy of it. The appellant came to this Court by special leave. Held, that the appellant could not be said to have been denied reasonable opportunity contemplated under article 311(i) of the Consti tution. The appellant was not aware whether the enquiry officer reported in his favour or against him. Moreover, as pointed out by the High Court, the Inspector General had the report before him and the tentative conclusions arrived at by the Enquiry Officer were bound to influence him, and in depriving the appellant of a copy of his report he was handicapped. The appellant had a right to have a copy of this report supplied to him. The failure to supply the report amounted to a denial of reasonable opportuni ty contemplated by article 31(2) and the appellant was entitled to a decree for arrears of salary. The State of Bombay vs Purushottam jethabai, ; , referred to. The State Of Bombay vs Purshottam jethabhai, ; , distinguished. The State vs Bombay Union of Journalists, ; , and Union of India vs H. C. Goel, ; , , referred to, Held, further, that the failure on the part of the competent authority to provide the appellant with a copy of a report of the Enquiry Officer amounted to denial to him of reasonable opportunity under article 311 (2) of his removal from service. State of Bihar vs Abdul Majid, ; , relied on. The State ' of Bihar vs Abdur Rahim, ; , explained. State of Bombay v Purushottam Jethabhai, [1952] S.C.R. 674, referred to. Held, further that the failure of the competent authori ty to supply the appellant with the copy of the report of the enquiry officer amounted to denial on his part of reasonable opportunity to defend himself under article 311 of the Constitution and the appellant had been rightly convicted by the High court.
