The respondents made an application to the Government of Bihar for exemption from the operation of the rule. The Government granted the exemption. The colleries were in the years 1932 and 1932. The coll Collieries were in the possession of the respondents for several years and the colliery was not in the possession for several years, but the colliery had been in the possession and occupation of the respondents from 1941. The coll colliery was removed from the colliery in the year 1933 and the respondents were in the occupation of the collieries for several years thereafter. The collields were in the management of the respondents. The coll mines were in the coal fields. The respondents filed a suit for recovery of the coll colliery and the collieries. The trial court held that the colliery and colliery were in the colliery from 1941 and the coll collieries were not in the collieries from 1932. The High Court in appeal accepted the finding of the trial court and dismissed the suit. The appellant contended that the coll coll colliery had not been in the collields for several years but had been in possession of it for several years; that the collieries were situated in the coal field and the coll mines were not in possession of them from 1941; that the respondents had not been able to prove that they had knowledge of the coll mines from 1941; and that the coll mines had been in their possession for several months. Held, that the colleries were not in collieries from 1941 and 1932 and the colleries and collieries were within the colliery. Under the Rules the respondents could ask the mining authorities to exempt them from the operation Of the rule. But the respondents could not claim exemption from the rule because they had not been asked to do so. The respondents had not proved that they had the knowledge of the appellant 's encroachment of their coll colliery. Held, further, that the respondents were entitled to the exemption claimed by them. The colli coll coll coll coll mines were within the coal fields and the colli coll mines were situated in them from 1941 and not in the coal mines from 1932. Held, also, that the appellant was entitled to the benefit of section 3 of the Limitation Act. The respondents could ask for exemption from operation of the Rule. The respondents did not prove that they were in possession for several 'years. The collies were in the mining lease from 1941 and were in possession and occupation from 1941. Held, the colliery could not be said to have been in the coal mine from 1941. There was no evidence to show that the collies were not in existence from 1941. In the absence of such evidence the colliery must be deemed to have been under the management of its owner for several years from 1941. Accordingly, the coll colleries and the collies had been in occupation of the coal mines for several years prior to 1941 and the respondents had failed to prove that the colli mines were in possession from 1941. Sundarji Shivji vs Secretary of State for India, (1931) L.R. 58 I.A. 259, referred to. Held, to the contrary, that the finding of fact arrived at by the courts was vitiated by an error of law by the burden of proof having been wrongly thrown on the appellant. The collocation of the words "burden of proof" in section 3 of Limitation Act means that the burden of proving that the person who is alleged to have committed a particular breach is or is not the owner of the property in respect of which the breach has taken place is on that person. The burden of proving the facts essential to the running of the period of limitation is on the party who wants to rely on the abstract doctrine of onus of proof. The onus of proving facts especially within knowledge of a person lies on such a person who would fail if no evidence is given on those facts. The burden is not on the person who wants to avail himself of the general doctrine of onus.

The appellant company was a public limited company and its employees were its employees. The company terminated the services of the appellant on the ground that it was in the habit of taking work from its employees without giving them proper notice or paying them wages in lieu of notice. The appellant raised an industrial dispute and the Government referred the dispute to the Industrial Tribunal. The Tribunal held that the appellant had intended to take disciplinary action against the workmen but subsequently departmental proceedings were dropped and action was taken under r. 18(a) of the Standing Orders. The Tribunal also held that the action taken under r 18(a), was a colourable exercise of the power given under that rule and therefore its action could not be upheld as a bona fide exercise of the powers conferred. The appellant contended that it was entitled under r.18(a) to dispense with the service of any employee after complying with its terms. The respondent contended that it could not be said that the appellant was empowered to take action under r. 17(a) and that having taken action under that rule, there was nothing for it to justify before the Tribunal. Held, that the appellant could not rely on r. 18 (a) and contend that it was not empowered to take any action under that Rule. The Tribunal was right in holding that the appellant did not have the power to take action in this case under r.17(a) as it was not a case of any misconduct on the part of the appellant but of the action taken by it under r. 14(a). Parshotam Lal Dhingra vs Union of India, [1958] S.C.R. 828, relied on. Held, further, that the Tribunal was right that the appellant having acted under r. 16(a) could not be heard to say that the action was not bona fide or was a result of victimisation or unfair labour practice. Held, also, that the industrial court had the right to inquire into the causes that led to the termination of service even under a rule like r. 18. Held, again, that the Industrial Court had the right under r. 19(a) read with r. 18 to enquire into the causes of the termination of the service of the appellant under r. 15(a) which was a term of the contract of employment or the specific service rule and if it was satisfied that the action of the appellant was a colourable or mala fide exercise of power, it would have jurisdiction to intervene and set aside such termination.

The appellant filed a suit against the respondent for a declaration that it was entitled to exhibit motion pictures in the theatre. The suit was based on the claim by Filmistan as lessees or sub lessees of the theatre and was exclusively triable by the Court of Small Causes by virtue of section 28 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947. The trial court held that the agreement dated November 27, 1954, created a lease and that the consent decree in suit No. 149 of 1960 had not decided that the transaction between the parties of the year 1954 was in the nature of a lease. The High Court in revision, held that the evidence as to the true nature of the transaction was not inadmissible by virtue of the provisions of section 92 of the Evidence Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The High Court had no jurisdiction to record any finding on the issue of res judicata in a revision application filed against an order refusing to uphold an objection to certain question asked to a witness under examination. The true nature of an order brought before the High Court and the dimensions of the dispute covered thereby apparently got blurred and the High Court proceeded to decide matters on which no decision was till then recorded by the trial court and which could not be decided by the High Court until the parties had opportunity to lead evidence thereon. The expression "case" is not limited in its import to the entirety of the matter in dispute in an action. F. J. Dillon 's case, [1959] S.C.R. 1332, referred to. The order passed by the High court was set aside and the Trial Court was directed to proceed and dispose of the suit. [441 B C] The true nature and effect of an order of the Court in the course of a suit, is not to be judged by the form which it has in fact taken. The order is not a decision of the Court and the consent decree is merely the record of a contract between the parties to a suit to which is superadded the seal of the Court. A matter in contest in a suit may operate as res judicata only if there is an adjudication by the Court. The order of the High Court is set aside and that of the Trial Court is restored. [442 B C] In the present case, the Court of the Small Causes had only decided that a question seeking information about the true legal relationship arising out of the agreement dated December 1, 1960, was not a case of a lease but of a lease of other character. The Court gave no finding expressly or by implication on the issue. In the view of the Trial court the question whether the legal relationship arising from the agreement dated March 27, 1954 was in 'the nature of a tenancy or of other character had to be decided at the trial and the previous judgment being a judgment by consent, could not operate as res judi cata. A consent decree accord ing to the decisions of this Court does not operate as a res judicata, because a consent decree is only the record of the contract between the par ties to a suit, to which is sui juris. [444 B D]

The respondent was appointed as a Pilot Officer in the State of Uttar Pradesh on contract basis for a fixed term which could be extended from time to time subject to the suitability of the official concerned but not beyond 58 years of age. The Governor of Uttar Pradesh issued a scheme for the benefit of ex military officials. The State Government also adopted the same scheme. Under that scheme the ex military officials were appointed on contract basis, for a fixed period which could be further extended from time tO time subject to suitability of the officials concerned but not exceeding 58 years of the age. The respondent was required to furnish his acceptance of the terms and conditions contained in the order including the term relating to the period of appointment and on his accepting the terms and condi tions he was appointed as Secretary in the District Soldiers Board in the district of Unnao in the State. The respondent challenged the order of termination of his service by filing a Writ Petition before the High Court. The High Court allowed the Writ Petition and directed the re spondent to be reinstated in service. The State of Uttar pradesh filed an appeal by special leave against the order of the High Court, contending that the order of appointment had been issued on the basis of Vigilance Report and no opportunity had been given to the respondent to show cause why such action should not be taken against him. The respondent contended that the order was invalid since it had been issued by the Governor of Uttar pramadesh and that the order could not be sustained and the Writ Petition was liable to be allowed. The State contended that the interim order that had been passed on 10.7.1986 entitled the respondent to be reinstated and that it was open for the State Government to consider the claim of the respondent for continua tion in service or of fresh appointment and no observations in this regard were made by the Court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in disposing of the Writ Petition on 24.3.1988 declaring that the respondent was entitled to salary upto the period he was entitled to remain in service. [243G] 1.2 The true position that emerges from the material on record is that the respondent had not urged before the High court that the order dated 10.7 1986 granting him extension of his service beyond 30th of August, 1985 was in the nature of a contract and the subsequent orders extending his period of appointment till 30th of 8th August, 1985 were liable to be ignored and that he should be treated as a person regularly appointed in Government service entitled to continue till he completed the age of 58 years. [243H, 244A] 1.3 The order passed on review on 26.7.1988 did not make out that the respondent having put forward a case that the interim orders conferred on him a right to continue in service beyond 30 th of August,1985, the High Court was wrong in making an order on review on that basis. [244B] 2.1 The order passed by the High Court on review is wholly unsustainable. The High court had not considered the question whether the interim order conferred a right on the respondent to continue in serv ice beyond 30th August,1985. [244C] 2.2 The order passed in the Writ Petition is set aside and the order passed by this Court on 10.2.1988 is restored. [244D]

The appellant was tried for an offence under section 302 I.P.C. for causing the death of his wife. The prosecution case was that the appellant and his brother, the deceased, were married about one and a half years before the occurrence. About three months before the occurrence the deceased gave birth to a female child in the house of the appellant. After the ninth day the mother and the child, according to customary practice, were taken by the mother of the deceased to her house at Krishna Kalva. The appellant and his mother went away. The deceased was found lying on the ground with a knife in his hand. The appellant was seen by the mother and grand mother of the child, P.W. 1, going towards the house of his mother in law. The appellant went to the house of P.W 1 and asked his mother to send his wife to his house. The mother and the grand mother of P. W. 1 went to the appellant 's house and found him tied to a pole. The appellant, the deceased and P. Ws. 1 to 3 went away. P.W, 1 went to his brother and the brother and the mother of P,W. 1 went away. After the deceased was tied to a peg, the appellant again came to the house and called his mother. The mother of P W. 1, P. W 2 and P.W 3 went to the scene. The appellant again came back to the house. The deceased intervened and interposed herself between P.W I and the appellant. She received a stab injury. She regained consciousness next morning. The appellant regained consciousness in the morning. The Doctor who examined the appellant found several abrasions and contusions on the person of the appellant and the plea of the appellant was one of denial. The Sessions Judge held that the prosecution had failed to establish any motive and that the evidence of the prosecution witnesses was 'discrepant, conflicting and improbable. He thought that the prosecution has made an attempt to improve its case which was originally based on circumstantial evidence to make it appear as if P.W 2 had also seen the stabbing. He observed that the prosecution evidence was more probable than the version of the prosecution. He, therefore, acquitted the appellant. The High Court reversed the finding of acquittal. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High court was justified in commenting that the discrepancies on the basis of which the Trial Court rejected the evidence of P.Ws. 1 to 4 were not at all material. The High, Court was also right in holding that the medical evidence supported the prosecution version and not the defence version. Merely because the Medical Officer stated that the victim could have received the injury if she was standing, it did not follow that the injury could have been received in the circumstances mentioned by the accused. The injury was inflicted with great force and its direction was upward. According to the accused the deceased received the injury when she placed herself between P W.1 and himself. The High 'Court was right in relying on the evidence of PW 1 to 3 which was corroborated by the evidence of PWs 4 and 5 who came to the scene soon afterwards. The High. Court was also justified in holding that there was no good reason to reject the evidence of. PW 3. The High Courts finding that the prosecution version was more probable was not based on any good reason. [368H 369A] 2. The High courts were right in relying upon the evidence of a child witness. The High was justified in relying on her evidence. The High is not right in holding from the medical evidence that the deceased was stabbed when she was lying down. The High has not been shown to be wrong in its appreciation of the evidence. [369B] 3. The medical evidence supported by the evidence. of PW 1 and PW 2, corroborated by the medical evidence, was sufficient to hold that the prosecution case was proved beyond reasonable doubt. [369C] 4. The High in the instant case was justified in interfering with the order of acquittal. [369D] 5. The High had not been shown that the view of the Trial Court was unreasonable or that the Trial Court had taken a view which was not reasonable or that the view taken by the Trial Court could not be said to be unreasonable. [369E] Sanwat Singh & Ors. vs State of Rajasthan, ; , referred to.

The appellant, a Judge of the Supreme Court, was convicted of the offence of criminal misconduct under section 5(1)(e) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for two years. The High Court of Delhi confirmed the conviction and sentence. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court of Punjab and Haryana challenging the validity of the order of his removal from service. The High court dismissed the petition. The appellant came to this Court by special leave. The appellant contended that the order of removal of a Judge of a High Court was not applicable to him as he was a Judge of that High Court and that the provisions of the Prevention Corruption Act, 1988, were not applicable to his case. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The provisions of the Act are applicable to Judges of the Supreme court and the High Courts. The Judge of the High Court is a constitutional functionary appointed under Article 124 and under the provisions of Article 217 of the Constitution. The Judge is a constitutional officer appointed under Article 217 and he is a Judge of this Court. He is a constitutional office. He is not a Judge of any other High Court. He has to be appointed by the President in consultation with the Chief Justice of India. The President may appoint a Judge of one High Court to be a Judge of another High Court. The Judge so appointed is a constitutional functionaries. He is appointed under Article 126 and is not a judge of any other Court. He cannot be removed from his office by the President save by an order of the President passed after an address by each House of Parliament supported by a majority of the total membership of that House and by a majority not less than two thirds of the members of that House present and voting, has been presented to the President in the same session for such removal on the ground of proved misbehaviour or incapacity. The power to punish a High Court Judge, if one may so describe it, is to be found only in Article 218 read with Article 124(4) and (5) of the Constitution, under which a Judge of High Court can be removed from office by an order passed by the President passed on the ground that the Judge is proved to have flagrantly abused his office or misbehaved in the discharge of his duties or he has shown disrespect to the Constitution or the law or has tendered an opinion according to the Constitution which is not in accordance with the law of the land. The power of the President to appoint a Judge under Article 124(1) is not an executive power but a constitutional power. The President is the authority to appoint and remove a Judge of his Court. He exercises this power in his capacity as the head of the State. He is the constitutional head who acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers. He is accountable to the people of the State, to the law of society and to the people. He is answerable to the people and to the law. He is charged with the duty of maintaining the highest standards of probity and propriety in the discharge and performance of his duties. He is also expected to protect the people and the people of India against any encroachment on their rights and liberties. He is required to maintain the highest standards to the people in the country and he is expected to rise above the nexus of a particular State. He has the power to appoint a High Court and to remove a Judge from his office on the ground specified in clause (1) of Article 124. The President, therefore, is the authority competent to appoint and to remove the Judge of the Court. [223E H; 224A B; 225A B] 1.2 The President, in exercise of the power vested under Article 124, is competent to appoint a judge of the Supreme Courts and the High Court. It is not necessary that the Judge should be a member of the Indian Civil Service or should be a person of impeccable integrity and standing having a record of service. The President can appoint a Judge to the Supreme Court and the High court on the basis of the recommendation of the Chief Justice or the Chief Justice, as the case may be. The President has the power under Article 124 to remove a judge of a High court if the Judge is found to be a contumacious, or is in any way, inconsistent with or unfit to continue in office. The President cannot be said to be the appointing authority of a Judge. [225D E; 226A B] 2.1 The power to remove a High Court judge is conferred on the President by Article 217(1) of the constitution. The President in exercise of this power can remove a Judge on the ground mentioned in clause (4) of Article 217. The President under Article 124 is the authority which can remove a High court Judge. The Judge, therefore, cannot be removed by the President except by an order under clause (4). [226C D] 2.2 The power to grant sanction for prosecution of a Judge under the Prevention of corruption Act, 1947, is conferred on a high dignitary of the State and the President is the competent authority to grant sanction in respect of a Judge for the purpose of prosecution. [226E F] 2.3 The President, while granting the sanction under Section 6(1)(c) of the Act, is required to act on the advice and recommendation of the Council. The expression "aid and advice" in Article 74(1) connotes that the Council of Minister must obtain the opinion of the Council on all matters relating to the administration of the State including the measures to be taken for the reduction of the strength of the Court and the like. The President while granting the prosecution sanction under Section 5(1) (c) of Prevention of Corruption, Act, 1947 is required to obtain the advice of Chief Justice of the High Courts and the Chief Justice is required to consult the Chief Justice. The President does not consult the Chief Justices of the High courts. The Chief Justice of a High is the head of a High Courts in India. The Chief justice of India is the head in the Indian Judiciary. The President of India is, therefore, the authority to grant the sanction for prosecution under the Prevention Corruption Acts. [226G H; 227A B] 3.1 The President, under Article 124 of the Constitution is the authority who can remove a judge from his office in accordance with Article 124 of Constitution. He exercises the power of the Supreme in his capacity, as the head or the head of State. He exercises that power in his own right. He is, therefore. the constitutional head of the executive. The President exercises the power under the Constitution not as an executive head but as the head and Chief Justice of High Court. [227B C] 3.2 The Chief Justice is the head and the Chief justice of the High court. He is an officer of the Court in the highest position. He is expected to maintain the dignity and decorum of the Court, and he is the head to see that the decisions of the Court are carried on in accordance with law. [227D E] 3.3 The Chief Justice enjoys the same position as the head. He is in charge of the Court as the head to the Court. He enjoys the confidence of the Court by representing the Court in all matters of importance. He is responsible for the maintenance of the Court 's dignity and decentralisation. He

The appellant was a member of a Scheduled Caste. He was a member in a Scheduled Caste which was a Scheduled Caste in the State of West Bengal. The respondent challenged the appellant 's election on the ground that he was not a member of the Scheduled Caste specified in item 40 of the President 's Order. The High Court held that the appellant was a Sunri by caste but was excluded from the Scheduled Caste group because he belonged to a smaller caste group of Sahas. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The appeal must be allowed. The appellant was a Scheduled caste and had not been proved to belong to the smaller caste group. The respondent called witnesses to establish that the appellant belonged to the smaller group of Sahash. All the courts in West Bengal came to the conclusion that it had not been provided in the case that the appellant had belonged to the larger caste group of the Sahas. The result then was that the appellant must be held to belong to a Scheduled Caste specified as such in item 40. [390 B D] The appellant was not proved to belong, to the smaller Caste group of SahAS. The respondent was therefore not entitled to challenge the appellant ' 's election. [390 E] The appeal must accordingly be allowed. [390 G] The respondent called witness to establish that he belonged to the bigger caste group of Shahas. The appellant called witnesses to prove that he belonged not to the smaller but to the smaller community of Sahas, and the High Court was in error in interpreting the item on the evidence in the case as it appeared to have done. [390 H] The appeal therefore must be allowed and the election petition dismissed. [391 A] The appeal to this court must be allowed on the ground of corrupt practice. [391 B] The respondent was not proved that the appellant did not belong to the larger Caste group of Shahash. The respondent had not been able to prove that the appellant 'did not belong to Shahash. [391 C] The appeal was allowed. [391 D] The respondent had failed to prove that Sahas were a distinct caste group of persons within the Sunri caste. The respondent could not therefore be declared elected. [391 E] The respondent 's election must be set aside. [391 F] The appeal is allowed. [392 A] The respondent is a Sunri and has not been proved that he belonged, to the larger group of Sahans. The respondent 'should be declared elected in the place of the appellant if the latter 's election was found to be invalid. [392 B]

The appellant was the tenant of a flat on the second floor of a building called "Ganga Vihar" Marine Drive, Bombay. The tenancy was a monthly one, the rent being Rs. 215. It was agreed that the appellant would be given a flat on rent of Rs. 215 per month. The appellant wanted to go to the United Kingdom for treatment of his failing eye sight and he got into touch with the complainant through one Sayed for the purpose of making necessary arrangements for the flat. The complainant paid the appellant two sums of money on 7th November, 1948 and 17th November,1948. The appellant was charged under section 18(1) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 for receiving a pugree of Rs. 29,500 and he was further charged under section 19(2) of the Act for receiving the said sum as a condition for the relinquishment of his tenancy. The appellant pleaded that he was in search of a partner to carry on his business and that he was also to act as caretaker of his flat. The Presidency Magistrate, who tried the case, dis missed the appellant 's plea and convicted him under section 19 (2) of Act. The appellant 's appeal to the High Court was summarily dismissed. The appellant came to this Court by special leave. Held, that the word "relinquishment" in section 19(1) Of the Act was not a term of art and was used in its comprehensive meaning as giving up of possession of the premises. The word "re relinquishment" was used in the section not in any strict technical sense but in its comprehensive sense as giving up possession of the promises. The section was not intended to apply to cases where the tenant had parted with possession of the whole or part of the premises in favour of another. The word 'relinquished ' in section 19 (1) of Act was used in a wide sense to include relinquishment of possession by the tenant. The word was used in section 19 in its comprehensive and not in any technical sense. The word relinquishment was used in that sense in section 19 of the Act and the word 're relinquishment ' in section 18 (1) was used in this wide sense in section 18(2) and section 19(3) of the said Act. The word used in section 18 was "relin quished" and not "relinBLE". The word "resistance" in section 18 of the Act was used to mean "relinatory". The word 'resistance ' in section 17(1) was not used in any technical or technical sense but was used in an ordinary sense to mean "to resist". The word was not used to mean 'to resist '. The word in section 19 was used in two parts, namely, "to resist" and "to resist altogether". The word used was "to resist", and the word "to resist was used in both parts to mean "not to resist". The section was intended to apply only to cases where a tenant had parted away with possession of his premises in favour to another. The section did not apply to cases in which the tenant had abandoned possession of the property. The word relinquished ' in section19(1) meant "to relinquish" and not to relinquish possession. The word, "relinchment" in section 17 (1) meant relinquishment of possession. The section in question was not intended by the legislature to apply to a case where the tenant was in possession of the entire premises. The section could not be read as applicable to cases where only one part of the building was occupied by the tenant and the other part was occupied by a tenant who was in possession thereof. The word could not be used to mean that the tenant had surrendered possession of the building in favour of the landlord. The word had to be read in the context of the entire Act and the section was not applicable to cases in the context where only one portion of the building had been occupied by the landlord.

The appellant company, which was engaged in the manufacture of textiles, was maintaining a wage scale of Rs. 200/ per month. The company had a large number of employees who were paid a salary of Rs. 150/ per month, and the company had to pay a salary of more than Rs. 200 per month. In the year 1976, the company had a revision of the wage scales and the company was paying a salary of less than Rs. 150 per month. On the question whether the company was justified in paying a salary less than Rs, 150/ per mensem, the Industrial Tribunal held that the company was not justified in paying the salary of Rs, 150 per month to the employees. The Tribunal directed that the company should pay the salary of the employees at the rate of Rs. 100/ per month and that the company would not be entitled to any increments. The company filed an appeal before the Supreme Court. The company contended that the Tribunal should have fixed the dearness allowance in the revised pay scales and that the Tribunal was wrong in fixing the dearness allowance at Rs. 100 per month. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The Tribunal was right in holding that the company could not bear the additional financial burden. The Tribunal was wrong, in the present case, in holding that a flat increase of Rs.150/ was intended to each workman. [181 B C] (2) The Tribunal had not taken into account the fact that the company had been paying a salary more than Rs, 200/ per mensem. The Tribunal had also not taken into consideration the fact that there was a large number, of employees who had to be paid a salary less. [181 D E] (3) The Tribunal has not taken into the matter the fact that a flat enhancement of Rs. 50/ was intended. [181 F G] (4) The Tribunal should have given a flat increase to each workman in the case of each workman. The Tribunal has relied on the statement of the appellant that a flat increased of Rs. 75/ was intended in the case. The Tribunal did not give any reasons for its conclusion. [181 G H] (5) The Tribunal, in the instant case, considered the matter and found it sufficient and in accord with justice that the wage scales should be restructured with suitable increments provided therein. [182 A B] (6) The award of the Industrial Tribunal was made on December 20, 1978. Thereafter the Tribunal made an order on the same day in the following terms: "There can be no doubt that a flat increases of Rs. 225/ per month to each workman, and that the fitment has also to be done only after the flat increase is added to the present basic salary of each workman". [182 C D] (7) The Tribunal did take into account the circumstances that the appellant had been paying the salary more than the beginning of the grade and that the appellant was not justified to pay more than Rs., 150/ per annum. [182 E F] (8) The Tribunal is not justified in fixing the wage scales of the appellant company at Rs. 150. [182 G H] The award of Industrial Tribunal is set aside and the matter remanded to the Tribunal for fixing the wage scale of the appellant. [183 A] (9) The Tribunal will fix the wage scale in accordance with the principles laid down in the award. [183 B] (10) The Tribunal would fix the dearness allowance on the basis of the present cost of living index. [183 C] (11) The Tribunal may fix the dearness allowances on the basis that the appellant is a profit making company. [183 D] (12) The Tribunal shall fix the dearness pay of each workman on the basis, of the present wage scale. [183 E] (13) The Tribunal 's direction that the company shall pay the salary at the rate Rs. 100.00 per month and the company shall not be entitled, to any increments, is set aside. [183 F G] The award is set aside, and the matter is remanded to the Industrial Tribunal for fixing a fair and just wage structure. [183 G H] [The Court directed that the appellant should pay the difference between the salary and dearness allowance as per the present wage structure.] [184 A] (14) The Tribunal directed the company to pay the salary to the employees at Rs. 50.00 per mensem and that the Company would not be liable to pay any increments. [184 B] (15) The Tribunal held that a flat rate of Rs, 50/ was not justified. [184 C] (16) The Tribunal fixed the dearness pay at Rs. 75.00 per day. [184 D] (17) The Tribunal also directed that the Company should pay the dearness allowance to the employees on the basis as if the appellant was a profit making Company. [184 E]

The respondent, an industrial dispute, was referred to the Industrial Tribunal for adjudication. The Tribunal held that the respondent was not entitled to the payment of wages at the rate of Rs. 2/ per day and that the refusal of the appellant to pay the same amounted to an illegal deduction from the wages. The appellant challenged the award before the High Court. The High Court held that the award did not amount to a contract of employment and that the claim of the respondent was barred by limitation. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: The appeal must be dismissed. The terms in question are not express and can be implied. But they must be terms which arise out of the contract of employment, and since an award made by an Industrial Tribunal cannot be said to amount to a con tract of employment, the wage structure prescribed by the award cannot fall within the definition prescribed by section 2(vi) of the Act. [422 B] The true legal position is that when industrial disputes are decided by industrial adjudication and awards are made, the said awards supplant contractual terms in respect of matters covered by them and are substituted for them. That being so, it is difficult to accede to the argument that the wages prescribed by the Tribunal cannot be treated as wages under section 2(v) of the Industrial Disputes Act before it was amended. [421 B] South Indian Bank Ltd. vs A. R. Chacko, A.I.R. 1951 Cal. 29, applied. Jogendra Nath (1) A.I,R. 1964 S.C. 15, followed. The South Indian Bank (2) A.T.R. , distinguished. South Indian Bank vs A.R. Chacko A.I.,R. , referred to. The result is, the appeal must be allowed. The appellant should be directed to pay the costs of the respondent.

The appellant was a Sub divisional Officer in the service of the State of Punjab. He was charged with criminal misappropriation of funds and was convicted by the trial Magistrate. The High Court, on appeal, held that the prosecution was not maintainable for want of sanction under section 197(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure for his prosecution. The appellant contended that the charge was one of misappropriation and not of criminal misappropriation and that sanction under section197(1) was necessary for his prosecution under that section. Held, that the charge under section 409 was not one of misappropriation but of criminal misappropriation. The appellant was not charged with criminal misappropriation and was not convicted for the same. The appellant received the sum of Rs. 51, alleged to have been misappropriated, as Sub divisional officer, and he admitted receipt of the same. He did not claim to have paid the amount to the khalasi, and the acquittance roll records the payment, and there was in acknowledgment thereof a thumb impression as against his name. The appellant did not claim that he paid the amount himself. The acquittance rolls were not produced in the case. The appellant could not be convicted for the offence of criminal misappropria tion unless he was able to prove that he had paid the amount. The appellant had not been able to prove his case. The conviction was illegal. Hori Ram Singh vs Emperor, (1943) L.R. 70 I.A. 216, distinguished. The appellant, as a public servant, was not entitled to the protection of section 197(I) of the Criminal Procedure Code, as he was not a public servant at the time of the alleged offence. The appellant 's conviction was illegal as sanction under section I5(1) Of the Code of Civil Procedure was not necessary for his conviction under section 409. The appellant should have been acquitted. The appellant cannot be convicted for criminal misappropriations unless he proves that he had received the amount from the khalashi. The appellant is not entitled to be acquitted on the ground that the charge against him was one of criminal misappropriation or criminal misappropriat. The appellant has not been able, to prove his claim that he had made the payment to the kahasi. The appellant must be acquitted. Hori Rain Singh vs Emperor (1943] L.R, 70 I. A. 216, referred to. The appellant having been acquitted by the High Court, the appellant could not have been convicted for the offences of criminal mis appropria tion and criminal breach of trust. The appellant bad not been able 'to prove his case that he had actually received the amount. He could not be held guilty of criminal mis misappropriation unless he could prove that he bad actually received the money.

The appellant, a Bank, was carrying on business at its head office in Cochin State and carried on business in the State of Cochin and also in the State in which the head office was situate. The assessment year was 1950 51, the corresponding accounting year being the year ending June 30, 1949. The appellant claimed that the loss incurred in the State was a loss in the State and was entitled to deduct it from its profits in British India. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax Officer. The Appellate Tribunal, however, held that the loss was not deductible from the profits of the appellant in British India and that the appellant was entitled to deduction of the loss from its profits. The High Court, on a reference, held that section 32(1) proviso (1) of the Travancore Income tax Act, which was in pari materia with section 24(1) of Indian Income tax Act was applicable to the appellant and that the loss in the appellant 's business was not deductible in British India, and that the profits and gains of the appellant were not taxable in British India under section 10 of the Indian Income tax. Held, that the words " business " in section 10 of Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, do not mean business in British India or business in an Indian State or so divide business, but mean business in the two territories, i.e., British India and the Indian States. The use of the words " loss of profits or gains " in section 24(2) of the Indian Act, which is in pari materia to section 10 of Travancore Income tax, is not sufficient to restrict the scope of the proviso to the profits and losses of business in the Indian States, i. e., British India. In re: Mishrimal Gulabchand, , relied on. Per Das, C. J., and Bhagwati, J., The proviso to section 24(i) of the Income Tax Act is not a proviso to section 10(1) but is a proviso to the main section. The proviso is not a substantive provision but is only a proviso to a substantive provision. The proviso, therefore, is not a provision which is controlled by the main provision and is not controlled by the proviso. The proviso to the section is not a new provision but is a substantive provision and is applicable to the assessment year 1950 51. The words " where the loss sustained is a loss of profits and gains " in the proviso to section 14(2) (e) of the Act are not words of limitation but of a qualified proviso and are not words which are to be read in the proviso. Per Sarkar, J. The proviso was not a proviso in the main section and was not a substantive section. The words used in the proviso were " where the business, profession or vocation in respect of which the loss sustained was a loss of profit or gains " and not " business ". The use in the proviso of the words loss of profits " or gains " to be set off against profits and gains would not be sufficient to restrict its scope. The proviso could not be used to limit the scope of section 10 of Income tax Act. The proviso must be construed harmoniously with the main enactment and if the language of the main enactment is clear it cannot be used for the purpose of interpreting the proviso or to exclude by implication what the enactment clearly says unless the words of the proviso are such that that is its necessary effect. The proper function of a proviso is to except and deal with a case which would otherwise fall within the general language of the principal enactment and its effect is confined to that case. The proper rule of construction is that a proviso must be considered with relation to the principal matter to which it stands as proviso. The proper test is not whether in enacting the proviso Parliament intended to restrict the enacting part of the section but whether by enacting the proviso, the legislature has expressed that intention. The proviso in the present case was not a new proviso but was a substantive provision which was applicable to assessment year 1950 50. The proviso did not apply to the assessment years 1951 52 and 1952 53 and the proviso was not applicable to the present assessment year. The proviso applied to the assessment of the appellant for the assessment year 1951 52 and not to the assessment for the assessment years 1952 53 and 1953 54. The proviso had to be read with the main provision of section 10(i) and not with the proviso.

The respondent company was incorporated in 1946 as a Private Limited Company to take over the business of the partnership firm of the Shaw Wallace & Co., which had been doing business in India for about 60 years. In July 1947 the private limited company was converted into a Public Limited Company. The Head Office of the company was at Calcutta. The general practice of the company both at the Head Office and the Branch Offices was to retire its employees at the age of 55. In September 1959 an agreement was entered into between the company and its employees at Calcutta under which the age of retirement was extended to 58 years subject to the employees passing a medical examination on reaching the age of 60. Shortly after this the company 's employees at Bombay raised a dispute regarding their retirement age. The Tribunal directed that the age of superannuation should be 58 but the company may in its discretion and with the express or implied consent of the employee continue an employee after he had attained that age. The company appealed to this Court by special leave. HELD: (i) The Tribunal was right in holding that the company was an All India concern and that changing the age of retire ment in one place might unsettle the uniformity and might have serious repercussions in other branches. The Tribunal had found that in all the awards in recent times in the Bombay region the trend had been to fix the age of retiring age at 60. But on a closer examination it was clear that this document was of little assistance for finding out the recent trend. [428 B D] Imperial Chemical Industries (India) Private Ltd. vs The Workmen, ; , referred to. (ii) The Tribunal had rightly rejected the company ' 's case on the ground that the trend in Bombay region had been to fixed the age of 58. The Tribunal was not justified in taking into account the fact that the company had kept the age of the retirement at 55 or 58. [429 B C] (iii) The Tribunal 's present conclusion that what was said by itself on an earlier occasion and was confirmed by this Court was in fact inaccurate, was not correct. [430 B C] Dunzlop Rubber Co. Ltd. vs Workmen, ; ; , referred. (iv) The Tribunal considered it to be its duty to enquire whether the conclusion recorded by this Court in some of its earlier decisions was accurate. Having embarked an this enquiry the Tribunal had taken considerable pains to perform this duty and it had ultimately persuaded itself to hold that no such trend was established in fact. [432 B C]

The appellants were the managing agents of a company which was a subsidiary of a public limited company. The Board of Directors of the company was constituted under section 237(b) of the Companies Act, 1913. The Board was to consist of a Chairman, a Managing Agent, a Secretary and a Treasurer. The Chairman was to be appointed by the Central Government. The Board had the power to appoint an Inspector to investigate the affairs of a company. The Chairman of the Board was to be a person who was or was not a member of the Board. The Chairman and the Secretary were to be appointed from amongst the members of the Board and the Chairman was to hold office for a term of three years. The Chairman, however, was to be paid a salary of Rs. 1,000 per month. The Chairman had the power of appointment of a Managing Agent. The Chairman appointed the appellants as the Managing Agent of the company. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Chairman. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the Chairman was not a person who could exercise the power of the Board under section 237 (b) and that the order was invalid because it was made by the Chairman who was not a Board. HELD: (i) The Chairman of a company is not a person within the meaning of section 237(a) of the Act. The power to appoint a Managing Agent is conferred on the Central Government under section 237. The Central Government has power to constitute a Company Law Board and to delegate its functions to the Board. [342 C] (ii) The power under section 237 is not a delegation of its authority. The power under that section is to be exercised by the Board independently of any rules framed by the Central Govern ment. The power is to be delegated to the Board independently. The Board has the power to distribute the business of the Board amongst the members. The power of the Central Government to make an order under section 237, is not a power which is conferred on it by section 237(1). [342 E F] (iii) The power to distribute business among the members of a company 's Board is not a delegated power. The power conferred by section 237 is to be read as a power conferred on the Board to be exercised in the same manner as the Board can exercise it. The power can be exercised by a Board consisting of two or more members. The Board is not constituted by the members of one company alone. The Board can exercise the power conferred on it independently of any of the rules framed by it. The Board cannot delegate its functions except with the consent of the Board, and the power to make an appointment of an Inspector is not conferred on the Chairman. [343 B C] (iv) The power conferred on a company by section 237 (a) is not a delegate of the Board but is a power conferred by the Board on the Chairman to be exercised independently of any rule framed by the Board. It is not possible to accept the contention that the Chairman is a delegate of his own authority. The Board may be a body corporate with a perpetual succession and a common seal. The power may be exercised by it only in the case of a Board. The power must be exercised by that body or authority which is competent to exercise it. [343 D E] (v) The power of delegation under section 237 can be exercised only by the Board and not by the Chairman. If the Board is a body corporate it can only be a body or authority exercising the power of a Board and not a Chairman. [344 A B] (vi) The power given to the Chairman under section 237 to distribute the work of the Board among the members is not a delega tion of his own power. The Chairman is not a Board and the power given to him is not a discretionary power. [344 C] (vii) The power is not a discretion. The power given by section 237 can only be exercised by an authority which is a Board. [344 D] (viii) The power can only be delegated to a Board consisting not only of the Chairman but also of the members. [344 E] (ix) The power cannot be delegated to an individual member. The power has to be exercised only in the manner provided in section 237(2). The power can also be delegated to any other person. [344 G] (x) The power must, therefore, be exercised by such authority as may be empowered by the Act. [344 H] (xi) The power could not be delegated to one of the members of another company. The power could be delegated to another member of the company and not to a member of another company, and the Chairman could not delegate his power to another member. [344 F] (xii) The power was not delegated to the Chairman. He was not a delegate. [344 B] (xiii) The power has been delegated to the Managing Agent. He was to be the Chairman of the company, and not to any other member. The Chairman could not exercise the power. [345 A B] The power to make appointment of an inspector is not conferred by section 235. The power cannot, therefore, he delegated to the Secretary. [345 B] (xiv) The power may not be delegated by the Chairman to any other officer. The power, however, can be delegated to such other officer as may be authorised by the Chairman in this behalf. [345 C] (xv) The power, if any, can be exercised in any of the ways mentioned in section 237. [345 D] (xvi) The power in the present case could not be exercised by any other person except the Chairman. It could not be said that the Chairman could delegate his power. [346 A] (xvii) The power would be exercised by him independently of any statutory rules. The power was to be exercised with the consent and approval of the Board of Directors. The power would not be delegated unless the rules were framed. The power in this case could not, therefore, have been delegated to any one of the other members of the company as the Board was not a body corporate. [348 C D] (xviii) The power had been delegated to a person who had been appointed by the Board to act as its Chairman. The power had not been delegated to anyone else. The power did not, therefore have to be delegated. [349 C] (xix) The power should be read as delegated to the other members. The other members of a Board could not delegate their power to the Chairman of another Board. [340 D] (xx) The power might be delegated to some other person. But the power could not have been delegated unless the rule making power was exercised by the Chairman of a Board consisting only of the members and not by any other member of the other Board. [349 A B] In the present case, the power could have been delegated by the Board consisting of the Chairman and the other members to the Managing Agents. The power might have been delegated in the present circumstances to the Managing Director. The power should have been delegated only to the Managing agent. [349 C D]

The appellants were convicted under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to 5 years ' rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs. 1,000/ each. The High Court, and the Court below, drew from this the conclusion that the appellants were themselves the dacoits and convicted them accordingly under section 395. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The law advocated by the appellants is not correct. If there is other evidence to connect an accused with the crime itself, however small, the finding of the stolen property with him is a piece of evidence which connects him further with the crime. There is then no question of presumption. The evidence strengthens the other evidence already against him. It is only when the accused cannot be connected with the crime except by reason of possession of the fruits of crime that the presumption may be drawn. In what circumstances the one presumption or the other may be drawn, it is not necessary to state categorically in this case. It all depends upon the circumstances under which the discovery of the fruits is made with a particular accused. It has been stated on more than one occasion that if the gap of time is too large, the presumption that the accused was concerned with the crime gets weakened. The presumption is stronger when the discovery of fruits of crime is made immediately after the crime is committed. The reason is obvious. disposal of the fruits requires the finding of a person ready to receive them and the shortness of time, the nature of the property which is disposed of, that is to say, its quantity and its character determine whether the person who had the goods in his possession received them from another or was himself the thief or the dacoit. In some cases there may be other elements which may point to the way as to how the presumption may he drawn. They need not be stated here for they differ from case to case. [723 B D] (ii) The evidence on record is not sufficient to show that the appellants had been in possession of the goods in their possession. The houses of 20 persons were searched and large quantities of the stolen goods were found. It is impossible to think that these 20 persons were merely receivers of stolen property from some other 20 persons who were the dacoits. It is legitimate therefore to raise the presumption in this case that the persons with whom the goods were found were the dacoits themselves. [724 B D]

The petitioners, who were manufacturers of 'thinner ' containing spirit and other soluble material, challenged the constitutional validity of Section 5 of the (12 of 1919) (hereinafter called 'the Act ') and the validity of the (13 of 1973) (hereinafter referred to as 'the Amending Act ') on the ground that the section gave an unguided, unchall ed and arbitrary power to the State Government to include any substance as poison for the purpose of restriction to be imposed on the posses sion for sale and sale of the same. The petitioners contended that the Act was a Central enactment and it was possible of unjust and unjustified discriminatory application as it was left to each State Government to determine what substance they would include as poison and regulated and the decision in one State to include the substance as poison was not automatically made applicable to the other States. The petitioners also contended that the restriction imposed on possession for sale and sell was not reasonable restrictions. Dismissing the petition, HELD: 1. The Act is intended to regulate the importation, possession and sale of poisons. Some substances were included in the Rules made in 1926 as poisons and that is not in dispute. Section 5 of Act, which deals with presumption and states that any substance specified as a poison in a Rule or noti fication issued under the Act shall be deemed to be a poison for the purposes of the Act. Rules of 1926 were made in exercise of the rule making power under Section 3 of the Act and that section enables the State Government by Rule to regulate the posses tion of any specified poison in any local area in which the use of such poison for the pur pose of committing murder or mischief by poisoning cattle appears to it to be of such frequent occurrence as to render restriction on the poss essor of such poison desirable. Any substance which is used for purposes mentioned therein can definitely be declared as poison. That is what the Government have done in this case. It has become a notorious fact, which is notorious, which is also the case of the petitioners. [223E H] 2. The nature of trade in poison is such that nobody can be considered to have an absolute right to carry on the same. It is a busi ness which can be termed even as inherently dangerous to health and safety of society in view of the rampant misuse and sale to the poor, weak and helpless as an intoxicant. A law in such circumstance can regulate the trade. This position is well settled and it would be pedantic to cite all the authorities of this Court on this point. [223H, 224A]

The appellants were partners of a firm carrying on business in Bombay. The firm was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1952 53. The Income tax Officer disallowed the claim of the appellants to deduct a sum of Rs. 2,68,385/ as bad debt due to the appellants from the firm as irrecoverable in their money lending business. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax Officer. The Income Tax Appellate Tribunal confirmed the order. The High Court, on a reference, held that the debt was not a bad and doubtful debt in its money lending business not a debt representing loss sustained in the other business. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The debt in question was not sent to the Bombay firm as loans made in the ordinary course of money lending business nor in respect of any other business of the assessee. The Tribunal has found that the monies sent by the assessee to the Bombay firms were not loans made in ordinary course of the money lending business of the appellants nor in respect Of any other business. The Tribunal, therefore, was right in holding that the debt in question did not arise in the course of the assessee 's business as Chemists and Druggists nor in the course Of their money lending. [419 B D] (2) The Tribunal has not raised any inference from the circumstances and has merely observed that charging of interest cannot make it a money lending account. [419 E] (3) The statement of the case submitted by the Tribunal is not a catalogue of the arguments advanced at the bar. It contains only a summary of the business relations between the appellants and the Bombay firm, a statement as to the amounts due at the end of each year at the foot of the account, the interest if any charged and a summary of orders made by the Income tax officer, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Tribunal. [419 F G] (4) The Tribunal had found that the moneys sent by the appellants to the Bombay Firm were not loans but were loans made in their ordinary course of business. The finding of the Tribunal was not supported by proper discussion of the material before it. [419 G] (5) The Tribunal was right in reframing the question referred to it. [420 B] (6) The Tribunal, in the circumstances of the case, was right that the sum in question was a bad and Doubtful debt in the assessee ' 's money lending business and was not a debt represented by loss sustained in other business. [420 C] (7) The Tribunal found that the money sent by the appellant to the Bombay 's Bombay firm was not loans made by the appellant in the ordinary ' course of his money lending business, nor in respect ' of any other 'business of the assessee, and that the sum was not a 'bad debt ' in its money ' lending business. [421 A]

The petitioners were the owners of certain lands which were acquired by the respondents under the provisions of the Bangalore Act. The awards were made on September 20, 1984. The petitioners obtained an interim order from this Court directing status quo with regard to the possession of the lands in question in Special Leave Petition No. 294 of 1985 preferred against the order of the Karnataka High Court dated August 14, 1984, with which this Court was not directly concerned. The said Special Leave Petition was dismissed on April 29, 1987. The petitioners filed two writ petitions challenging the acquisition on the ground that the awards were not made within the stipulated time. In these two writ petitions, the Karnataka High court granted interim stay of further proceedings in respect of the acquisition of the said lands. These petitions were dismissed by a Single Judge of that High Court on November 29, 1988. Appeals against the decision of a Single Judge were dismissed by the Karnataka High. The petitioners preferred Special Leave Petitions against the decision in the Special Leave Petitions. The petitioners contended that as the awards in these cases had not been made within two years of the notification making the declaration under Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act, the entire acquisition proceedings had lapsed. Dismissing the petitions, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The fact of the stay orders was highly material in the determination of these Special Leave Petitions and the non disclosure of the same certainly amounts to suppression of material facts. [566C] 1.2 The interim orders have a direct bearing on the question raised and the non furnishing of the same definitely amounts to suppression. [565C] 1:3. The fact of stay orders was very material in the determinations of these Special leave Petitions. [567B] 1.4. The fact that the stay orders were obtained by the petitioners by practising fraud on the Court is of no consequence. [568B] 1:5. The fact whether the stay orders obtained by the petitioner by practising fraud is material or not is a matter of fact which has to be established by the petitioners. [569B] 1 :6. The fact, that the stay order was obtained by the peti tioners by practising fraud, is of no consequences. [570C] 1 :7. The fact as to whether the stay order obtained by the petition er by practising fraud was material or not, is a matter which has to he established by the petitioner. [575C] 1 8. The fact is that the stay was obtained by practising fraud. [549D] 1:7. The petitioners have not disclosed the fact that the awards in the cases were not made by the Land Acquisition Officer within the stipulated period. [548E] 1:8. The fact remains that the awards have been made within the time prescribed. [545F] 1:9. The fact the stay orders have been obtained by the petitions by practising fraud cannot be a ground for not disclosing the facts. [547B]

The appellant bank was a bank which was a subsidiary bank of the Punjab National Bank. The appellant bank was governed by the Punjab National bank (Employees) Pension and Guarantee Fund Rules, 1952. The appellant Bank was a nationalised bank and was governed by these rules. The appellant was a bank governed by the State Bank of India (Supervising Staff) Service Rules, 1960. The appellant had a branch office at Delhi and branches at various places in India. The appellant made a request to the Punjab National Tribunal for revision of pay scales of its employees. The Tribunal allowed the claim of the appellant bank. The appellant contended that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to entertain the claim. The respondent contended that the appellant was not a bank governed under the State Bank 's Pension and Guarantee Funds Act, 1961 and that the Tribunal was not competent to entertain the appellant 's claim. The Tribunal held that the appellant bank was not a "bank" as defined in section 2(1) of the Act and that the appellant had no jurisdiction under the Act to entertain the claims. The Tribunal further held that the claim of appellant bank was barred by limitation. The Tribunal also held that the Tribunal did not have jurisdiction to entertain a claim for revision of scales of pay. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The Tribunal was right in holding that the appellant Bank was not a 'bank ' as defined in the State Bank Act. The appellant 's case was that once the maximum arrived at by point to point adjustment as on January 1, 1962 was reached under cl. (ii) of the Desai award, no further increments even under sub cl. (1) (d) of cl. (iv) could be allowed. [904 C] (ii) The appellant bank claimed that under cl. 2(ii) of Desai award the adjusted basic pay in the new scale was not to exceed what point to point fitment would give an employee on January 1. 1962. The appellant could not be allowed to raise this contention for the first time in this Court. [905 B] (iii) The appellant had no right to raise this question for the first two years after the date of the award. The appellant did not raise this question in the High Court. The appellant raised this question in this Court for the first three years after the award. [906 B] (iv) The appellant was not entitled to any relief from the labour court. The award of the labour court was correct. [907 C] (v) The appellant could have raised the question of limitation before the labour court and the labour court would have been bound to give the appellant a decision on the question of law. [908 C] (vi) The appellant did raise the question of jurisdiction of the Tribunal to entertain the application for revision of the scales of pay of its employees and the Tribunal was right that the appellant should have raised the same before the labour Court. [907 C] (vii) The appellant ' was not entitled under the State bank 's Pension Fund Rules to claim revision of scales. The appellant claimed revision of scales on the basis of the award of the Labour Court. The Tribunal was wrong in holding that it was not open to the appellant to raise the question that the Tribunal has no jurisdiction to decide the question of revision of scales because the appellant was a nationalised Bank. [907 D E] (viii) The appellant claimed that the Tribunal should have given the appellant a direction to the effect that the appellant would be entitled to increments under sub cl.(d) of el. (iv). The appellant could claim increments under sub el. (d) only if it was entitled to increments on the basis that it was entitled under sub cl (i) to increments on account of having worked as a bank employee. [907 F] (ix) The appellant would not be entitled to any increments under sub cls. (b) and (c) of cl.(iv) of the State Bank Service Rules. The appellant would be only entitled to two increments under sub clause (d) for the years 1960 and 1961 and his salary as on January, 1962 would be Rs. 182. The appellant thus would not be able to get increments under sub clauses (b) & (c) for the year 1960 and 1961. [907 G] (x) The appellant should have been given the benefit of the increments under subcl. (d). [908 H]

The Government of West Bengal, in exercise of its powers under the Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act, 1949, transferred the land belonging to the Zoo to the Taj Group of Hotels. The Taj Group of hotels, in turn, transferred the lands to the Government of West Bangal. The Government of West Benga tal, in exercise, of its powers, under the CalcuttaThika Tenancy Act 1949, transferred to the Taj group of Hotels, the lands belonging to the Government. The Government also transferred to the Government the lands belonging, to the Zoological Garden. The Government, in turn transferred to the Zooo group of Hotels the lands belonging the Zoo. The Government was also the owner of the land. The Government had also the right to dispose of the land by way of lease. The Government took a decision to lease the land to the Zoloo group of hotels. The Government issued a lease deed in favour of the Government. In the lease deed, the Government stated that the land was to be used for the purpose of acclimatization only. The Government further stated that the Government had the right to construct the Five Star Hotels and the land was not to be leased to anyone. The Government 's case was that the land could not be leased to the Zola Group of Hotels without inviting tenders from willing persons and without complying with the requirements of para 166 of the Land Manual. The lease deed was executed by the Government in favour of Government. The land could not, however, be leased to any one. The Government contended that the land had been leased to the Government for a specified number of years and that the land should be used for a public purpose. The lease was for a specified period and the Government had no right to lease the same to anyone. It was further contended that the Government was not the owner of land but the Government of the Zoo and that the Government did not apply its mind to relevant facts before disposing of the land in discharge of the public interest. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Government of India had no power to transfer the land to a private party and that the lease deed was not a lease by the Government. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The public interest litigation is a remedy for the enforcement of a legal right, not for the purpose ot enforcement of a private right. The Supreme Court, in exercise its jurisdiction under Article 32, has the power to issue a writ of mandamus or a writ in the nature of mandamus or any other appropriate writ, order or direction to any person or authority, directing them to perform any of the functions which is properly vested in them. [277C D] 1.2 The public interest litigations are not in the nature, of adversarial litigation but are essentially of a private character where by reason of the nature of the functions and duties of the State, the interest of the people in general and the revenue of the State as a whole is involved. The Court is not a con cerned with the merits of the dispute between the private parties in litigation. The dispute between the parties is only in regard to the lease of the land to be granted to the Zonoo Group of Hotels and the question of the title to the land is not involved in the dispute. [277E G] 1.3 The Government of India, in its affidavit, has stated that the lease was granted to the Government in exercise of the power under the Calcutta Land Reforms Act, 1955. The Government has also stated that the lands were leased to the State Government for a period of five years. The Government is the owner of all the lands. The Government cannot, therefore, be said to have no right to the land. [278B C] 1.4 The Government has the right to lease out the land to any one but the Government has no right to transfer the lease to anyone. [278D] 1.5 The Government has a right to dispose the land by public auction or by inviting tenders. The Government can transfer the land either by way of public auction or on lease. The assessee, a Hindu undivided family, was carrying on business of banking and had a branch office in Delhi. The assessee was a partner in a firm which carried on the business of banking. The assessee gifted certain amounts to his sons and grand sons and the balance of the amount was credited to the account of the donees. The assessee claimed that the amounts had been gifted by him to his sons by transfer entries in the books of account of the firm and by his letter dated 1.1.1957. The Income Tax Officer rejected the assessee 's claim and held that the amounts were validly gifted by him. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Tribunal upheld the order of the Income Tax Officer. The High Court, on a reference, held that the assessee did not make valid gifts aggregating Rs.1,50,000 on 1.1 .1957. The High Courts decision in the case of India Glass Agency vs Commissioner of Income Tax, New Delhi, was overruled by the Supreme Court in the case Commissioner of Income tax, Ahmedabad vs Digvijaysinghji Tin Factory, ; New India Colour Co. vs Commissioner of income Tax, New Deihi, ; New Delhi Municipal Committee vs Commissioner of Wealth Tax, Delhi, ; Commissioner of Wealth tax, U.P.v. Smt. Shyamo Bibi, ; and Commissioner of Wealthtax vs Gulab Rai Govind Prajapati, ; , and that the assessee had made a valid gift of the amount to his sons. The assessee contended that a total sum of Rs.1.50,000 was validly gifted by the assessee to his sons, and hence the amounts had rightly been included in his net wealth by the Income Tax officer and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Revenue contended that the said sum was properly included in the assessee ' s net wealth by Income Tax Officer and the Appellate Asstt. Commissioner. The Tribunal held that there was no valid gift. The High court, on a Reference, affirmed the view of the Tribunal. The assessee appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in holding that the assessee was not entitled to the benefit of section 10 of the Income tax Act, 1922, as the amounts had not been gifted to his sons on 1. 1. 1957. [129F] 1.2 The High Court had rightly held that the gifts were valid. [129G] 1.3 The High Court has rightly held that there is no completed gift of the principal amount as there was no registered deed and as there was a gift of Rs.2 lakhs to each of the sons, the gift was valid. [130B] 1.4 The Tribunal had rightly held in the instant case that the gifts in question were valid. The High courts decision in the instant cases is affirmed. [130C] 1.5 The High Court in the instant appeals has rightly held, that the assessee has made a valid gifts of the amount of Rs.50,00,000 to his sons which was available to him on the date of the gifts. [130D] 1.6 The High Court rightly held that in the instant ease, the assessee had not made a valid transfer of the amount gifted to his son. [130E] 1.7 The High Court held that the amount of the gift was not properly included in his income. [130F] 1:8 The High Court correctly held that the gift was invalid. [130G] 1:9 The High Court also correctly held that there were no valid gifts. [131B] 1:10 The High Court did not accept the contention of the assessee that the amount was gifted to his wife and son. [131C] 1:11 The High Court accepted the contention of assessee that the amounts gifted to his two sons were not valid gifts. Court rightly held on the facts that the amount is not properly includible. [131G] 1 :15 The High Court considered the question whether there was a valid gift or trust in respect of the said amounts. [131H; 132A] 1:16 The High Court further held that the sum of Rs,1,50.000 could not be included in the net wealth of the assessee because the said amount was not gifted to his daughters.
