The appellant, a judicial officer, was posted as a member of the Orissa Superior Judicial Service. He was promoted as a District and Sessions Judge and was posted as Additional District and Sessions judge. In the year 1964, he was posted as an Additional District and Session judge. In February 1965, the High Court took a policy decision to the effect that as a general rule, judicial officers working in special posts whether cadre or non cadre outside their regular line should be recalled to the regular line after the completion of three years. The High Court was anxious that a judicial officer occupying one of the administrative posts should not, in the interest of judicial work, continue in that post for an unduly long time. The High court insisted that ordinarily judicial officers should not hold those posts for more than three years. In view of article 229 of the Constitution, the power to appoint the Registrar of the High Court was exclusively that of the Chief Justice. Neither the High Court as such nor the Governor had any hand in his appointment. The power to appoint a judicial officer was exclusively that which the Chief Justice had under article 229 of Constitution. Neither the Government nor the High Court could have posted any officer as the Registrar of that High Court as that post could be filled only by the Chief Justice and not by the Governor. The High Courts were anxious that a Judicial officer occupying one or the other administrative posts should be transferred to the regular post. The High courts were anxious that the officers should not be kept away from judicial work for a long time. In view, of the decisions of this Court in State of West Bengal vs Nripendra Nath Bagchi, ; and State of Assam vs Ranga Mahammad, ; , the High Court insisted that ordinarily the judicial officers should be recalled and postings made by the High Court. The High. Court was anxious to have the orders of the Government implemented on the basis of the orders of this Court. The Government as well as the concerned officers in the returns made by them justified the action taken by the Government. The High, Court overruled the prayer made on behalf of the Government to stay the operation of its decision till necessary orders were obtained from this Court. It directed the Government to re post the officers and to post them in the regular cadre. The High 'Court directed the Government not to appoint any judicial officer to the post of the Registrar of Orissa Superior Judicial Services. The High .Court directed the State Government to appoint the officers to the regular cadre of the Orissa Higher Judicial Service. The High ,Court directed the government to post the officers to a regular cadre of Orissa Higher Judicial Services. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the High Court had no power to post a judicial officer to a regular post. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High High Court was entitled to recall the appellant and post him as a District Judge. [161 E] 2. The cadre of the superior judicial service consisted of not only the posts of District and Sessions Judges and Additional District and sessions Judges but also officers holding other posts. One of the officers included there was the Registrar of High Court. Neither the government nor the High court could have posted a judicial officer as the. Registrar of the Orissa High Court as this was a cadre post. [161 G] 3. The High Judicial Service consisted of not merely the posts of district and sessions judges and additional district and sessions Judges, but also officers who were holding other posts and who were not included in the cadre of superior judicial service. [161 H] 4. The cadre consisted of not even the posts of a District and Session Judge and Additional District Judge but also officers of the judicial service of the State. [162 A] 5. The High judicial service consisted not only of the posts of the District and Sessions judges and Additional District Judges but also of officers holding other post and who were neither in the cadre nor in the cadre. [162 B] 6. The High Judiciary was better suited to make transfers than a Minister. The policy displayed by the Constitution has been in this direction as has been explained in earlier cases of this Court.[162 C] 7. The High judiciary is better suited for making transfers than a minister. Just as the executive cannot know the requirements of a particular court, the High Courts also cannot know the requirement of any post in the secretariat. Just as a minister is taken over by the Government, the High court cannot, as contended by the learned Attorney General, foist any officer on the government. The cadre with which the High Court is concerned consists of three parts i.e., (1) presiding officers of district courts, (2) the Registrar of, the High 'Court and (3) the judicial officers working In the secretariat.[162 D E] 8. The High Judges are appointed by the Governor on the advice of the Chief Minister. The Chief Minister is the most competent person to advise the Governor on a matter of this kind. The Chief Justice of the High Courts is the most suitable person to advise on such matters. The Chief justice of the High ' Court is the most appropriate person to advise him on such matters.[162 F] 9. The High judges are better suited than the Chief Justice of India. The Chief Justices of the High courts are better su unsuitable to the office of the Chief justice. The Chief justices of the High. Courts are better suoushed to the office. The Chief Secretary is the most suited person to advise. The Chief. Justice of the State is the most. suitable person to advice the Chief Justice on such matters as may be referred to him by the Chief Minister.[163 B C] 10. The High magistrates are better sused to see that the executive functions are not abused to their advantage. The High Magis trate is better sused with the task of seeing that the executive function is not abused to the advantage of the executive. [163 D] 11. The High public officers are better suted than the executive. The High officers are better equipped to advise the Government on such matters and they are not expected to abuse the powers vested in them. [163 E] 12. The High Executive is better suted to see that executive functions are exercised in a manner which is not mala fide. [163 F] 13. The High executive is better suckered to see that its executive functions are. exercised in a proper and satisfactory manner. [163 G] 14. The High offices of the judicial officers are not only the post of District and Session Judges but also the post of Additional District and session Judges. The High office of the judicial officer is a non cadre post. The post of the judicial office is a cadre post of the District Judge. The post is not a cadre post in the cadre, but is a cadre one. The High cadre consists of not only judicial officers but also judicial officers working as Additional District Judges. The post has been held by judicial officers for several years. The post was held by judicial officer for several years and the High Court has not shown any reason why the post should not have been held by the judicial officer for a longer period. [164 B C] 15. The Chief Ministers are the most competent persons to advise the Chief Minister on such matters, and they are also not expected to misuse the powers vested on them.

The workmen of the appellant companies claimed sickness leave for a period of 7 days with full pay and dearness allowance in a year. The company, however, contended that the benefit of the sickness leave was not available to the workmen as the company had not given any such benefit to its workmen. The workmen contended that the sickness benefit was not a benefit which could be granted to them as a matter of right and that the workmen were entitled to the benefit of sick leave on full pay on the ground of sickness. The workmen also contended that the company had given the benefit of sickness leave to its workmen in the past and that the company was not justified in denying the benefit of such leave to the workmen. The company contended that the workmen had benefited a lot under the entire scheme of the Act and that the sickness leave could not be granted retrospectively or allowed to accumulate. The Tribunal, however, allowed the workmen 's demand and set aside the award of the Tribunal. The workmen 's appeals to this Court were dismissed. The workmen filed a writ petition in the High Court which was also dismissed. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that as the benefits of sections 47 and 49 of the Act were already admissible to workmen in Baroda with effect from December 14, 1969 and they were quite adequate, the Tribunal committed an error of law in granting the additional benefits mentioned above. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The benefit of sections 47, 48 and 49 of Act is available to workmen in the matter of the grant of sick leave. The Act does not in fact deal with the question of sickness leave. The other question regarding the adequacy of the sick ness benefit under the provisions of the Act has been examined by the Tribunal with reference to the reports of the National Commission of Labour, 1969, the Labour Laws Review Committee and the Norms Committee of Gujarat State, which go to show that the benefit cannot be said to be adequate for it works out to about half the average wage of a workman, and even that amount is not admissible for the first two days of sickness except in the case of a spell of sickness following at an interval of not more than 15 days, the spell of sickness for which the sickness benefit is last paid. [83D F] (2) The Tribunal was justified in its view that the workmen are entitled to 7 days sick leave with wages on pro duction of a medical certificate. [83G] (3) The Tribunal could not be said to have erred in restoring the benefit which the workmen were getting under the award of 1958, for it was taken away under the mistaken impression that it had been adequately replaced by the new provisions on the coming into force of the Act. [83H] (4) The workmen were not entitled to the additional benefit of sickle leave for 7 days in the garb of sick leave as the benefit of section 49 of the was available only in the case Of actual sickness certified by a registered medical practitioner. [84A] (5) The workmen did not deserve anything more than sickness benefit for the first 2 days of sickness under the first proviso to section 49 of Act. [84B] (6) The workmen had not been able to show that they were entitled to any additional benefit of sickness. [84C]

The appellant was detained under the Bombay Prevention of Anti Social Activities Act, 1947. The grounds of detention were supplied to him on the 8th June, 1955. The appellant was informed that the grounds on which a detention order was made against him were not specific and no particulars of the grounds could be furnished in public interest. He was also informed that he could make a representation against the order of detention. The appellant challenged the validity of the order of his detention on the grounds, inter alia, (1) that the order of the detention was mala fide and that the detaining authority in passing the order of preventive detention had not applied its mind to the existence or otherwise of the legitimate objects of detention; (2) that the grounds of detention are vague; (3) that the claim of non disclosure of the grounds made in the affidavit of the Under Secretary was not justified; (4) that the appellant was denied the right of making a representation under article 22(5) of the Constitution; and (5) that the detention was not bona fide. Held, that the constitutional right of a detenue under article 22 (5) of, the Constitution includes the right to be furnished particulars and information as well as the right to make a representation. The right to be supplied particulars and information is subject to the limitation under article 22. The authority is under a constitutional obligation to furnish reasonably definite grounds, as well as adequate particulars then and there, or shortly thereafter. But the right of the detenue to be furnished the earliest opportunity of making a represen tation against his detention is subject to such limitation as the Constitution has under article 22, and the authority is under an obligation to consider whether the disclosure of facts involved in the grounds is against public interest. The authority was therefore under a constitutional duty to furnish reasonably probable grounds, as also adequate particulars, before the order of its detention was made. The fact that the grounds are not specific and are not adequate to the requirements of the law under which the order of pre detention was made, is a circumstance which may well be taken into consideration in deciding whether the grounds can be considered to be vague. The fact, however, that the grounds were not specific, and were not adequate to enable the detenue to make a proper representation, is a relevant circumstance which may be taken into account in deciding whether he should be detained. The fact of non disclosure is not necessarily irrelevant. The fact whether the grounds are adequate or not is not a relevant circumstance. The fact as to whether the grounds were adequate or not, is a matter which is to be decided by the detaining authority. The fact in the present case that the grounds furnished to the appellant were not specific is a circumstance, which may well, be taken into, consideration in deciding the question whether the grounds could he considered to be reasonable. The fact is that the grounds have been furnished to the detenue and he has been informed that he can make a representation to the Advisory Board against the order. The fact also that the detenue was furnished the information at the time of the hearing of the case, is a material circumstance which may properly be taken into considera tion in deciding whether to disclose the grounds.

The respondent was a commissioned officer in the Indian Army. He was attached to the Army Ordnance Corps Training Centre, Secundrabad, where he was tried by a General Court Martial for offences under section 52(a) of the . The General Court Martial found him guilty of the offences and sentenced him to suffer rigorous imprisonment for three years. The respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order of removal from service on the ground that the rule 14 of the Army Rules, 1954, was ultra vires the and that the action taken thereunder was without any authority. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The rule is not ultra vires. The power under section 19 of the read with r. 14 of the Indian Army Rules, is an independent power. Although section 19 uses the words "subject to the provisions of this Act", it speaks of removal of a person from the service. Section 45 provides that on conviction by court martial an officer is liable to be cashiered or to suffer such less punishment as is in this Act mentioned. For removal from service under section 19, read with r 14 of the, Army Rules, the Central Government has power to remove from the service any person subject to the Act. [450 G H] The words "subject" in section 19 of ' the Act is not used in the sense in which it is used in section 45 of the Act. The words " subject to the provisions" in section19 of the Act are not used in that sense. The words in section 19 are used in the context of the other provisions of the Act and are not used to qualify the words " subject" in section 45. [451 A B] The words in the context in which they are used in section 19, are not used. The words are used in a sense which is different from that in section 45 and are not intended to qualify the word "subject". [451 C]

The appellant was a Panchayat. The respondent was the Panchayat. The appellant filed an appeal under section 124(5) of the Bombay Village Panchayat Act, 1958, before the Panchayat Samiti, Parseoni. The Panchayat passed a resolution on February 25, 1963, fixing octroi limits and number of octroi nakas and their places. The resolution was approved by the Collector. The Panchayat was required to submit its resolution to the Collector for approval. The Collector approved the resolution on January 14, 1964. The Panchayat filed an appeal on April 6, 1964, under section 124 (5) of that Act. The Panchayat contended that the resolution was invalid as it was not passed by the Panchayat within six months of the date of its passing. The Panchayat also contended that the approval of the Collector was not necessary as the Panchayat was not importing tea within the limits of the Panchayat for consumption, use or sale. The Panchayat 's contention was that the tea was imported into the Panchayat limits for consumption,use or sale. On the question whether the Panchayat was liable to pay octroi duty for the period January 14, 1963 to April 1, 1964, the Panchayat contended that it was not importing the tea for consumption, sale. The High Court held that the Panchayat was entitled to levy octroi duty from January 14,1964, in accordance with the resolution dated February 25,1963, and the Panchayat was also entitled to levy the octroi duty from April 1,1964. The Panchayat appealed to this Court. HELD: (i) The resolution dated February 14, 1963, was not invalid. The Panchayat had not fixed the octroi limits in the resolution. The resolution fixed the number of octroi Nakas and the places. The Panchayat could not fix the octroi limits without the sanction of the Collector. [217 B] (ii) The fixing of the octroi limits with the approval of Collector is an essential condition precedent to the levy of octroi duty. The resolution dated March 17, 1963, fixed the octroi limit and the number of the octroi naka and their places, and the resolution was not challenged. [217 C] (iii) The fixing the octroi limits and the number and location of octroi naka within the limits was an essential condition. The resolution fixing the octroi limit was not challenged and the resolution fixing the number and the location of octroi Naka within the octroi limits was not challenged in the High Court. [217 D] (iv) The High Court was right in holding that the Panchayat could validly impose octroi duty from the date of the resolution. [218 B] (v) The High court was right in not dealing with the question whether r.5 applied to all appeals under section 124 of the Act. [218 C] (vi) The High 'Court was right in its conclusion that the Panchayat had not established sufficient facts to enable it to deal with the question. [218 D] (vii) The High, Court was right that the Panchayat should have been given an opportunity to explain the basis on which the resolution was passed. [218 E] (viii) The High. Court was right, in holding that r.5 of the Rules was ultra vires the powers of the rule making authority. [218 F] (ix) The High Courts have power to decide all questions of law and fact arising in a case. The High Courts are not bound to give an opportunity to the parties to make their submissions on questions of law. [218 G]

The petitioner was detained under section 3(2) of the , on the ground that his activities were prejudicial to the maintenance of public order. The order of detention was served on the petitioner on the date of the order. The petitioner made representation on 22nd January, 1986 and the same was rejected on 22nd February, 1986. The petitioner 's writ petition in the High Court was dismissed. In the special leave petition to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the order of detention could only be justified against a person in detention if the detaining authority was satisfied that his release from detention was imminent and the order of the detention was necessary for putting him back in jail. Dismissing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The service of order of detention on the petitioner while he was in jail was futile and useless since such an order had no application under section 3 (2) of The Act. [910F] 2. The service on the petitioner of the order of approval of the order was not properly made. The order was not in proper form. The service was not in accordance with the provisions of the Act. [911B] 3. The grounds of challenge are all stated in the writ petition as well as in the special leave. The petitioner was in detention when the petitioner was served with the order of his detention. There were criminal cases against the petitioner. There was a murder case in respect of the said incident. In the said case investigation was in progress and the defence of the petitioner in the murder case was that he was falsely implicated and was not at all concerned with the murder. When the order was passed, the petitioner had not surrendered but when the order was served, the petitioner was taken into custody. [911B C] 4. The service upon the petitioner of an order of detention is not a mechanical formality. It is the result of a satisfaction of the detaining authority that the detenu is likely to be released from detention. The words "likely to be released" in the context of the section mean that there should be a release from detention. [912B C] 5. The order is not invalid on the ground of delay. [913C] 6. The order does not show that the detaining authority had considered the question of the petitioner being released on bail or that there was such a possibility of his release. [914D] 7. The order cannot be said to be invalid on the grounds of delay. The order could have been served on the detenu only after the detenu was taken into detention. [911E] 8. The order must be deemed to have been made on the date when the order of its approval was passed. [915A] 9. The order in the instant case is set aside. The writ petition and the appeal are allowed to the extent indicated above. [916B]

The appellant, a dealer in gold, was carrying on business as a money lender and a dealer in ornaments. The Administrator of the Union of India, exercising powers under section 28 of the Gold Control Act, 1968, refused permission to the appellant to carry on business as money lender on the ground that the appellant was carrying on money lending business. The appellant challenged the validity of section 28 of that Act on the ground, inter alia, that it suffers from the vice of excessive delegation of legislative power inasmuch as no criteria or guidelines have been provided by reference to which the power conferred on the Administrator to refuse permission or grant permission should be exercised and that the section confers an arbitrary and uncanalised power upon the Administrator with the result that the licensed dealer is at his mercy while seeking permission to carry on money lending or banking business on the security of any article, ornament or both in the same premises in which he carried on business as such dealer. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that section 28 confers an arbitrary, uncanalized power without any criteria for guiding the discretion of the Administrator. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The object of the enactment and the scheme of the Act together with the necessity to ensure prevention of circumvention of the other provisions of the Act afford more than sufficient guidance to the Administrator in the matter of exercising his discretion under that section. [955 B] (2) The objective, the policy and the Scheme of the Act, together with the need to ensure prevention and circumvention of other provisions of law, afford more than adequate guidance to the administrator in the matter. [954 B] (3) The object, the policy, the scheme of section 28 and the necessity to prevent circumvention of section 28 are sufficient guidance to enable the Administrator to exercise his power under section 28. [956 B] (4) The High Court was right in holding that section 28 was valid. [959 C] (5) The analogy drawn by the High Court from the reasoning adopted by this Court in Harakchand Banthia 's case is not applicable. [951 C] (6) The High Courts have upheld the validity of the section. [957 D] (7) The analogy of the reasoning adopted in Harak Chand Banthia ' 's case does not help the appellant. [957 E] (8) The High court was right in declaring section 28 invalid on the ground of excessive delegation. [957 G] (9) The High courts have upheld the section on the ground 'that it conferred a very wide and vague power on the Administrator. [957 H] (10) The High 'Court was right in striking down section 28 on the ground it conferred a wide and vague discretionary power on the administrator. [958 A] (11) The High, Court was right that the section did not impose any blanket or absolute prohibition upon a dealer from carrying on moneylending, banking or any other business in the same, premises in which the applicant was intending to carry on, business as a dealer but he was prevented only from carrying on business, as money lender or banker on the security, of any article or ornament or two or more articles of gold and that he was prevented from carrying on the business in the licensed premises of the dealer and while implementing such limited restrictions or granting relief against the same he will be guided by the policy and purposes of the Act and by the prime consideration that circumvention of provisions of the other sections of the Act shall not be premitted. [958 B C] (12) The High. Court was right, in the present case, in holding that the section was valid.

The appellants filed a suit against the respondents for a declaration that the properties in suit belonged to the temple and for possession of the same. The trial Court dismissed the suit. The lower appellate Court held that the properties belonged to the idol and that the appellants had acquired title to them by prescription. The High Court, in second appeal, held that the appellants ' title in respect of the properties in question was open to challenge. The appellants contended that article 134 B of the Limitation Act, 1908, did not apply to the facts of the case, and that the suit was barred by limitation. Held, that the suit filed by the appellants was barred by article 134 B. The appellants had failed to prove that the properties were comprised in the endowment and that they had been transferred by the previous manager for valuable consideration. The properties belonged to a temple and were not the properties of the idol. The appellants were not the trustees of the idols. The appellants ' title was not lost by adverse possession before the suit was filed. The appellants could not be allowed to raise the plea of adverse possession in the present case. The question as to whether on facts proved in the present ease, an inference can be drawn that the previous manager or trustee had been removed, was a mixed question of fact and law and the High Court was in error in reversing the decisions of the courts below. Held, further, that the question as to the applicability of article 134 B was a mixed one of fact and of law and the appellants ' case was not covered by that article. The question whether on facts, an inference could be drawn that a previous manager or a trustee had been removing the property for valuable consideration, was a question of fact. The appellants failed to prove the existence of any temple in the temple and the properties were not the property of the idole. The appellants did not prove that the temple was a public temple. The appellants claimed that the properties had been granted to the idols and their matam, and that they were entitled to the properties by prescription. Held, also, that the appellants were not entitled to raise the question of adverse possession. The question of adverse Possession was a mixed matter of fact and a mixed question Of law and fact and the appellants had failed in proving the existence of a temple in the idol, and the properties belonged not to the idole but to the temple. The question was not one of fact. Held, again, that the High Court had rightly reversed the decisions of all the courts below, and the appeal must be dismissed. The question that article 134B applied to the facts was a mixed ques tion of fact and the law applicable to the facts. The appellants, therefore, had failed to establish that the suit had been filed within 12 years of the date of the removal of the previous manager. The appellants must fail in their suit. The suit was not barred by limitation under article 134 B, because, the suit was not one for possession of immovable property, but for a declaration of title to immovable property. The appellants would be entitled to succeed if the suit were brought within 12 years from the date of their removal. The appellants relied on the decision of the Privy Council in Vidya Varuthi vs Balusami, (1916) L.R. 43 I.A. 147, and contended that the suit should be dismissed. Held,, further, (i) that the suit must be dismissed as it was not one brought within 12 year of the date on which the suit was brought, and the appellants were entitled to succeed on the ground that article 134 had no application. The appellants cannot be allowed to take the plea of limitation in the present suit. The question in the present appeal was not one which was a mixed questions of fact and Law, but one of law. The appellants have failed to prove their case. The appellants are not entitled to any relief. (ii) that the question whether on the facts proved in this case an inference could have been drawn that the appellants have been removed from the office of the previous managers for valuable consideration was a mixed issue of fact and an issue of law and that the High court was in error, in reversing the decision of all the Courts below.

The appellant, a partnership firm, was granted a licence by the District Magistrate, Jammu, for running a Theatre in the Theatre. The licence was renewed by the District magistrate in the name of the firm. The licence for the Theatres was renewed by him. The District Magistrate rejected the application of the appellant for renewal of the licence on the ground that the appellant had not obtained the necessary licence for running the Theatere. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the legality and validity of the orders passed by the District Magis trate and the appellate authority. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the licence was granted for premises permanently equipped for cinematograph exhibition in the name and style of the appellant firm and that it was not a grant for premises and that the licence could not be renewed under any of the provisions of the Act or the Rules. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The licence is granted for premises, permanently equipped for the cinematograph exhibition in a place. The licence may be granted for a period not exceeding one year. The licence can be renewed for a period of one year at a time. The licence could be renewed for one year at the option of the licensee. The licensee may be required to obtain a fresh licence for a period less than one year. [591F G] 2. The licence granted to the appellant was for a period which was not less than one month. The licence cannot be renewed for more than one year at one time. The appellant was a partner of the firm and had no right whatever to exhibit cinematograph films in the Theater without a licence. Any such operation by them would have been in clear and gross contravention of the law. The principles of natural justice are not attracted to such a situation and there was no obligation on the part of the District Magistrate to give a notice or hearing to the firm or its partners before he passed the impugned order. [592A B] 3. The order passed by the district Magistrate directing the suspension of the exhibition of the Theatrecorder in the Theate is not violative of the principles of natural Justice. [592C] 4. The appellant could not have any legitimate expectation that they will be allowed to run the Theatare without a licence in violation of the law and the rules. [592D] 5. The appellant had no legal right whatever to conduct the Theatricgo without a licence and the order passed by District Magisti tor directing the suspension was one passed by him in the exercise of his function of administering the provision of the Act and the Rules and the aforesaid implied power to take all incidental steps necessary for effective enforcement of the statute. [592E] 6. The order of the District Magistra tor is not violative or principles of natural justi fies. [592F] 7. The order is not violative nor is it vitiated by any error of law apparent on the face of the record. [592G] 8. The High court was right in holding that the order of the district Magis trator was not violative of principles of natural juri sce. [592H] 9. The appellant has no right whatever, to conduct the cinema shows in the Theated Theatre without a licence, in violation of law. The writ petitioners could not also have any legitimate expecta tion that they will he allowed to run their Theatre, without a licence for one year. In the absence of any legal right or legitimate expectation being available to the writ petitioners, there was no infraction of the principles. [593A B] 10. The order was one passed in the exercise or his function of adminis tration and the order was not violative or violation of any statutory or legal right of the writ petitioners. [594B] 11. The order cannot be said to have visited the writ petitioners with any adverse civil consequences. They had no legal rights whatever to conduct their Theatres without a licence or to exhibit cinematograph film in the Theating Theatre and the order cannot be assailed on the ground of violation of principles of audi alteram partem. [594B] 12. The order dated September 26, 1980 passed by the Superintendent of Police, Jammu, is quashed. [595B] 13. The District Magis tors of the State of Jammu and Kashmir are directed to immediately take immediate steps to ensure that the Theaters are not allowed to exhibit cinematographs in the Theantre without a license. [596B] 14. The District Magistrates are directed to ensure that no person other than the licensee is allowed to exhibit films in the theater without a license and that no person who is not a licensee is allowed any film which is not certified as suitable for unrestricted public exhibition by the District Magistrates. [597B]

The appellants were displaced persons from Pakistan and were declared evacuees under the provisions of the , and were allotted certain mills and the factory. The appellants were served with notices under section 12 of the , requiring them to show cause why the lease should not be cancelled and why they should not be evicted. The notices were challenged by the appellants on the grounds, inter alia, that section 12 of Act XXXI of 1950 did not authorise the Custodian to cancel leases granted by himself and not by the evacuee, and that the notices were ultra vires the powers of the Custodian under that section. Held, that the Custodian had the power under section 12 to cancel leases and the notices were valid. The Custodian had the authority under section 12(1) to cancel leases in respect of property belonging to the evacuee, that the lease was in respect of the property belonging to him and not in respect of evacuee property, and that in consequence the directions given by the Custodian were unauthorised. The Custodian could not cancel a lease granted by himself, and the notices issued by him were valid. Section 12 of the Act was not intended to repeal the provisions of any other law for the time being in force. The words "any other law for time being inforce" in section 12(2) of the Act were wide enough to include any law which was in force before the amendment of section 12(i) of the 1950 Act. The words of the section "any other laws for the time be in force" in section 10(1) of the Administration of Evacuee Property (Amendment) Act, 1954, were wide enough and did not include any law other than the one which was in operation before the amendment. The words in section 12 of that Act "any other Act for the time ' being in force" were wide enough, and did not take in the Act of 1954. The words 'any other law ' in section 12 were wide enough. The words, "any other property" in section 11(1) were wide enough in their amplitude and did not cover property of the evacuee which was not evacuee property. The words used in section 12 did not include property of the evacuees which was not an evacuee property.

The appellant was a minor son of the respondent. The respondent was a minor at the time of the commencement of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1955. The respondent filed an application before the Sub Divisional Officer, Hanumangarh, for determining the ceiling area of the appellant. The Sub Divisional Officer held that the appellant was a major son of the father and used to study in Punjab and that the land in possession of the father was ancestral. The Sub Division Officer, after holding an enquiry, determined the ceiling area, but an appeal by the respondent was dismissed by the Revenue Appellate Authority. The respondent then filed a revision application before the Board of Revenue for Rajasthan. The Board held that the father and the son constituted two separate units and each one of them was entitled to get 62 Bighas and 8 Biswas. The Board also held that the provisions of the old ceiling law applied to the case but the Sub Divisional officer had committed an error of law in determining the ceiling. The Board remanded the case to the Sub Divisional Magistrate for fresh determination of the ceiling area. The Sub Divi sional Officer held that there was a gross and patent illegality in the order of the Sub Divisional Offi cer and, consequently, set aside the order of Sub Divisional Officer. The Board, however, upheld the order of remand of the Sub Division Officer. The respondent challenged the order of Board of Revenue before the High Court. The High Court upheld the order. Hence the appeal by the appellant. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Board of Revenue has general powers of superintendence and control over all revenue courts. It is both administrative as well as judicial powers. It is open to the Board to exercise its powers of superintendence on all its subordinate courts in order to regulate the functioning of the subordinate courts so as to keep them within their spheres of jurisdiction. If the subordinate court disregards any specific provision of law and does something illegal it is open to Board to interfere and set the matter right. A similar question arose before the Rajasthan High Court in Kana and others vs Board of Revenue, Rajasthan, ILR (1964) 1 Raj. 10 (F.B.) and it was held that Section 12 of the Rajasthan Land Revenue Act, 1956, which provides that the Board may revise any order passed by any subordinate officer, does not apply to judicial proceedings. The Board has power to revise judicial orders also passed by courts in appropriate cases. [728F H; 729A] 2. The Board had by its order dated 14th April, 1975 directed that the ceiling area may be determined according to old law i.e. Act of 1955 and it did not give any power of superintendence to the Board on judicial side. The Board could not, therefore, make use of its powers of supervision and control and the order of Collector could not be held proper with reference to Section 9 of the Land Revenue Act. [729B C] 3. The Board noticed that there was no provision for separate unit in Chapter III B of the Act of 1955. The appellant and his son constituted one unit and not two units and the case was remanded to Sub Divisional Officer for de novo determination of the Ceiling Area. The Sub divisional Officer committed the grave illegality on not merely ignoring the law but also ignoring the directions of the Board of Reve nue. [727A B] 4. The Board was right in holding that the Sub Divisional Officers had committed an illegality in not only ignoring the law, but also ignoring directions of the Sub divisional officer. [726C] 5. The Board rightly remanded the case. [725D]

The first respondent, All India Reporter Limited, was not served with any individual notice by the Tribunal before it passed its award. The first respondent submitted its reply in October, 1981 inter alia contending that it was not running a newspaper and publications published by it were not the newspapers and as such the Palekar Award was not applicable to it. The Deputy Labour Commissioner, Nagpur, wrote to the Manager of the first respondent that the first respondent was liable to implement the order of the Central Government made on the recommendations of the Palekkar Tribunal in respect of its employees since the first respondent had not been able to function effectively. The first Respondent, All India Journalists and the All India Reporter, filed a writ petition in the High Court of Bombay, Nagpur Bench, challenging the validity of the notice served on it by the Deputy Labour Commissioner. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the law reports published by the first respondent were not newspapers within the meaning of the Act and that the employees engaged in their production or publication of the said law reports were not entitled to the benefits conferred upon the employees of the newspaper establishments by the Act. Hence this appeal by the first Respondent. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The law reports which are being published by the Ist respondent are reports of recent decisions of the Supreme Court of India and of the High Courts in India which are supplied to it by its agents appointed at New Delhi and other places where High Courts are situated. It cannot be disputed that these decisions are of public importance. [782E F] 1.2 The law reports contain information about the recent events which have taken place in the Supreme Court or in the High Courts which are public bodies and these are matters in which the public is interested. Strong reliance was placed on behalf of the first Respondent on the decision of the High Court in Commissoner of Sales Tax vs M/s. In the course of the said report it is obtained that in this case the Paleker Award was not a newspaper and the establishment in which the said law report was being published was a newspaper establishment which attracted the provisions of that Act. The first respond ent cannot derive any assistance from the deci sion of the High court of Bombay in Commissioner of Sales tax vs M/S. In the Course of the said Report it is ob tained that the Press Registrar scrutinised reports published in certain foreign countries regarding their own Press and it was noticed that in the catalogues prepared by them specialised newspapers such as the one under consideration were not excluded from the list of newspapers. The Act in question is a beneficent legislation which is enacted for the purpose of improving the conditions of service of the employees of newspaper establishments and hence even if it is possible to have two opinions on the construction of the provisions of the Act the one which advances the object of the Act, and is in favour of the employees for whose benefit the Act is passed has to be accepted. [783B D] 1.3 The law reports published in the country are public documents and the employees engaged by the first respond ent in their production of the said Law reports are entitled to the benefit of the orders passed by the Central Government on the basis of the recommendations made by the Paleakkar Tribunal. [784B]

The appellant was a monthly tenant of the suit premises since about 2nd February, 1965. The respondent wanted to charge more rent or mesne profits. The appellant was a tenant of the premises since about the year 1965. The appellant filed a suit for eviction against the respondent on the ground that he was a licensee and not a tenant. The trial court passed a decree in ejectment petition filed by the respondent and ordered the appellant to vacate the premises before 31st January, 1975. The appellant preferred an appeal against the said decree. The respondent filed a revision petition under section 115 of the C.P.C. in the High Court. The High Court held that the respondent was a licensee. The High court also held that the appellant was a licensee since the period of the agreement was over. The High, Court also held that there was no sub tenancy by the respondent. The High. Court also held the appellant was not entitled to the protection of section 15A of the Bombay Rent Act. The High 'Court dismissed the revision petition. The appellant appealed to this Court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The respondent was a monthly tenancy of the suit property since about 2.2.1965. The appellant had entered into an agreement with the respondent for the purpose of running a business of selling liquor. The agreement recited that the licensee shall not allow any other person to use and occupy the said premises and shall not do any unlawful or illegal business therein. The agreement was only for the purpose that the licensee should not allow any person to use the premises and occupy the premises. The appellant, therefore, was a licensee as defined in section 5(4A) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947. [1062C D] 1.2 The respondent was not a licensee as contemplated by section 5(1) of the Act. The respondent was in occupation of the premises on 1st February, 1973 under a subsisting agreement for licence. The respondent had filed a suit against the appellant for eviction on the ground of sub tenancy. The trial Court decreed the suit. The High Courts in revision under section 115 C.P C. refused to interfere with the finding of the trial Court that the respondent had failed to prove that he was licensee. The Bombay High Court affirmed the decision of the trial court. [1063B C] 1.3 The respondent was entitled to the benefit of section 15 A of the Bombay. Rent Act. [1064D] 1.4 The respondent was, therefore, a licensee and was not a tenant within the meaning of section 5(11) of the Rent Act. He was, therefore. not entitled to protection under the Bombay Rent Control Act. [104C] 1.5 The respondent was also entitled to the benefits of section 15(1) and (2) of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, as amended by Maharashtra Act 17 of 1973. [104D] 1:6 The respondent was liable to pay the rent and damages for use and occupation. [104E] 1.6 The respondent had not filed a suit under section 41 of the Bombay Small Causes Courts Act against the appellant. The respondent could not be called a licensee. He was not a sub tenant. He was in occupation as a monthly tenant. The respondent did not have any right to continue in possession after the termination of the licence. The licence was not put an end to by the appellant. [104F G] 1.7 The respondent was bound to pay the monthly compensation for use and possession. The respondent cannot be called a sub tenant as he was not a licencee. He was a licensee, and not a subtenant. [104G] 1.8 The respondent was therefore, a tenant and not a licensee. [105A] 1.9 The respondent was thus a licensee. It was not necessary to decide whether he was a sub tenant or not. [105B] 1.10 The respondent was rightly held to be a licensee. There was no subtenancy. [105C] 1:11 The respondent was only a licensee. His possession was not unlawful. [105D] 1 :12 The respondent was held to be entitled to the relief of eviction. [105E] 1:12 The respondent had failed in his defence. The High was right in holding that the respondent could not succeed in his defence and that the appellant could not be said to be a sub tenant of the respondent. [105F] 1:13 The respondent was holding the premises on a monthly tenancy. The respondent paid the rent and the appellant was in possession of the premises. [105G] 1:14 The respondent was the licensee. He had filed a civil suit against the appel lant for eviction. The suit was decreed. The High courts in revision affirmed the decree. [105H] 1:15 The respondent was paying the rent regularly. The appellant paid the rent regularly and the respondent was in possession. The appellant did not pay the rent regularly, and the respondent did not pay any rent regularly. [105I] 1:16 The respondent was under no obligation to pay any rent. He was under no legal obligation to pay rent. He had paid the rent. The respondent, therefore, could not be treated as a sub tenant and the appellant could have no right to remain in possession after determination of the licence, and the appellant had no right to continue to remain in occupation after the determination of the agreement. [105J] 1:17 The respondent was an employee of the appellant. He was also a licensee. Therefore, he was a tenant. [105K] 1:18 The respondent was protected under the Maharashtra Rent Act. There was a clear finding by the courts below that the respondent did have a right to remain on the premises. He was entitled to remain in the premises. There was nothing to show that the respondent ever raised any objection to the appellant continuing in possession of any part of the premises after the termination or the agreement. The respondent never raised any objection. [105L] 1:19 The respondent was neither a licensee nor a sub tenant, and was not entitled, under the Bombay Rents Act, to continue in occupation after determination of his licence. [105M] 1:20 The respondent was guilty of breach of the terms of the agreement and was liable to be evicted. [105N] 1:21 The respondent was required to pay the amount of compensation for use of the premises and the amount of damages for use of occupation. [105OB] 1:22 The respondent was at all material times a tenant. He had no right of sub tenancy in the premises in question. [105P] 1:23 The respondent was merely a licensee. In the circumstances, he was not entitled under the Bombay Act to continue in the premises after determination of licence. [1066B] 1 :24 The respondent was given the benefit of the provisions of section 15C of the Bombay Act. [105GH] 1:25 The respondent was always a licensee. But he was not in occupation of any part or premises of the premises in his occupation. The respondent continued to be a tenant. There was, therefore no question of the respondent being a sub tenant in the premises and of the appellant being a licensee in the premises, and the High Court was right in dismissing the revision petition filed by him. [1067B

The respondent was a resident of the former State of Dholpur State and the dispute related to a time before the merger of the former Dholpur State into the Matsya Union. The United State of Rajasthan merged in 1949 and became the Part B State of Rajasthan. The respondent was a member of the Matsya union. The United States of Rajasthan merged with the Matsya State in 1949. The United state of Rajasthan was a new sovereign and was not bound by any obligation against the old sovereign of the former state of Dholpur. The respondent filed a suit for recovery of the amount due to it from the State of Rajasthan on the basis of the covenant of merger. The trial court dismissed the suit but the High Court decreed the suit. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The liability of the State of the United State of Rajas than Rajasthan arose on the merger of that State in 1949 and the liability of the respondent arose on the coming into force of the Constitution of India. The respondent could not therefore be made liable for the amount due from the State. [180 D] (ii) The liability arose on the continued existence of the old laws and the valuable evidence afforded by article VI of the Covenant and there was nothing to show that the right to claim refund was taken away by any law competently passed. [180 E] (iii) The respondent was not entitled to claim refund of the amount paid by it under the covenant of the merger because the covenant was not a special law. [180 F] (iv) The liability was not incurred by the respondent because the covenant of 1949 was not a general law. [181 B] (v) The liability lay on the State of Rajs than Rajasthan because there was recognition of the liability even on the principles enunciate in Dalmia Dadri Cement Co. Ltd. vs The Commissioner of Income tax, ; , referred to. (vi) The liability to pay the amount was not incurred because the respondent was not a Ruler of the State. The liability arose from the covenant of accession of the State to the Dominion of India. [181 G] (vii) The liability under the covenant was incurred by the State of Dholpur because the respondent had agreed to pay the liability. [182 A] (viii) The liability could not be enforced against the respondent because there was no recognition of the right to exemption by the new sovereign. [182 B] (ix) The liability in the present case arose on the continuance of the old law and the valuable document afforded by article V of the Covenant of Merger. [182 C] (x) The liability arises on the continued operation of the laws of the State and the respondent was therefore liable under article 295(2) of the Constitution. [182 D] (xi) The liability for the amount was incurred by reason of the Covenant. [182 E] (xii) The liability incurred by the appellant was not a liability incurred by it because the respondent did not take advantage of the Covenant or the agreement. [182 F] (xiii) The liability did not arise because the respondent took advantage of the agreement. The liability was incurred by virtue of the Covenant which was not a law. [182 G] (xiv) The liability arising under the agreement was not incurred on account of the respondent because it was not a new sovereign. The liability could be enforced against it because the new sovereign had not recognised the liability. The liability did arise on the continued establishment of the old sovereign. [183 A] (xv) The liability which arose on the commencement of the Constitution was not incurred when the Constitution came into force. The liability which accrued on the commencement was not incurred if the respondent took the advantage of the covenant or the agreement and the respondent took it. [183 B] (xvi) The liability, therefore, arose on the date of the commencement of Constitution. [183 C] (xvii) The liability is not incurred because of the respondent taking advantage of the contract. [183 D] (xviii) The liability does not arise because of the Covenant, because the respondent never took advantage of it. [184 A]

The appellants were the owners of cotton and groundnut seeds in the State of Madras. They were registered as dealers under the Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1939, and were carrying on business in cotton and ground nut. The State Government issued a notification under section 5(1) of the Act declaring its intention to exercise control over the purchase and sale of cotton and the groundnut. The appellants challenged the validity of the Act and the Rules framed thereunder on the ground that the restrictions imposed by the Act and Rules were unreasonable and that the Act and rules were not in conformity with article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. Held, that the Act was not in conformity either with article 19 (1) (f) or with article 19 of the Constitution and was not invalid. The Act was an integrated one and it regulates the buying and selling of commercial crops. If the small traders were exempted, it created to them a monopoly of the trade in the produce of the notified crops. The Act did not create unreasonable restrictions on the appellants ' right to do business. The Act imposed reasonable restrictions on the right of the appellants to do business and the restrictions imposed were reasonable within the meaning of section 14 of the Act. The Act and the rules were not unreasonable restrictions on a citizen 's right to do trade or business. The fact that the appellants were not prohibited from carrying on their business did not affect their right to do so. The fact of the appellants being exempted from the operation of the Act did not affect the appellants ' rights to do business, and the restrictions were reasonable within article 19(6) of the constitution. The Act, in its true nature and character, was a law relating to the carrying on of a business and the Act was a law imposing reasonable restrictions on that business within the meaning Of article 19(5) of the Constitu tion. The Act in its true character and character, did not create any unreasonable restrictions on any citizen 's rights to do trade business. The restrictions imposed by it were reasonable within section 14 of Act. The fact, that the appellants had to pay the price of the cotton and the commodity agreed to be paid, did not affect them 's right of carrying on business. The question whether a particular payment is a trade allowance or not depends upon the facts of each case. Held, further, that the impugned provisions of the Act constituted reasonable restrictions on a person 's right under article 19(i)(g) and were not in conflict with article 19. The Act provided for the regulation of the buying and the selling of commercial crop and the restrictions on the trade of the appellants were reasonable within Article 19(6). The Act was not, therefore, invalid. The fact as to the amount of the price of cotton and commodity agreed to, did not alter the nature of the transaction. The Act only imposed reasonable restrictions in the interest of the general public on the right to carry on trade. The Act also imposed reasonable restrictions upon the right of a trader to carry on his business. The impugned provisions did not create a monopoly in the trade of cotton and oil seeds. The Act merely imposed reasonable restrictions and did not contravene article 19(ii) of the Consti tution. The Act could not be said to be unreasonable within the meaning section 14 of that Act. The question as to whether a particular trade allowance was a trade allowance within the meaning, of section 14 was a question of fact and could not be decided on the basis of any material placed before the Court. The reasonableness of the restrictions would depend upon the circumstances obtaining at the time the market was established. The reasonableness could be determined by reference to the circumstances obtaining in the market at the time of the market. The question was not whether the deduction was a trade allowances but whether the deduction in any transaction was a trade or business allowance. The reasonableness was to be determined by the facts of the particular case. The fact whether the deduction is a trade allowances or not depended upon the facts and circumstances of each case and the reasonableness of the deductions could not be determined on the basis only of the facts and circumstance of each case, and the reasonableness was to he determined on the facts of that particular case. Held also, that the restrictions were not unreasonable within the section. The Act authorised the State Government to make rules for the regulation and control of the buying, selling and storage for commercial crops. The rules were not inconsistent with the Act and were not unreasonable. The Act made no discrimination between the appellants and the growers of cotton and their trade. The fact was that the appellants could not carry on their trade without the permission of the State Government. The fact did not affect any of the rights of the appellants. The Act conferred upon the appellants a right to carry business and the fact that the growers could not carry their trade without permission of the Government did not affect that right. The fact could not be a ground for holding that the Act imposed unreasonable restrictions on their right to carry trade. The question of reasonableness of the restriction was a matter of inference to be drawn from the facts and the circumstances of each particular case.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. The appellants contended that the conviction was bad on the ground that the evidence showed that there was a large crowd there and that the witnesses were agreed that there was no point in sending up a report without names the next morning if the idea of delay was to concoct a story and implicate innocent persons. Held, that the evidence did not show that there was any prior arrangement to murder from which a common intention could be inferred. The fact that the witnesses arrived at a time when the beating was already in progress, and that they knew nothing about what went before, showed that there must have been a prior meeting of minds. The fact of the witnesses being too lazy, mentally, to differentiate, could not be used to determine the conclusion of the guilt of the accused. The fact, however, that the witnesses could not be relied on, was not a ground for rejecting their evidence. The fact could not be said to be of such a nature as to lead to the conclusion that they were not speaking the truth. The fact was that the witnesses had no interest in the case and the evidence showed no connection between the appellants and the murder. The fact did not show any previous arrangement to murder. The evidence did not establish that the appellants had the common intention to murder. There was no evidence of any prior meeting. The fact showed that the witnesses did not know anything about the murder. There could be no presumption of common intention in the absence of any evidence of prior arrangement. The fact also showed that the appellants were not present at the scene of the offence and that the evidence was not sufficient to establish that they had the common object to murder. Held, further, that the fact that the appellants joined in the attack but had no hand in the killing, was not of such a character as to lead the court to the conclusion of a common intention to kill. The fact however that the witnesses came to a time when they were going to the scene of offence and that they had no interest to speak about the murder, could not lead to the inference of a common object. The fact therefore that the witnesses met a time when he was going to the field and that they were all agreed that there should be no delay in sending up the report without names, could not show that they were speaking the truth and that the appellants could not be convicted on the basis of their mere presence. The fact in the present case that the witnesses knew nothing about the murder could not be a ground for holding that they were present at the time of the murder. Held further, that in the case of a joint trial, the conviction could be maintained only if it was shown that the accused had the common motive to commit the offence. In the present case, there was no evidence that there was such a motive. The fact had been that the witnesses, who were interested in the accused, were not speaking their truth. The conviction of the appellants was therefore bad. The fact might not have been of such a degree as to lead an inference of common intention. The fact would not have been sufficient to establish the guilt of an accused person unless it was shown by evidence that he had the common mental intention to commit the murder. In the case of joint trial, it was not necessary that there must be a prior meeting in the course of the same transaction. The fact must be such that it was impossible for the accused to know with certainty and precision the exact place where the crime was committed. The fact may be proved by a variety of facts and circumstances which must vary from case to case and from circumstances to circumstances. In the instant case, the facts showed that the accused were not present when the murder was committed. They were not present in the house when the murder took place. They were present in the field when the deceased was attacked. They were all agreed to have the common intention of killing the deceased. The fact there was no previous arrangement to kill, could not mean that they were acting in concert with the murder.

The petitioner was employed in the Central Public Works Department under the Ministry of Works and Housing in Government of India and was compulsorily retired by order dated 3.8.1976 made under Rule 56(j) of the Fundamental Rules. The petitioner challenged the order of compulsory retirement in a writ petition under Article 32 of the Constitution. The petitioner contended that the order of retirement was violative of Article 311(2) of the Constitution as the petitioner was an officiating government servant and could not have been compulsorily retired under Rule 56 (j) of Fundamental Rules. Dismissing the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The petitioner was holding a class II post when the impugned order was served on him. The appropriate authority is entitled to exercise power under clause (j) in the case of a Government servant in Class I or Class II service or post where he entered into service before attaining the age of 35 years after the said servant attained the age of 50 years. [638C D] 1.2 The appropriate authority was entitled to exercise the power under clause(j) in case of a government servant in Class II service, or post where the government servant entered into service after attaining the age 35 years. [637B] 1.3 The petitioner was promoted as officiating Assistant Engineer which is a Class II post on 25.5.1954 and continued to hold that post when the order of compulsorily retirement was passed. By 25.5,1954 the petitioner had not at all at any time attained the age Of 50 years. As a result of the order of the compulsory retirement the petitioner had no right to the post and could not be reverted to his substantive post before the order of his compulsory retirement was passed on 3.8,1976. [637C D] 2.1 The order of compulsory retire ment was not violative of Article 31 1(2) or Article 311(1) of the constitution. [637D] 2.2 The petitioner was not entitled to the benefit of Fundamental Rule 56(1)(i) as he was not in Class II post. [637E] 2.3 The contention that the petitioner was entitled to the benefits of Fundamental Rule 54(1)(a) is not correct. The petitioner was in Class II Post when the impugned orders of compulsory retirement were passed. [637F] 2.4 The petitioner was entitled, therefore, to the benefit under Rule 54(i)(a) of the Central Civil Services (Pension) Rules, 1972. [637G] 2.5 The petitioner would have superannuated from service on 29.2.1980 if he had not been compulsorily retired with effect from 6.5.1976. Even if the writ petition is allowed and the order of Compulsory retirement is set aside the petitioner cannot go back to service. But he would be entitled to pecuniary benefit of salary and allowances admissible under the rules. [637H, 638A]

The respondent No. 1, widow of the deceased, had taken a life insurance policy from the appellant Corporation. The policy was valid for a period of one year commencing from 11th January, 1961 and ending on 11th January 1962. The policy contained a clause that the policy was subject to the terms and conditions of the policy. The policy holder died on the same day. The respondent No. I filed a suit for recovery of the amount due under the policy. In the plaint it was stated that the Divisional Manager of the appellant Corporation had accepted the proposal of the deceased and had credited the amount in the account of the deceased. The respondent claimed that the amount was not credited towards the premium account of the proposal but was kept in suspense account without any liability of the appellant. The appellant Corporation contested the suit on the ground that the proposal was not accepted and as such there was no concluded insurance contract between the deceased and the appellant Corporation and that the policy holder had not fulfilled his part of the contract. The Trial Court held that there was a concluded contract between the respondent No.1 and the appellant and that the respondent No 1 was entitled to the amount. The Trial court further held that the proposal had been accepted by the Divisional Manager and that the amount had been credited in the account. The Trial Judge further held that there were no further steps to be taken by the deceased to get the amount credited in his account. The respondent filed an appeal in the High Court. The High Court held that the respondent was entitled to a decree for the amount. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the proposal having been accepted by a higher authority, the respondent was not entitled to any relief. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was in error in holding that there was no valid contract of insurance between the deceased on the one hand and the appellant on the other. The expression "underwrite" signifies accept liability under '. The dictionary meaning also indicates that. It is true that normally the expression "underwriting" is used in Marine Insurance but the expression used in Chapter III of the Financial Powers of the Standing Order in this case specifically used the expression "Underwriting and revivals" of policies in case of Life Insurance Corporation and stated that it was the Divisional Manager who was competent to underwrite policy for Rs 50,000 and above. The mere receipt and retention of premium until after the death of the applicant or the mere preparation of the policy document is not acceptance. Acceptance must be signified by some act or acts agreed on by the parties or from which the law raises a presumption of acceptance. The mere execution of the policy is not an acceptance; an acceptance, to be complete must be communicated to the offeror, either directly, or by some definite act, such as placing the contract in the mail. The test is not intention alone. When the application so requires, the acceptance must be evidenced by the signature of one of the company 's executive officers. [359B D] In the instant case, the High Court was of the opinion that the respondent had not taken a decision to accept the proposal. The High court was of the view that the respondent could not have been under a misapprehension that the Divisional Officer was the only authority to accept the proposer. The High, Court was of opinion that the Divisional manager was the only competent authority to accept a proposal for Rs. 50,000. The High. Court was of view that having regard to the conduct of the parties, there was a valid contract. [358B D] 2. The expression 'underwrite ' signifies accept liability. It is a term of art. It is not defined in the Insurance Act. The dictionary meanings also indicate that. It means accept liability. [356B] In the present case, the expression 'underwriting ' signifies acceptability. The expression is used in the policy in the present case. The expression used in the Policy is "underwriting and revivial of policies in the case of Life Insurers". The expression is not defined. The dictionary sense also indicates that the expression is used. [357B] 3. The expression in the policy is "underwriting and reviving" and the expression is not used in the Insurance policy. The expression has been used in the insurance policy in the instant case. The policy is not a contract of insurance. [354B] 4. The expression underwrite ' means accept liability under a contract of Insurance. The expression, therefore, has been used to indicate that the insurer is accepting liability under a Contract of Insurance. [355B] In this case, the respondent No I had not taken any decision to accept his proposal. The respondent was not under a mis impression that the Divisional Office was the only Authority to accept the policy. [353C]

The appellant filed a suit against the respondents for the recovery of certain amounts due to them from the respondents. The respondents filed an application for revocation of the certificate granted by the High Court under article 133(1)(a) and (b) of the Constitution. The High Court granted an interim injunction restraining the appellant from encashing the cheques issued by the respondents. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) An order passed by the High court in appeal which does not finally dispose of the suit or proceeding and leave the rights and obligations of the parties for determination in the suit or proceedings from which appeal has arisen, is not final within the meaning of article 133( 1) of the constitution. [701 B] (2) An order is final within the mean of article 133 of the Constitution under section 109 of the Code of Civil Procedure or section 205 of the Government of India Act, 1935, if it amounts to final decision on the rights of the parties in dispute in the suit, or proceeding; if after the order is made, the suit or the proceeding still remains to be tried, and the rights in dispute have to be determined, the order is interlocutory. [702 B] (3) An order refusing to grant an interim injunction does not determine the rights and obligation of the parties to the suit or of the proceeding in the suit. [703 B] (4) An order by the High Courts in appeals under the Letters Patent is not a final order within the meaning Of section 109 of Code of Civil Proce dure or section 205 Of the Government of Indian Act, 1935. [704 B] (5) The order of the High Court in appeal which did not finally dispose the suit or proceed ing and leave the parties to seek amendment of the plaint to get effective relief, is not a 'final order ' within the meaning 'of article 133(i) of the Constitu tion. [705 C] (6) The order passed by this Court in the present case is not a "final order" within the meaning. of article 133 (1) of the Consti tution. [706 B] (7) The order refusing to stay the execution of the decree under appeal was not a "judgment" within the contemplation of article 133. [707 C] (8) The order was not a 'judgment ' within the contemplation Of article 133. The order was a final order. [708 C] (9) The order in appeal was not final within article 133(I) of the . [708 D] (10) The order is not a judgment within the meaning, of article 133 and the appeal was not maintainable. [709 E] (11) The order granting interim injunction was not a final 'order ' within the mean ing of article 133, because, the controversy between the parties when the order was made was finally decided by the order of the Court. [710 A] (12) The order appealed against was not a judgment, because, it was not a decree. The order did not finally determine the rights of parties in relation to the matter in dispute in suit. [718 C] (13) The order did no more than to decide the question of the maintainability of the suit and the rights of both the parties in the suit and did not determine the right and obligation of parties in the matter in issue in the suit; it was a final ' order ' within article 133 of Constitution. [718 D] (14) The order under appeal was a final one. [718 E]

The petitioners contended that the value of the grey cloth in the hands of the processor was not included in the assessable value of the processed fabric and that the value was to be included in the value of job work done plus manufacturing profit and manufacturing expenses. Dismissing the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The assessable value of processed fabric would be the value of grey cloth plus the value of manufacturing profit and the manufacturing expenses. [345C] 1.2. The value of the goods processed in the hands o f the processor would be the price of the processed fabrics plus the value or deemed price at the factory gate for the processed fabric plus his profit. [345D] 1.3. The factory gate here means the "deemed" factory gate as if the processed fabric was sold by the processor. [345E] 1.4. The factory 's gate means the "final" "deemed "factory" as if the processing fabric was sold. [345F] 1.5. The factory "deemed to be" factory gate is the "final "deemed factory gate as it is the "de deemed" factory gate. [345G] 1.6. The value would be the "value" of the glycerol at the factory. [345H] 1.7. The value is the "value", which is the "grey cloth" in the hands Of the processor plus the valueof the job work done and the manufacturing profit and expenses. [346A] 1.8.
