The value should be the "good" or "good material" which is obtained by the processors from the processing machine or by any other processor from the factory. The value will be the "goods". [348C] 1,10. The value has to be the "market value" of the processed goods. [349C] 1:9. The "market value", in the context of the Central Excise Act, 1944, means the price at which the goods are sold by the assessee to

The appellant was appointed as a clerk by the Panchayat Samiti, Loharu, in 1963, long before the Amending Act came into force. He was, therefore, entitled to be absorbed in Government service as a clerk in any event. But, as a result of the deletion of section 33 of the Punjab Panchayat Samitis and Zilla Parishads Act, 1961, the Panchayat Samiti lost its power to make appointments to the Panchayat. The fact that the appellant was promoted as a Head Clerk on an ad hoc basis in January 1974, or the further fact that he was appointed as Head Clerk on April 1, 1975, cannot improve his position for the simple reason that these appointments were made after June 13, 1973, being the date on which the Amending Act of 1973 came into force, and that the Panchayat Samiti had lost its power in that regard. [737E G] The fact that he had been promoted as a head clerk on an ad hoe basis in January, 1974, or that he was promoted as Head Clerk in April, 1975, could not improve his position. [738A B] The appellant was entitled to be considered for promotion to the post of a Head Clerk, his appointment as a Clerk prior to his absorption in Government service had to be recognised and protected, notwithstanding the fact that such appointment was made after June, 1973 when the Amending Act had come into force. [739B C] The fact, that the appellant had been promoted to the post in January, 1975, or that the appellant 's appointment as a Head clerk was made without the authority of law, could not, therefore, have appointed him as a Head Clerks, as it purported to do, in January, 197. [740C D]

The appellants filed a suit claiming that the property in dispute belonged to the Math Sauna or the deity Sri Thakur Gokarneshwar Mahadeo. The property was purchased by the appellants in 1921 from the personal funds of the predecessor in title of the appellants. The property in dispute was purchased by Mahant Shivshanker Yati for Rs. 40,000 forming part of a fund left behind by his predecessor Mahant Shivshana Yati. The appellants claimed that the property was the personal property of the Mahant and that the fund was not his personal property. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court allowed the appeal. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The fund from which the Amauli properties were acquired constituted the personal property and did not form part of the properties of the Math Saana or the deity. [663 B] The fund from the personal property was not the personal property. It was the personal income of the Mahant. The property from which the fund was acquired constituted the property of the Math and the fund was the personal money of the Mahant, and did not belong to the Math or the deity, and the appellants were not entitled to claim exemption from the levy of the tax. [664 B] The High Court was right in the view that the fund from which Amauli property was acquired constituted its personal property and that the appellants were entitled to claim the exemption from the tax. The fund from out of which Amaul properties were acquired was not the property of Math Sauna. [662 C] The fund was the property of Mahant Shivsnagh, and the property from which Amiuli properties were purchased was the property belonging to the Math. [661 D] The fund of the Amaul property was the property which was the personal fund of the Mahant of the Math. The property did not belong either to the Math, or the deity or to the Mahant. [669 E]

The appellants were displaced persons from West Pakistan. They were allotted certain lands in the State of Punjab. The lands were allotted to them under the notification of the Government of Punjab dated March 24, 1955, under section 12(1) of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954. The appellants moved the Custodian of Evacuee Property for the cancellation of the allotment of lands in their favour on the ground that they were entitled to allotment of suburban land a had been wrongly fitted in the village Karodian. The Custodian cancelled the allotment of land in favour of the appellants on the ground, inter alia, that the lands were not available in the village. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Custodian. The High Court dismissed the petition. The appellants came to this Court by special leave. The appellants contended that the Custodian had no jurisdiction to cancel the allotment of the lands in the village in view of the provisions of section 10 of the Act. Held, that the Custodian was competent to cancel the allotments of the lands. The Custodian was competent under section 10 of Act to cancel allotments made in favour of displaced persons. The Custodian had no power to cancel the order of allotment in favour of a displaced person. The order of the Deputy Custodian cancelling the allotment of displaced land was erroneous. The Custodian could not cancel the allotment in favour. of a displaced land holder. The Custodian, by reason of the divesting of the property, as from March 24,1955, had become functus officio with respect to it and could not rectify any error made by him in the past in the matter of cancellation of allotment. The appellants had lost their possession before the publication of the notification and were thus not entitled to the protection of the section. The Custodian by reason of r. 102 of the Rules framed under the Act was competent to set aside the allotment. The power of the Custodian to cancel an allotment was not confined to the property which was entrusted to him for management and not to any other property. The rule was in Chapter X headed "Payment of compensation under section 10" and dealt with a transfer of property to an allottee by way of final settlement of his claim to compensation and did not deal with the question of allotment on a quasi permanent basis. The appellants were, therefore, not entitled to any relief. The special leave petition must be dismissed. The Custodian General had no power under section 19(1) to cancel the orders of the Deputy or the Custodian. Held, further, that the appellants had lost the right to the lands in question before the publication. of the notification under section 12 of the Act and the Custodian had the power to cancel them. The Custodian bad no power to set aside an allotment in favour a displaced person in the sense that it could be set aside only on certain specified grounds. The appellants could not be said to have lost their property before the publication and could not be entitled to the benefit of section 19(i) of the Act, as the Custodian had not cancelled the allotment in their favour. The Custodian 's power to cancel an order of allotment was not restricted to the property entrusted to him. The Custodian did not have the power to set it aside in the sense of cancelling an allotment on a ground other than those specified in section 19(2) of the 1954 Act.

The Uttar Pradesh Public Service Commission invited applications from eligible candidates for recruitment to the post of Upper Zila Basic Shiksha Adhikari (Women) District Inspectress of Girls Schools/Associate Regional Inspectress of girls Schools in Uttar Pradesh Educational Service Junior Scale (Women 's Branch) The advertisement inviting applications from eligible candidate was published on May 5, 1985 and a corrigendum was published on June 8, 1985. The recruitment examination was in two stages written and interview/personality test. After the written examina tion was over, on the basis of the results thereof, success ful candidates upto a base limit have to be called to be interviewed. On account of improper feeding into the comput er some of the candidates who had better performance in the written examination were not called and candidates securing lesser marks in the written examin a tion were not only called for interview but were also finally selected. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In the appeals to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court was not right in upholding the decision of the Public Service Commission to re hold the recruitment examination. On behalf of the respondents it was contended that the High court was right in upholding that the Public Service Com mission had no power to cancel the written part of the recruitment examination and that the High Courts were right in dismissing the writ petitions and that the selection of the candidates was not vitiated. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in holding that the Public Commis sion had no power in cancelling the written part or the recruitment examination, and that the Public Services Commission was not justified in cancelling the examination. [126G] 1.2 The Public Service Commission was not right to cancel the examination and the High Court has rightly dismissed the writ peti tions. [126H; 127A] 1.3 The High Court has not been able to appreciate the justification for cancellation of the written part and the examina tion. [127B] 1.4 The situation could have been appropriately met by setting aside the recruitment and asking for a fresh interview of all eligible candidates on the basis Of the written examination and select those who on the basis o f the written and the freshly held interview became eligible for selection. [127C] 1.5 The State Public Service Commission should have been more careful in dealing with the matter so that four years in the process of recruitment would not have been lost and the public cause would not have suffered. [127D] 1.6 The Public Service Commis ssion should have been careful in dealing With the matter so as to enable the State Public Service Commissi on to have a fresh interview. [127E]

The appellant brought the suit on the allegation that there was one Shiromani Nirankari Dera at Patiala, that this institution had two branches one at Landeke in Moga Tehsil and the other at Nanga Kheri in the erstwhile Patiala State, and that he, as mahant in charge of the Shiromani Dera at Landeka, had the right to manage the properties attached to the Dera at Nanga, and that the appellant was entitled to be in possession of the properties. The appellant contended that the Dera was an independent Dera and that he was in possession of properties of the Dera as its lawfully appointed mahant. The trial court decreed the suit. The decree was reversed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that there was no devolution of the interest in the subject matter of the suit on his death, since there was no certainty as to the person who would be elected as mahants to succeed him. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The suit was brought on the basis that the appellant as the lawfully appointed mamdar was entitled to manage the Dera and the properties of the dera, and that it devolved upon the appellant by virtue of his election as mahatant of the Derhi. [488 B] (2) The devolution of the interests in the subject of the suit took place when Shiam Dass was elected as mamdar of the Dershi. [490 C] (3) The subject matter of suit was the interest of Shiromani Darbar in the Dera, and its properties and it devolved upon Shiam Dass by virtue of the election of Shiroman Dass as mahdar of the deredari. [490 D] (4) The subject of the appeal was the interest in Dera and its properties, and it devolved on the appellant by succession. [490 E] (5) The subject property was in a representative capacity that the appellant and Shiam Dass were sued and as it was in a represented Dera, the appellant could be added as a party under Order 22, rule 10, C.P.C. [490 F] (6) The appellant could be impleaded as a party to the appeal if he was a necessary party. [490 G] (7) The High Court was right in holding that the appellant had no knowledge of the date of the death of Shiam Dass and that he did not know about the death of Som Dass. [490 H]

The Andhra Pradesh Government issued a notification dated October 29, 1979, purporting to amend the Andhra Pradesh Government Servants (Conditions of Service) Rules, 1979, by adding a proviso to the effect that the age of retirement of all Government employees other than in the last Grade Service, shall be 58 years. The petitioners who were employed in the Andhra Pradesh Secretariat Service challenged the validity of the said notification on the ground that the age was fixed arbitrarily without any reasonable basis and that the Government had acted unreasonably in not giving any previous notice to the employees which would have enabled them to arrange their affairs on the eve of retirement. The petitioners contended that the Government was estopped from reducing the age of their retirement to 55 years since the employees had acted on the representation made to them in 1979 by increasing the age of superannuation from 55 to 58 years in 1976. The petitioners also contended that the age fixed by the Government was too low and that the decision of the Government was arbitrary and irrational. The respondents contended that the decision was taken bona fide and was not arbitrary and that the petitioners had acted on a representation made to the Government in 1979 by the increase in the age of super annuation. Allowing the writ petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The Government is justified in its contention that the question of the age of retire ment was not referred to the Commission and that the Commission recommended that the age be continued to be 58 years for the Central Government employees with the modification that the retirement should take effect from the afternoon of the last day of the month in which the employee attains the age of 58 years. [586B C] 2. The question as to what should be the proper age of retirement is not a novel or unprecedented question which the State Legislative had to consider. If reduction of the retirement age from 58 to 55 is to be regarded as arbitrary on the ground of non application of mind, the Court 's interference would be called for, though not for fixing the age of refixation. [588C D] 3. The power to issue an ordinance is not an executive power but is the power of the executive to legislate. An executive act is liable to be struck down on the ground it is ultra vires or unconstitutional. [589C D] 4. The power of the Government to amend the rules retrospectively is of a legislative character and is to be distinguished from an ordinary rule making power. The power conferred by the proviso to Article 309 is of a ' legislative character and ' is to be distinct from an executive act. [584E] 5. The power under the proviso to Rule 2(2) of the Andhra Pradesh Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1963, to amend the said rules retrospectively is a legislative power. The rule making power under the Proviso to Article 309, by which the proviso to rule 2(2), was deleted retrospectively, was a valid exercise of legislative power. [582C] 6. The power is not an ordinary rule of law but a legislative power and is to he distinguished from an executive power. [575B] 7. The power given by the proviso is of a "peculiar or special nature" and is to operate in special cases. The power can be exercised in respect of all government employees notwithstanding that their age of retirement on the date of their retirement is 58 or 55 as the case may be. [565C] 8. The power granted by the proviso can be exercised by the Government only in respect of those government employees who are in the last grade service. The power cannot be exercised in regard to those employees who are not in the last grades service. [566B] 9. The power must be exercised in public interest and for public good. The power could be exercised for preventing the affairs of the State being conducted in a manner which is not in public interest. The power may be exercised to achieve a purpose which is not conducive to the general interest of the State or whose interests are not safeguarded. The power, however, cannot be exercised to affect or take away a right of an employee which has been conferred or conferred by statute. [567B] 10. The power which is conferred by the rule is not an absolute power. It is a power to be exercised in the public interest and to meet the exigencies of the service. The rule does not confer a right on an employee to claim that he should be retired on the date on which he attains the age specified in the rule. The rule is not open to the exception which is carved out by the proviso. [568C] 11. The power vested by the proviso cannot be exercised so as to affect or impair the right of an individual employee to claim his superannuation at the age of 55. The rule, however, is not open either to the rule of superannuation or to the exception carved out by proviso. [569C] 12. The power in the rule is of a general nature and cannot be equated with the power of legislation. The rule cannot be said to be arbitrary or irrational. [564D] 13. The power has been conferred on the Government to meet the administrative exigencies. The power does not mean that the rule making power is absolute. The rule can be altered or amended by the Government. The power would be exercised in larger public interest. [548D] 14. The power being of a legislative nature, it cannot be exercised by a rule making authority. The rule must be in conformity with the provisions of the Constitution. [549B] 15. The power was not an ordinary one but a 'peculiar power ' and is to ' operate in special situations. The power should be exercised in such a way as to avoid discrimination. [544C] 16. The power that is conferred by Rule 2(1) is not an 'ordinary power ' but a 'special power '. The power thereunder can be exercised for the purpose of preventing the affairs or the State being investigated in a manner that is not in the public interests. The power so conferred is not an unguided power. The exercise of the power is not subject to any rules or regulations. [545C] 17. The power contained in Rule 2(3) is not a 'special ' power. It can be exercised only in respect to the employees of the State Government. The rule has been framed in exercise of the rule making powers conferred by the Proviso to article 309. The power thus conferred is not a special power. It cannot be exercised for any other purpose. [546D] 18. The power includes the power to amend the rule. [547E] 19. The power confers by the proviso on the Government is of a similar character. The power enables the Government to make an order in respect of a class of employees without affecting the rights of the employees. The power also enables the Government by an order to remove difficulties in implementing the order. The power therefore, can be exercised to meet the situation. [543F] 20. The power not to retire an employee on the date he attains the superannuation age is a power which is not an inherent power. It must be exercised for public good and for public interest. It cannot, therefore, be exercised to override or affect the right of the employee. [540B] 21. The power exercisable by the Government under the proviso is not an "ordinary" power.

The appellant was a registered dealer under the Bombay Sales Tax Act, 1953. The sales tax authorities assessed him to purchase tax on the sales of castor oil. The appellant contended that the sales were exempted from tax under article 286(1)(b) of the Constitution of India on the ground that the goods were not exported out of the territory of India and that the exemption under article 286 (1) (b) would not apply to the sales. Held, that the sales tax authorities were right in holding that the sales in question were exempted from sales tax under article 19(1)(f) of the constitution. The word " a person " in section 10(b) of Bombay Sales Tax, Act, 1953, includes a registered dealer or a person who has given a false certificate of his intention. The certificate of the intention of the purchasing dealer is a necessary condition for the application of the exemption. The words " a person" in section 10 (b) of Act, 1953 are wide enough to include a registered dealer and an unregistered dealer. The words in section 10 are wide enough and the Legislature was anxious to secure that the declaration as regards intention of the goods being despatched outside the State of Bombay should be carried out by despatch by a registered dealer to whom he sells the goods. If such despatch outside the State is by a person to whom the certifying dealer has sold the goods but who is not a registered dealer the certificate has not been complied with. Held, further, that the words " a registered dealer " in section 8(b) are wide enough. The words used in section 10 of the Bombay Sales tax Act, 1953 include a registered dealers or a person to whose intention the goods have been despatched outside the territory of Bombay. The scheme of the Act clearly is that where the intention as declared has not been carried out purchase tax should be levied. Held, also, that the word " a " person " in the section includes a registered dealers and an unregistered dealers. The words of the section are wide enough, and the Legislature is anxious to secure the declaration as to intention of the person being despatched outside. Held, therefore, that the courts below were right in interpreting the words "a person " in that section as a " registered dealer " and that the purchasing dealers have rightly been assessed to purchase tax under section 10(B) of the Bombay Act. Held, however, that the certificate of the purchasing dealers is a necessary prerequisite for the application under section 10 (B) of Act 1953. The words, " a person ' in section 10, (b) includes a registered, dealer or a registered dealer. The word ' a person ' is wide enough to cover a registered dealer also. The words ' a person " are wide enough in section 10 and the Legislature has not used the word ' a registered dealer ' instead of the words " registered dealer ". The words "a registered dealer " are wide and the Legislature intended to cover a person who is not registered as a dealer.

The appellant married the respondent in 1956. A few years later, she had a son by her. 15 The initial warmth vanished and the jealousies of a triangular situation erupted, marring mutual affection. The respondent divorced the appellant around July 1962. A suit relating to a flat in which the husband had housed the wife resulted in a consent decree which also settled the marital disputes. The appellant moved the magistrate under section 125 of the Criminal Procedure Code 1973 for a monthly allowance for the maintenance of herself and her child. She proceeded on the footing that she was still a wife while the respondent rejected this status and asserted that she was a divorce and therefore ineligible for maintenance. The magistrate who tried the petition for maintenance held that the appellant was a subsisting wife and awarded monthly maintenance of Rs. 300/ for the son and Rs. 400/ for the mother for their subsistence, taking due note of the fact that the cost of living in Bombay where the parties lived was high and that the respondent had provided residential accommodation to the appellant. The High Court summarily dismissed a revision petition. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Courts have not spoken at all. The husband has not examined himself to prove that he has been giving allowances to the divorced wife. His case, on the contrary, is that she has forfeited her claim because of divorce and the consent decree. Obviously he has no case of non neglect. His plea is his right to ignore. [78D E] 2. Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1973 is a social piece of legislation designed to protect women from being turned into desperate and vagrant women. The social perspective granted the resolution of all the disputes projected is easy. Surely, Parliament, in keeping with article 15(3) and deliberate by design, made a special provision to help women in distress cast away by divorce. Protection against moral and material abandonment manifest in article 39 is part of social and economic justice, specificated in article 38, fulfilment of which is fundamental to the governance of the country. [81B C] 3. The legislative intent is to recognise the substitute maintenance arrangement by lump sum payment organised by the custom of the community or the personal law of the parties. There must be a rational relation between the sum so paid and its potential as provision for maintenance. To interpret otherwise is to stultify the project. [81D E] 4. The payment of illusory amounts by way of customary or personal law requirement will be considered in the reduction of maintenance rate but cannot annihilate that rate unless it is a reasonable substitute. The legal sanctity of the payment is certified by the fulfilment of the social obligation, not by a ritual exercise rooted in custom. No construction which leads to frustration of the statutory project can secure validation if the court is to pay true homage to the Constitution. [81E F] 5. The whole scheme of section 127(3) (b) is manifestly to recognise the substitution maintenance arrangement by a lump sum payment in lieu of maintenance. The purpose of the payment under any customary or personal Law must be to obviate destitution of the divorcee and to provide her with wherewithal to maintain herself. The whole purpose of the provision is to recognise substitute maintenance arrangement. [81G H] 6. The payment under any custom or personal law must be a reasonable substitute for the order under section 125. [82A] 7. The payment must be a substitute for maintenance. [82B]

The appellant was a successful bidder for the sale of country liquor shop in an auction held on 27th March, 1988. He was given the shop on the basis of a bid of Rs.11,900. The name of the appellant was placed in the black list for future under the orders of the Collector. The Collector, however, did not give any notice to the appellant of the proposal of black listing him. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of black listing. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that there was no requirement in the rule of giving any prior notice before black listing any person. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: The last portion of the order in so far as it directs black listing of the appellant in respect of future contracts, cannot be sustained in law. [867D] PG NO 869 PG NO 870 The order of blackging of the appellant 's bid is set aside. The order of the Collector is set aside and the appellant is directed to be placed in the Black List in respect of the future contracts. [868A]

The appellant tenant filed a suit for recovery of arrears of rent on the basis of the fair rents fixed, which were computed at Rs.98,250.97 in respect of the two items of property. While the former had an inherent jurisdiction to decide a question raised about its own jurisdiction and such a decision cannot be challenged in another court after it has become final, the latter is strictly confined to the terms of the statute creating it. When a petition under section 4 of the was filed, the Rent Controller, on the language of section 4, had to decide: (1) whether the applicant was a tenant in or landlord of the building and (2) what the fair rent of the premises should be in accordance with the provisions of the Act. At any rate, it was not open to one of the parties to contend that the decision given by the Court of Small Causes, which had become final between the parties, was a total nullity which could be completely ignored. It was, therefore, not open to the High Court to entertain a collateral attack on the validity of the order of the Court of small Causes and to consider afresh the issue as to whether the L.I.C. was the owner of the premises as claimed or not. Thereafter the tenant filed a civil suit for a declaration that the order of eviction was ultra vires in that no notice to quit had been given as required by law. That being so, if the Rent Controller did not decide that question properly, the matter would have to be raised in appeal to the Court of the Small Causes and would give the Court no jurisdiction to entertain a suit by the defeated party. The High Court, however, held that the question whether the provisions of section 4 of Act had been complied with or not was a matter that was directly and substantially in issue in the earlier proceedings to which any finality could be attached, as the Rent Controller had no jurisdiction to decide questions of title. The High court, therefore, held that it was not necessary to decide the issue as it was not a matter that could be gone into in a civil suit. The High Courts in appeal, however, took the view that the question as to whether there was a relationship of landlord and tenant between the parties was a matter which could be decided only by a civil court and not by the Rent Controller. The High courts, therefore, dismissed the appeal. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant tenant that the High Court was in error in holding that the question of the applicability of the Act was res judicata and that the High Courts were in error in dismissing the suit on the ground that the question was not a question that could be decided in a civil court. On behalf of the respondent, it was submitted that the High court was in error because the question as regards the applicability of section 4 was not directly and substantially involved in the earlier proceeding to which the Rent Controller was a party. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High 'Court was in error on both the points. [566C] 2. The Rent Controller has to satisfy himself that the person seeking eviction or fixation of fair rent is a landlord who has, prima facie, the right to receive the rents of the property in question. That the Rent Controller 's jurisdiction on this issue is limited is clear from the proviso to section 10(1) of the Act, which, inter alia, provides that in an application under section 4, the Rent Control Court "shall, if it is satisfied that the rent is bona fide required" by the landlord for occupation by himself or any member of his family dependent on him, call upon the landlord to show cause why the application should not be granted and if the Rent Control court is satisfied that no hardship would be caused to the tenant by making the application, it may pass a decree for eviction. [565C E] 3. The Rent Control Court has to satisfy itself that the person sought to be evicted or fixation of rent is a "landlord" who has, Prima facie, the rights to receive the rent of the property. That the rent is not payable in respect of a building, is a question that has to be decided by the Rent Control Tribunal. The Rent control Court has to decide the question whether a relationship of the landlord and tenant exists between the parties. [567B C] 4. The Rent Act does not exclude those cases where the provisions of a particular Act have not been complied with, or the statutory tribunal has not acted in conformity with the fundamental principles of judicial procedure. The Rent Courts are competent to decide the questions of title to the premises. [569C] 6. The Rent Court has to determine the question as a "final" authority under the Act. The jurisdiction to decide the dispute is a matter which is exclusively within the jurisdiction of the Rent Controller and, therefore, impliedly excluded from the purview of the civil Court. [575D] 7. The Rent Tribunal has to decide whether the relationship of landlord tenant exists between them. The jurisdiction is not ousted. [595F] 8. The Rent Authority has to satisfy herself that the person for whose benefit the application is filed is a "Landlord" and that the premises are bona fide required by the landlord. [596B] 9. The Rent controller has to satisfy, as to the amount of fair rent, that is, the fair rent fixed by the Rent Contrator. If, and only if, this relationship exists between the landlord and the tenant, the Rent Controllers jurisdiction to decide upon the question of fair rent will not be ousted. [592C] 11. The Rent Authorities have no power to decide a dispute which is not between a landlord and tenant. Therefore, the decision on the question whether there is a relationship of a landlord and a tenant, is a decision regarding jurisdictional facts and such a dispute can never be referred to the Civil Court. [592D] 12. The Rent authorities cannot grant the reliefs of declaration of occupancy rights. The State Government 's plea was rejected by the High Court. Therefore, it was urged that the civil court 's jurisdiction to adjudicate upon the nature or character of the suit lands must be held to have been exclu sively ousted. [593B] 13. The petitioner, who was a Forester in the State of Mysore, was given in the final integration list a position to which he objected. The petitioner, however, was given an opportunity to object to the provisional list. The petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the final list. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The petitioner had ample opportunity to make a representation against the preliminary list. The concession in Shankari 's case (supra) was confined to the facts of that case. There the list was provisional. The most that could be urged in the light of the decisions of this Court was that a person whose seniority was to be determined under section 115 of the Act must be given an opportunity of object ing to the proposed assignment of a place to him in the seniority list. As no such opportunity was furnished to the respondents with regard to these two matters, the combined final gradation list dated April 6, 1962, so far as category 6 was concerned, was ultra vires and illegal and that part of the notification alone must be quashed by grant of a writ in the nature of certiorari. [829 C E] The petitioner had no right to have a representation against his final seniority list. The respondents were entitled to an opportunity to make representation against the two points urged by the petitioner. [830 C] The petitioner was not entitled to have any further opportunity against the final seniority list, as he was given ample opportunity to object. [831 A] The petitioner 's contention that he was not heard after the final list was prepared was not correct. The petitioner was given ample opportuni ty to make a represen tation against the preliminary seniority list. [832 C] The respondents were, therefore, entitled to an opportuni ty of making a representation against their final seniority list and the final gradation list was not ultra vires and void. [833 C] Union of India vs G.M. Shankariah & Ors. ; , referred to. The petitioner had a right to have his representation considered before the final gradation List was published. [834 C] The Court did not consider it necessary to express any opinion on the merits of the case.

The petitioners, who were granted Additional Licences under the Import Policy 1978 79, and the Import Policy 1988 91, challenged the validity of the Import & Export Policy 1988 91 on the ground that they were entitled to the grant of Additional Licences in terms of the Import Policy 1985 88. The petitioners also contended that the Additional licences were granted to the petitioners under the Import Trade Control Policy 1985 88, and that they were also entitled to the benefit of the said Policy. Dismissing the writ petitions, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The petitioners have failed to make out a case for interference by this Court under Article 32 of the Constitution. [246C] 1.2 The petitioners have not made out a case that the Additional Licence were granted under the Import policy 1985 88. [246D] 1.3 The petitioners have been subjected to arbitrary and hostile discrimination. The appellant was an Accountant cum Head Clerk in the Tamil Nadu Forest Training School at Vaigai Dam. He took charge of the office on 6.10.1975 and had been residing in a house opposite the training school. PW 3, the Principal of the training school, issued exhibit P 2 show cause notice to the appellant, asking him to explain why his licence for running the canteen should not be cancelled. The appellant, who was an Accountant, was asked to explain why the money should not be confiscated. The appellant stated that he had returned the money due to him and that he had no objection to the forfeiture of the money. The appellant was charged under section 5(2) read with section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The Trial Court accepted the prosecution evidence, rejected the plea of the appellant and recorded the conviction. The High Court, however, held that the evidence of PW 1, the principal of the training college, was sufficient to prove the guilt of the appellant. In the appeal to this Court, on behalf of the appellant it was contended that there was no independent evidence regarding the demand, the messenger who had contacted PW 1 at the behest of the appellant had not been examined, the solitary evidence of PW I was insufficient, the explanation offered by the appellant was probable and there was no conclusive evi dence to hold that the appellant was guilty. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The presumption under section 4(1) of the Act is rebutted by the evidence of the prosecution witnesses. The appellant had failed to rebut the presumption. [339C] 2. He had been charged under section 161 I.P.C. and section 5(i)(d) read with 5(1) (d) of Prevention of Corruption Ac t. The case that has been developed in the course of the trial is not that of a loan transaction but payment of an advance of Rs. 125 in the canteen when the appellant started to take food there. The case of Dipawali gift or return of a loan given to PW 1 has not been even suggested. It cannot, therefore, be said that there had been consistent explanation for the appellant. [338C D] 3. The presumption arising under section 4 is rebutted by proof and not by a bare explanation which is merely plausible. A fact is said to be proved when its existence is directly established or when upon the material before it the Court finds its existence to be so probable that a reasonable man would act on the supposition that it exists. Unless there is a presumption, the presumption created by the provision cannot be said to be rebutted. The appellant, a public limited company, was carrying on the business of running a port and was maintaining a record of the hours of work and overtime work done by the workmen. The work of the workmen was to do night duty and to watch the work of the port. The work was to be done at 9 hours per day. The work at the Alexandra Docks was to be carried out at 9 hours a day. The workmen were to be paid overtime wages at the rate of twice the ordinary rate for work done in the ordinary course. The work done at the Axandra Docks, however, was to be at 9 hours on every day. The workers were to be given work at the port at the rate fixed by the Port Trust. The work in the Axra Docks was of a simple nature and the workmen were to get the work done at 9.30 hours per day and the rest at 9.00 hours per day, if the work was to take place at 9.45 hours per day or more. The workmen claimed that the hours of rest and overtime work should be at least 3 hours per day in the work of a day and that the hours should be 9.30 and not 9.45. The Trustees of the Port of Bombay, the Port Trust of Madras and the Port Trust, Bombay pleaded that the work done by workmen at the Aixandra Docks could not be taken into account in calculating the hours of duty and overtime work and that the workmen were entitled to overtime wages at twice the ordinary rates for work done beyond 9.45 and not 9, and that the work in the Port was of a kind of work which was not of a normal nature and that the workers were entitled to the overtime wages at double the ordinary rates. The Trustees also claimed that the workmen should be paid overtime for the work done beyond the normal hours of work. The workmen contended that the hours were of a kind which was not ordinary work and that they were entitled to work overtime at double the rate for work of a kind done in the Aixra Docks. The Trustees further claimed that the work of overtime was of a permanent nature and that they had fixed the hours of overtime work at 9.50 hours per day for the work of 8 hours per day of work and that in any case the hours of working should be 9 hours on any day and not 9 hours on a day. Held, that the work at the Port was not ordinary and ordinary work and the workmen could not claim overtime wages at 9.80 hours per day as they were entitled, if present for work, to overtime wages for work of 8.30 hours. The work carried out at the AIXRA Docks was not ordinary or ordinary work and was not of the kind which was of a normal kind and was not ordinary working day. The hours of work were 9.30, 9.45, 9.50 and 9.50. The workmen could not be said to be entitled to overtime payment at twice the rate for the work. The Trustees were not compelled to break up the hours of employment by interposing intervals for rest, if owing to the nature of the work there was difficulty in giving the intervals for rest in that manner on any particular day. The Trustees could fix two or three or even four without in any way going against the provisions of section 13 or Rule 24. The workmen had to be paid for work done at 8.30 and 9.00. The work that was done at the Port at 9.40 hours per day was to be 9.50, 9.30. and 9.75 hours per day if the work of 9.30 was to take time. The workmen, therefore, were entitled to three hours ' overtime if required to work beyond 9.30 in the AIXhra Docks.

Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972. The suit was decreed by the trial court. The High Court set aside the decree. The appellant tenant filed an appeal in this Court. The respondent tenant contended that the provisions of the Act will not be applicable to the case as the suit was filed within a period of exemption. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The suit was not pending on the date on which the Act came into force. The Act came into effect on 15th July, 1972. Therefore, if the suit was pending on the day on which the applicability of the Act came to an end, the provisions of section 39 will come to the assistance of the tenant appellant. [165C D] 1.2 The restriction on the right of a landlord to evict a tenant has been provided for in section 20 of the Act under which the landlord can evict a tenant only if the conditions contemplated in clauses (a) to (1) of section 20(2) are satisfied. [165D] 1.3 The restriction on a landlord to institute a suit as provided for in clause (1) is not applicable to the present case. [165E] 1.4 The restriction on landlord to institute the suit as provided in clause (2) of section 2 is not applicable as the suit has been instituted within a period Of exemption. [165F] 1.5 The restriction on right of a land lord to evict a land lords has been provided under section 20 of Act. The restriction on such right will not be attracted as the suit had been instituted within 10 years and therefore restriction as provided for under section 20 can not be attracted. [165G] 1.6 The appellant tenant could not be given the advantage of the provisions contained in the Act. [166A] 1.7 The appellant tenant cannot be given the benefit of the provisions of this Act. [165B] 1.8 The appellant tenant is entitled to the benefit of section 20 of U.P Act. [167C] 1.9 The appellant tenant can be given the benefits of the provisions under the U. P Act. [168C] Firms Amar Nath Basheshar Dass vs Tek Chand, 11972] 3 SCR 922, referred to. 1.10 The restriction on eviction will not be available to the appellant tenant if the suit from which revision or appeal arose was pending on 15th of July, 1972 i.e. the date on the commencement of the Act. The suit itself was filed much after the coming into force of this Act, and therefore, the restriction will not be of any avail to the appellant. [167D] 1:11 The restriction on rights of a landlord will not be made applicable to the appellant if the suit is pending on the said date. [167E] 1:12 The appellant tenant has been carrying out the business in the premises for a long time for it would be proper to permit the appellant time to make their arrangements for shifting. [167F]

The respondent No. 1 was a thika tenant of the appellant 's land. The appellant 's suit for ejectment was dismissed by the Subordinate Judge. The respondent No. I filed an appeal to the High Court. The High Court held that the appellant was not liable to ejectment in the absence of any grounds therefor in the notice to quit in accordance with section 3 of the Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act, 1949, as he was a thikadar within the meaning of that Act. The High court also held that the respondent No. 2 was a thakadar within the definition of that Act and was a tho tenant within the meaning thereof. The appellant came to this Court by special leave. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the respondent was not entitled to the benefit of the Calcutta Act, 1949 as amended by the Calcutta T.hika Tenancy (Amendment) Act, 1953, as he had not erected any structures on the land and was not a successor in interest of the tenant but only a transferee. Held, that the respondent 's suit was not barred by the Calcutta Act. The respondent was a thukadar within the terms of the Act and was entitled to the protection of the Act. The Act was not retrospective in operation. The Act did not apply to the facts of the case. The Act applied to all suits, appeals and proceedings pending on 21st October, 1952, and the respondent was entitled to succeed. The Act could not apply to pre Act suits by the circuitous process of sections 4 and 5 of the Act as the respondent was a transferee of the rights of the appellant. Mahadeolal Kanodia vs Administrator General of West Bengal, [1962] Supp. 3 S.C.R. 49, referred to. The Act, as amended by Act of 1953, was applicable to all suits and proceedings pending in the Calcutta Tika Tenancy Act, 1948, and the suit was not a suit or proceeding pending in a court or before a Controller. The Act had no retrospective operation. The respondent 's claim to ejectment was not barred under the Act as he was not a thika tenants within the meaning Of the Act as it was finally amended by the Act of 1953. Mahadeolalsal Kanodia 's case, [1962], Supp. 3, S.C,R. 49 and The Calcutta Thika Tenant 's case. , referred to. Section 4 of the Act was not applicable to pre Act suit by the circutar. The respondent could not succeed in his suit. The appeal must be dismissed. The respondent had not established any of the grounds specified in section 3 of Act, 1949. The Act would not apply to cases where the decree was made after the Act had come into force. Mahadeolall Kanodia vs The Administrator General of W. Bengal, [1961] 1 S.C R. 158, distinguished. The Act is not retrospective in its operation. The provisions of sections 4, 5 and 6 of the Act are not couched in the same kind of language as section 3 of section 2 of the CalcuttaThika Tenancy Act. The legislature clearly meant section 4 to be prospective. The language of section 5 being closely similar to that used in section 4 that section should also be held to be prospective only. The effect of omission of section 28 has been considered by this Court in Mahadeolal ' Kanodia ' 's case and it was held that the legislature always proceeded on the basis that section 4 was prospective. The legislature never intended that the grounds mentioned in section 3 should be stated in the notice of ejectment. The legislature could not be taken to have imposed a ban on all pre Act suits on the ground of sections 4 & 5 of the Calcutta Tenancy Act. [184 D, G H] Mahadeolal Khettryal Kanodia V. Administrator General of Bengal, [1943] L.R. 70 I.A. 180, referred to and distinguished. The respondent did not establish any of the ground specified in section 4 of the Calcutta Rent Act. The suit was not one for ejectment of the respondent. The respondent having not established any ground specified in the section, the appeal must be allowed. The appeal was accordingly dismissed. The appellant was entitled to his costs. The respondent filed a suit for ejectment of his tenant. The suit had been dismissed by the trial court. The High 'Court in appeal reversed the decree of the trial court and dismissed the respondent ' 's suit. The appellant contended that the respondent had not been able to establish any of these grounds. The respondent contended that the suit was barred by the Act as his suit was not for ejectment of a thika tenanee but for ejectment of an intermediary. The respondent relied on section 4 of Act, and contended that the Act was applicable to the facts. The contention was that the Act applied to pre Act cases. The contention of the respondent was that the suit for ejectment had been dismissed on the ground that the respondent did not have any right to the land. The respondent also relied on section 5 of the West Bengal Act, and claimed that the suit had been rightly dismissed. Held, (per Kapur and Shah, JJ.) that the respondent could not be allowed to raise the contention that the suit should have been dismissed on grounds other than those mentioned in section 4. The Act as amended by section 2 of Act, 1953 was applicable to pre and post Act suits. The Act in terms did not apply. The Act came into force on 21st January, 1952. The respondent, therefore, had not established that he was a tenant within the terms Of the Act. Mahadeolali Kanodia vs Secretary of State for India in Council, (1943) L.R 70 I. A. 180, distinguished.

The appellant, a driver constable in the Delhi Police Force, was appointed as a Section Officer in the pay scale of Rs. 160 320. He was promoted as a Section officer in the pay scales of Rs. 120 300 to Rs. 500 1,000. The pay scale of Section officers was Rs. 500 I,000. In the pay scale Rs. 500 l,000, the post of Section officer was Rs. 100 1,000 and the post of Bench Secretaries was Rs. 200 1,000, while the post of a Section officer was of Rs. 200 I,000 and that of a Bench Secretary was Rs. 400 I,000, The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the two different pay scales of Section officers. The High Court dismissed the petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that: (1) The High Court was in error in equating Bench Secretaries with Section officers in view of their differential duties; (2) The nature of duties and responsibilities of Bench Secretaries were different from that of Section officers; (3) The creation of two different grades with different pay scales in the cadre of Bench Secretaries who were doing the same or similar work was violative of the principle of equal pay for equal work; and (4) The creation and creation of two grades with different scales of pay in the cadre was violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The principle of "equal pay for equal Work" is not an abstract doctrine but one of substance. It is not necessary that it should be directed to be 1.5% of the total posts in a cadre. The percentage of posts may be increased or decreased but must be left to the discretion of the Government. The purpose of the principle is to prevent discrimination between similarly situated persons. It is now well settled that the principle of " equal pay for unequal work" is not a fundamental right but a constitutional goal. It is indeed the duty of the State to ensure that all workers are treated equally. The doctrine of "equal work for equal pay" is not alien to the concept of "equal wages". The doctrine ofequal pay for unequal working is indeed a significant constitutional principle but not an absolute one. It is a very useful principle because it gives to many things their fair equivalent, and it is calculated to bring about a real and substantial equality. [293C E] 1.2. The principle is not an inexorable one. It admits of no doubt that Article l4 of the Constitution proclaims "equal pay foe for equal work for both men and women" as a Directive Principle of State Policy. "Equal pay for equalwork for both men an women" has been accepted as a constitutional goal capable of being achieved through constitutional remedies. [293F G] 1.3. The principle has been accepted and applied in many other situations also. The doctrine is a mere abstract doctrine and cannot be enforced in a vacuum. [293H; 294A] 1.4. The doctrine has been evolved out of experience and its application in the constitutional law of some countries. The doctrine itself has undergone a great deal of change in recent years. The reason why the doctrine of "equality for equal work" was evolved over the years has been that there has been a a constant and gradual increase in the number of men and women in our country. Today there are well marked rise in the number Of women in our age, particularly in the lower sex sex. [294B C] 1.5. The doctrine does not remain merely a platitudinous guiding light but has a dynamic check. It seeks to remove the existing inequality by bringing about a qualitative improvement in the conditions of women and children. It has a definite purpose and a purpose. It has to take within its sweep all those who are equal and to achieve a social purpose by securing to all those who really need to be the same. [294C D] 1.6. The principle that all workers, legitimate as they are, must be treated alike is not only an abstract doctrine, but a valuable aid to the interpretation of social and economic legislation. [294D E] 1:7. The principle underlying the doctrine of 'equal pay for Equal work ' is not an inflexible rule. It is essentially for a legislature to consider what measures can be taken in give effect to it. [294E F] 1.8. The Court cannot strike down the pay scale granted to a section officer because it is not shown how it is violative of the constitutional principle of 'equal work forequal pay '. [294F] 1.9. The Court can strike down the rule which is the result of an intelligible differentia having a rational nexus with the object to be achieved. [294G] 1.10. The Court has to consider the nature of the duties attached to the posts and the responsibilities attached to the post. The doctrine that all those who discharge the same duties should be treated alike has no application to the facts of the present case. [294H; 295A] 1:11. The doctrine cannot be extended to the extent of equating the post of an Assistant Sub Inspector with that of a Section Officer. [295B] 1.12. The principle cannot be extended by the Court to the extent to which it is contrary to the constitutional principle. [295C] 1.13. The doctrine was evolved out of the experience and its applicability in the constitutional sense. [295D] 1.14. The doctrine, in the context of Article l4, is not an invariable rule. It has an element of flexibility. It is capable of being moulded to meet the requirements of different situations. [295E F] 2. The principle which is sought to be invoked by the appellant is that the Bench Secretaries in the High Courts should be given the same pay scale as that of Section Officers. The Bench Secretaries Grade I are in a higher pay scale than that of Section Officer. The entitlement to higher pay scale depends upon selection based on merit cum seniority. It is only in the case of Bench Secretaries Grade II that the selection is based on merit with due regard to seniority. [295F G] 2.1. It is open to the Government to provide for the same pay scales, after taking into account the nature of duties attached to such posts. The principle can be extended to such posts as well. [295H; 296A] 2.2. It is for the Government to consider what measure can be taken to bring about uniformity in the pay structure of the employees. [296B] 2.3. The appellant companies were carrying on the business of mining coal and were also carrying on the mining operations for the purpose of winning coal. The appellant companies were assessed to property tax under the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957, for the years 1976 77 and 1977 78. The Delhi High Court held that the Delhi Municipal Corpora tion had no power to levy property tax on the lands and buildings of the appellant companies. The Delhi Municipal Corporation appealed to this Court. The appellant company contended that the Delhi Development Act, 1957 was a special Act and the provisions of the Delhi Municipal Act, 1957 must be taken to have been incorporated in the Delhi Municipal Corporations Act, 1957 and any subsequent amendments made to the Municipal Corporation Act and the Municipalities Act will also apply to the power of taxation provided for in section 69(d) of the Delhi Development. Act, 1957. Dismissing the appeals, the Court, HELD: 1. The Delhi Development Act 1957 was enacted by the Parliament under Entry 52, List I of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. The power to impose tax on lands and buildings is derived by the State Legislature from Entry 49 of List II: "Taxes on lands and building". The power to levy tax on lands or buildings is derived from Entry 49, List II: 'Taxes on land and buildings '. The power of the municipalities to levy tax is derived from the power conferred by Entry 54, List I: 'Tax on lands and Buildings '. The Delhi Corporation Act, 1956 was enacted by Parliament under Entry 23, List II. The power conferred by the State Act on the Municipal Corporation to levy property taxes on lands and. buildings is therefore not in conflict with the power conferred on the State Government to regulate and develop the coal mines so as to ensure rational and scientific utilisation of coal resources. [20E G] 2. The power under the Delhi Development Autho rity Act, 1957 to levy property Tax on lands and Building is derived by it from Entry 49 List II: tax on lands. The power is not in conflict With the power conferred upon the State Government by Entry 52, list I read with Entry 24, List II, to impose tax. The power must, therefore, be held to be not in conflict 'with the power conferred ' by Entry 54 List I read with the Constitution. [20H; 21A] 3. The power given by the State legislature to the Municipal Corporations to impose the property tax on lands is not in any manner in conflict with or repugnant to the power conferred under Entry 49 List 11. The power has been given to the Municipal Corporat or to the State Government under Entry 23 List II. [21B] 4. The power cannot be said to be in conflict with any other power conferred by any other provision of the Constitution. It is not the Crown and has none of the immunities or privileges of the Crown. [21C] 5. The power granted by the State Government is not in the nature of a fee. The power was given to the appellant companies to impose the tax. The tax is not in, the nature of fee. [21D] 6. The power can be exercised only by the Municipal Corporation. The power could be exercised only in respect of the properties of the appellant company. The properties of the company are not the properties of any other person. The properties are not the property of the shareholders. The properties belong to the company. The company is not the owner of the properties. The properties have been leased to the appellant company for a period of 30 years. The company has been carrying on the trade of mining coal. The company had been paying the royalty to the State. The company was not the owner. The company cannot be taxed. The company could not be taxed. [21E G] 7. The power vested in the Municipal Corporation is not in dispute. The power, therefore, cannot be said, to be in any manner repugnant to the powers conferred by Entry 49 List I read. with the Constitution, on the State Govern ment to impose tax in respect of lands and buildings. [22A B] 8. The power in the State Government cannot be said not to be in the nature or a fee. [22C] 9. The power and the duty of the municipalities are derived from Entry 5, List II of the Seventh schedule to the Constitution and the power to levy the property tax is derived by them from Entry 49. List II. It is true that on account of the declaration contained in section 2 of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 the legislative field covered by Entry 23 of List II will pass on to Parliament by virtue of Entry 54, list I. But in order to judge whether, on that account, the State legislature loses its competence to pass the Act of 1973, it is necessary to have regard to the object and purpose of that Act and to the relevant provisions thereof, under which Special Area Development Authorities are given the power to tax lands and buildings within their jurisdiction. [22E G] 10. The power which is conferred by the Delhi Development Authority Act, 1957 on the Municipal Corporations is not in con nection with the ownership of the industrial undertakings. The power does not flow from the power to legislate. The power would be available to the Municipal Authorities only if the lands and the buildings on which they are constructed belong to the Corporation. The Corporation has no power to impose the properties tax on the land and buildings of a company. The property tax provided for in the Delhi Development Authori ty Act, 1957 is not in connection with the ownership or management of industrial undertakings. [23A B] 11. The tax provided for by the Delhi Municipal corporation Act, 1957 in respect of properties of the companies is not in excess of the maximum rate permissible under the Act. The tax, however, is not in respect of any property of the company. It is in respect of a building owned by the company. [23C D] 12. The power reserved by the State Govern ments to the Municipal corporations to impose the Property Tax on lands is derived from Article 246(3) of the Constitution read with Entry 49 of the State List. The power also cannot be said. not in con tect with the ownership, management or control of industrial undertakings, because, the power is not the power to impose property tax on industrial undertakings. It is the power to provide for the levy of property tax on land and building. The power may be exercised in respect of property of the Company or may be exercised by the State in respect of land and building owned by a company. [24A B] 13. The power provided by the State is not in contra vention of the power conferred in Entry 49 List 1. The power will be available to a Municipal Corporation only if the land and the building on which they stand belong to the Corpora tee. The Corporation cannot be taxed on the basis of the property owned by the Company. [24C D] 14. The power contained in the State Governm ent cannot be said be in conflict ' with any other provision ' of the Constitution, because, it is not in accord with the power to make laws conferred by the Constitution. The appellant was a lessee of a large area of land in the State of Andhra Pradesh. The Government of Andhra Pradesh issued a notice to him under section 20(1) of the Andhra Pradesh (Andhra Area) Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, terminating his lease. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notice. The High Court dismissed the petition. The appellant came up in appeal to the Supreme Court. The appellant contended that the second proviso to section 20(2) of the Act was merely declaratory and the third proviso was merely declaratory of the rights created on or after July 1, 1945. Held, that the third proviso to section 2(2) Of the Act was not merely declaratory of rights created on the date of the notice but was a new clause added to the lease itself. The second proviso to the section was not merely a declaratory provision but was a part of the substantive law and was protected by article 31B of the Constitution. The third proviso to the said section was not an independent proviso but was a sort of proviso to the second proviso. The words " such right " in the third proviso relate to the rights mentioned in the second proviso, that is to say, rights created on and after July 1. 1945. The scheme of the Act is to render ineffective all rights created after July 1 1945, for a period exceeding one year. In one view of the matter it may well be taken as meaning that the creation of rights after July 1st, 1945, is by the force of the second proviso itself, and that the second Proviso would be otiose and need not have been enacted at all. The true effect of the section can be stated in three ways : (i) Rights validly created prior to July 1, 1948, will be valid; (ii) such rights, however, may be determined under the third proviso if it is in the public interest to do so and in such cases compensation will be payable under section 20 (2); and (iii) rights created after 1st July, 1945, if they are for a period of one year, are liable to be avoided under the second proviso and the Government must do something to avoid them. The third and the fourth provisos deal with the termination of rights created before July 1, 1946, and the second proviso deals with the termination Of rights created after that date. The third is not a new clause but is merely a new clause. The true intention of the third proviso is that the rights created after the expiry of the lease should be deemed to be valid and all rights and obligations arising thereunder on or after the notified date should be enforceable by or against the Government. The words ' such right ' in the third and the proviso are not used in the sense of extinguishing rights and obligations which had already accrued or been incurred before the notified date. The words are used in the context of rights created after a specified date and not in the sense that they are used in a loose sense. The words in the third are not used to limit the operation of the rights which had already been created. The words of the third are used in their widest amplitude and they clearly indicate that the rights which were created after July, 1, 1945, are only voidable at the instance of the Government and that being the position, the Government must, in the present case, do something to terminate the lease and that further, in such cases, the lessee will also be entitled to compensation under section 20. The words, ' such right " do not refer to the rights created before the notified period. The words used in the third is not used to restrict the operation of rights created in the past but to restrict the rights created in future. The words do not refer only to rights created before but they also refer to rights created after such rights are terminated. The words must be read as meaning that such rights must be terminated under the third and that the rights must be determined under section 20 of the Act. The words were not used to give a new meaning to the words " such rights " but to indicate that the right created after July. 1, 1945 was only voidable at their instance and that the Government must terminate the lease at its option and unconditionally. The words could not be construed as meaning that rights created after 745 July, 1945 were only voidable at its instance and that, therefore, the Government could terminate the lease only if it was in the public interests to do so. The words did not refer to rights which had been created before the date of notice but only to those which were created before the notice was issued. The words would not be used to limit their operation to rights which were already created. The third was not a new provision but was merely a new one. The words which were used in the proviso were not used in their fullest sense to mean that the rights were to be terminated under section 20 but only those which were validly created. The intention of the legislature was that the rights should be terminated under that section and not under the Act.
